Chapter 14 · Building a potential from point responses

Solve one source problem exactly, reuse it for a distributed charge, and find what an electrode measures without solving for its surface charge point by point.

Start with the response to one thin sheet

Two large grounded conducting plates occupy \(x=0\) and \(x=L\). A charge sheet of surface density \(\sigma\) sits at \(x=s\), far from plate edges. Translational symmetry along each plate makes the potential a function of \(x\) alone. Integrating Poisson’s equation across the charge shows that \(V\) is continuous and \(V'(s^+)-V'(s^-)=-\sigma/\epsilon_0\). The potential is linear in each empty gap. It is helpful to remove the scale \(\sigma/\epsilon_0\) and call the remaining function \(G(x,s)\).

On the left write \(G=A x\) to satisfy the first plate. On the right write \(G=B(L-x)\) to satisfy the second. Continuity imposes \(As=B(L-s)\). The derivative jump gives \(-B-A=-1\), so \(A=(L-s)/L\) and \(B=s/L\). A single expression covers both segments:

\[G(x,s)=\frac{\min(x,s)[L-\max(x,s)]}{L},\]
\[-\partial_x^2G(x,s)=\delta(x-s).\]

This Green function has units of length in this one-dimensional reduction. A source near the left plate produces a steep left slope and a shallow right slope. The left conductor acquires the greater magnitude of induced charge. Exchanging detector and source coordinates leaves \(G\) unchanged. This symmetry will turn out to be a physical consequence of the linear field equation.

Background · Reciprocity
\[\int \rho_1 V_2\,dV=\int \rho_2 V_1\,dV\]

The displayed form assumes compatible homogeneous boundary conditions and a reciprocal linear medium. Boundary work terms matter for separately driven electrodes.

Assemble many sheets and retain the boundary voltages

A slice of thickness \(ds\) has sheet charge \(\rho(s)\,ds\). Linearity allows its contribution \(\rho(s)G(x,s)\,ds/\epsilon_0\) to be added to every other slice. If the plate voltages are \(V_0,V_L\), a straight line accounts for the source-free solution satisfying those voltages:

\[V(x)=V_0(1-x/L)+V_L x/L+\frac1{\epsilon_0}\int_0^L G(x,s)\rho(s)\,ds .\]

For uniform positive \(\rho\), split the integral at \(s=x\). The left piece is \((L-x)x^2/(2L)\), and the right piece is \(x(L-x)^2/(2L)\), before multiplication by \(\rho/\epsilon_0\). Together they yield

\[V_{\rm charge}=\rho x(L-x)/(2\epsilon_0).\]

Twice differentiating recovers the volume charge everywhere, and at either plate the charge contribution is zero.

Worked field measurement between unequal plates

Let \(L=10\) mm, \(V_0=0\), \(V_L=2.0\) V, and \(\rho=1.00\,\mu{\rm C/m^3}\). The straight-line background contributes 1.00 V at the midpoint. The uniform space charge contributes \(\rho L^2/(8\epsilon_0)=1.41\) V. The maximum potential can exceed both conductor voltages in the presence of a positive source. At the midpoint the charge contribution to the field vanishes by symmetry, so the field there still has its background value \(-200\) V/m. This gives two independent observables for the same solution.

Prove that source and detector can exchange roles

For two electrostatic states occupying the same region with a linear, symmetric permittivity tensor, define potentials \(V_1,V_2\) and charges \(\rho_1,\rho_2\). Multiply the first Poisson equation by \(V_2\), the second by \(V_1\), then subtract and integrate. The two terms containing products of gradients cancel after integration by parts because of tensor symmetry. With outward normal from the dielectric region one obtains

\[\int_\Omega (V_2\rho_1-V_1\rho_2)\,d^3x=\oint_{\partial\Omega}\big[V_1\mathbf n\cdot\epsilon\nabla V_2-V_2\mathbf n\cdot\epsilon\nabla V_1\big]\,dA .\]

With both outer boundary potentials zero, the surface term vanishes. Choosing a point source for each state shows that the potential per unit charge at the other point is the same in either order. Fixed geometry, material response and boundary type matter. Replacing a grounded electrode by an isolated electrode between the two measurements changes the problem.

Worked electrode reading from a weighting potential

Take state 1 to be the real charge \(q\) inside a cavity whose electrodes are all grounded. For state 2 remove the charge, set the right electrode to 1 V and the others to zero, and divide this potential by 1 V to define \(w\). The surface normal in the identity points into the metal, so \(\mathbf n\cdot\epsilon\nabla V_1\) is the free charge density on the metal face. The identity now gives

\[Q_R=-q\,w(\mathbf x_q).\]

For parallel plates \(w=x/L\). Moving \(12\) pC from \(0.20L\) to \(0.65L\) changes the right-electrode charge by \(-5.4\) pC. Its change on the other plate is \(+5.4\) pC, as an independent sum check. Device designers can reuse one computed \(w\) for many charge positions.

Move a charge sheet between grounded electrodes

Keep the plate separation at 10 mm. At 30% of the gap, a positive sheet of 3 nC/m² induces −2.1 and −0.9 nC/m² on the left and right plates. Move the sheet through the midpoint, then reverse its charge. Predict the sign of the slope jump each time.

Open this experiment online

Practise splitting the integral and reading an induced signal

Locate a hidden sheet using both electrodes

A grounded pair of plates has induced charges of \(-3.0\) pC on the left and \(-7.0\) pC on the right from a single positive sheet of finite illuminated area in the large-plate approximation. Infer its charge and dimensionless position. Does the pair determine the width if several sheets may be present?

Work through the solution

All induced charge sums to \(-q\), so \(q=10.0\) pC. The right fraction \(0.700\) places the sheet at \(s=0.700L\). For a cloud, linearity gives

\[Q_R=-\int(x/L)\,dq.\]

The two readings yield total charge and first moment only. Two equal sheets at \(0.60L\) and \(0.80L\) give identical readings.

Bound a numerical influence coefficient

A discretisation gives

\[G(0.2L,0.7L)=0.062L,\]
\[G(0.7L,0.2L)=0.058L.\]

Which exact value should both approach? Does averaging establish convergence?

Work through the solution

Their target is

\[0.2(1-0.7)L=0.060L.\]

The discrepancy may come from depositing source charge and sampling voltage with different weights. The two errors happen to cancel in the mean here. Refine the grid and perform each measurement separately. Reciprocity alone also cannot reveal a common bias in both entries.

Further reading

  • Fließbach, Randwertprobleme, pp. 59–67
  • Griffiths, §§3.1–3.2, boundary conditions, uniqueness and images

Study the full derivation

Green functions, the Poisson kernel and what a small electrode can influence · Electrostatic field theory and measurement

A Green function is the response of an entire boundary-value problem to a unit source. Once that response is known, a continuous charge distribution and a patterned boundary voltage can both be treated by integration. The two integrations require different kernels.

Chapter 15 · How far does an electrode pattern reach?

Solve Laplace’s equation in a strip, read decay lengths straight from boundary data and decide when a truncated series can predict an interior measurement.

Specify all the boundaries before searching for a formula

A long rectangular cross-section occupies \(0<x<a,\ y>0\). The side walls are grounded, the bottom edge carries a prescribed voltage \(f(x)\), and the potential decays as \(y\) grows. Physically the bottom edge may be an array of narrow driven electrodes separated by insulating gaps. The idealisation prescribes voltage in the limit of small gaps. There is no free charge in the interior and the dielectric is homogeneous. The problem is thus

\[V_{xx}+V_{yy}=0.\]

A single field line or Gaussian surface does not tell us how a complicated \(f\) propagates upwards.

Try one product \(X(x)Y(y)\). Dividing the equation by the product gives

\[X''/X=-Y''/Y.\]

Each side depends on a different variable, so both must be constant. Write the first constant as \(-k^2\). Testing zero and positive values for \(X''/X\) yields only the trivial solution satisfying both grounded sides. The negative choice yields

\[X=A\sin kx+B\cos kx.\]

The left wall sets \(B=0\); the right wall requires

\[k_n=n\pi/a,\]
\[n=1,2,\ldots.\]

For a fixed \(n\), \(Y\) is a sum of growing and decaying exponentials. The far boundary eliminates the growing branch.

Determine the coefficients by asking one question per mode

No individual mode can fit general data at the base. Add the admissible products and enforce the bottom voltage. Multiply by \(\sin(m\pi x/a)\) and integrate over the width. Products of distinct sine modes average to zero, while the squared sine integrates to \(a/2\). These measurements recover independent coefficients:

\[b_n=\frac2a\int_0^a f(x)\sin(n\pi x/a)\,dx,\]
\[V(x,y)=\sum_{n=1}^\infty b_n\sin(n\pi x/a)e^{-n\pi y/a}.\]

Physically every extra oscillation across the base shortens the vertical penetration length. For \(a=40\) mm the first mode decays by a factor \(e\) every 12.7 mm; the third takes only 4.24 mm. Complicated boundary structure can leave a very simple interior field.

Worked cancellation that moves with height

Drive the base with \(f=3\sin(\pi x/a)+3\sin(3\pi x/a)\) volts. At the centre the two boundary voltages cancel since \(\sin(3\pi/2)=-1\). Above it the voltage becomes \(3(e^{-t}-e^{-3t})\) with \(t=\pi y/a\). Differentiate to locate its maximum: \(-e^{-t}+3e^{-3t}=0\) gives

\[t=\frac12\ln3.\]

Thus \(y=0.175a\) and the reading reaches \(2/\sqrt3=1.155\) V, even above a point set to zero volts. A full solution at the centre depends on the surrounding boundary data.

Predict the influence of a finite electrode

Place a 5 V electrode on the central half of the base and ground the remainder. Direct integration yields

\[b_n=\frac{10\ {\rm V}}{n\pi}\big[\cos(n\pi/4)-\cos(3n\pi/4)\big].\]

Even modes vanish by reflection symmetry. The first two nonzero coefficients are \(b_1=4.50\) V and \(b_3=-1.50\) V. At \(x=a/2,y=a/4\), their combined central reading is

\[4.50e^{-\pi/4}+1.50e^{-3\pi/4}=2.19\,\mathrm{V}.\]

A conservative bound on the discarded tail uses \(|b_n|\le20/(n\pi)\) V. Summing a geometric bound from \(n=5\) gives a maximum error of \(20e^{-5\pi/4}/[5\pi(1-e^{-\pi/4})]\approx0.046\) V. Away from the base this is an inexpensive error certificate.

At the electrode edge itself the series approaches the midpoint of the voltage jump and overshoots nearby when truncated. A real electrode has a gap and finite edge radius. Estimating the maximum surface field from this discontinuous idealisation makes the result depend on the chosen resolution. An interior voltage at a specified positive height is much better conditioned.

Change a physical boundary and rebuild the mode

An enclosure of finite height \(H\) with a grounded lid needs a mode which vanishes at \(H\) and equals one at the base. Solving the same vertical ODE now gives

\[Y_n=\sinh[k_n(H-y)]/\sinh(k_nH).\]

The transverse eigenvalues stay fixed because the side walls have not moved. For \(H=a/2\) and \(y=H/2\), the fundamental is transmitted with factor \(\sinh(\pi/4)/\sinh(\pi/2)=0.377\) instead of the open-strip value \(e^{-\pi/4}=0.456\). This difference is a way to diagnose an unmodelled nearby conductor.

Move a measurement plane away from patterned electrodes

The first boundary harmonic is fixed at 3 V. Set the third to 3 V as well. At the midpoint the boundary values cancel; 0.18 strip widths above it the two terms leave about 1.15 V. Follow the two curves to see which boundary details survive propagation into the gap.

Open this experiment online

Use a measurement to judge which boundary details survive

How accurately could the third harmonic be recovered?

At \(y=a/2\) an instrument can resolve a 10 mV Fourier amplitude. How large must the third harmonic at the base be? Compare the fundamental.

Work through the solution

Third-mode attenuation is \(e^{-3\pi/2}=0.00898\), so about \(1.11\) V is needed at the boundary. The fundamental needs only \(0.010e^{\pi/2}=0.0481\) V. Back-propagating a noisy field magnifies its finest scales first. Improving the number of model harmonics cannot compensate for a missing signal.

Check the energy of one harmonic

The base drives \(b\sin(kx)\) for one admissible \(k\). Integrate the electric energy per unit length perpendicular to the strip and check its dimensions.

Work through the solution

The two field components are \(-kb\cos(kx)e^{-ky}\) and \(kb\sin(kx)e^{-ky}\), so their squares sum to \(k^2b^2e^{-2ky}\). Integrating \(\epsilon E^2/2\) across \(a\) and upwards to infinity gives \(U'=\epsilon a k b^2/4\), in J/m. At fixed boundary amplitude a shorter wavelength stores more energy near the base despite penetrating less far.

Further reading

  • Griffiths, §3.3.1, Cartesian separation of variables
  • Fließbach, Randwertprobleme

Rectangular geometries, orthogonality and sources that drive individual modes · Electrostatic field theory and measurement

Fourier modes are solutions selected by their electrode walls. On a rectangle they turn a boundary-voltage problem into independent vertical equations. When a charge fills the rectangle the same eigenfunctions give a different denominator and a different physical response.

Chapter 16 · Spherical harmonics as measurements of boundary voltage

Reconstruct interior and exterior potentials from an angular voltage scan. Use orthogonality to isolate a dipole or quadrupole and quantify how rapidly fine angular structure disappears.

Why a sphere selects angular patterns

Consider a spherical surface of radius \(a\) covered by closely spaced insulated electrodes. They can prescribe a voltage varying with position, whereas a single connected conductor in electrostatic equilibrium can have only one voltage. Suppose there are no other charges, the surrounding permittivity is \(\epsilon_0\), and the reference is zero at infinity. At first let the applied voltage be independent of azimuth. In spherical coordinates the charge-free equation becomes

\[\frac1{r^2}\partial_r(r^2\partial_r V)+\frac1{r^2\sin\theta}\partial_\theta(\sin\theta\,\partial_\theta V)=0 .\]

Writing \(V=R(r)P(u)\) with \(u=\cos\theta\) and multiplying by \(r^2/(RP)\) separates the radial and angular parts. The angular operator becomes \(d[(1-u^2)dP/du]/du\); regularity at both poles selects eigenvalues \(\ell(\ell+1)\) for nonnegative integer \(\ell\). The regular eigenfunctions are the Legendre polynomials. The first three are \(1,u,(3u^2-1)/2\). Substitution of any of these into the angular equation verifies its eigenvalue.

For each angular order the radial equation reads \((r^2R')'=\ell(\ell+1)R\). Insert \(R=r^p\) to obtain

\[p(p+1)=\ell(\ell+1).\]

The two choices are \(p=\ell\) and \(p=-\ell-1\). The first stays regular at the centre; the second decays at infinity. These choices describe different physical domains for the same measured surface voltage.

Infer coefficients and the surface charge they require

On the spherical surface write \(f(u)=\sum_\ell b_\ell P_\ell(u)\). Legendre polynomials are orthogonal under the integral \(du\) from \(-1\) to 1; for equal indices the integral is \(2/(2\ell+1)\). The weight has a geometric origin: a narrow latitude strip subtends solid angle \(2\pi\sin\theta\,d\theta=-2\pi\,du\). Uniform steps in polar angle must be weighted by \(\sin\theta\) before estimating the angular coefficients.

\[b_\ell=\frac{2\ell+1}{2}\int_{-1}^{1}f(u)P_\ell(u)\,du,\]
\[V_{\rm in}=\sum_\ell b_\ell(r/a)^\ell P_\ell(u),\]
\[V_{\rm out}=\sum_\ell b_\ell(a/r)^{\ell+1}P_\ell(u).\]

At the boundary both sides have the prescribed potential. Their normal derivatives generally differ. For each order the outward fields at \(a\) are \(+(\ell+1)b_\ell P_\ell/a\) outside and \(-\ell b_\ell P_\ell/a\) inside. Gauss’s pillbox therefore assigns the thin electrode array a net sheet charge density

\[\sigma(u)=\frac{\epsilon_0}{a}\sum_\ell (2\ell+1)b_\ell P_\ell(u).\]

Worked inverse problem with three voltmeter readings

Suppose independent measurements establish that orders above two are negligible. At the north pole, equator and south pole a scan gives 4, 1 and 2 V. The first and last readings differ only in the odd term, hence

\[b_1=(4-2)/2=1\,\mathrm{V}.\]

Their average gives \(b_0+b_2=3\) V and the equator gives

\[b_0-b_2/2=1\,\mathrm{V}.\]

Solving yields \(b_0=5/3\) V and \(b_2=4/3\) V. On the north axis at \(r=a/2\) the predicted voltage is

\[5/3+1/2+1/3=2.50\,\mathrm{V}.\]

The three readings alone would not exclude a higher-order angular pattern. Additional sample positions are needed to test that assumption.

Use radial decay to design a measurement

The exterior radial factor contains one extra power of \(a/r\) compared with the relative angular order. At \(r=2a\) a quadrupole potential has fallen to one eighth of its surface value. An order-six pattern has fallen to \(1/128\). A 20 mV order-six component at a distant detector would require 2.56 V at the surface. A 20 mV instrumental uncertainty has exactly the same amplification if one attempts a surface reconstruction from that single radius.

Worked cancellation and a charge measurement

For a pure quadrupole set \(a=50\) mm and \(b_2=3.0\) V. The north-pole surface density is \(5\epsilon_0 b_2/a=2.66\) nC/m²; at the equator it is half that magnitude with opposite sign. The net charge vanishes because \(\int_{-1}^{1}P_2\,du=0\). A charge meter that captures the entire array would read zero while a local probe measures finite voltage and field. Net charge measures precisely the \(\ell=0\) coefficient.

Recognise when a latitude scan is insufficient

A painted voltage pattern can vary with longitude as well. A periodic azimuthal factor has form \(e^{im\phi}\) with integer \(m\). The extra angular term in Laplace’s equation introduces \(-m^2/(1-u^2)\) into the Legendre equation. Regular solutions are associated Legendre functions with \(|m|\le\ell\). Combined with the azimuthal factor and normalisation they form \(Y_{\ell m}\). For an orthonormal convention the coefficient is the surface integral of \(Y_{\ell m}^*f\) over solid angle. The radial powers remain unchanged. In particular, \(f\propto\sin\theta\cos\phi\) is a dipolar pattern oriented along the \(x\) direction. Averaging every latitude ring would completely erase it.

Continue three boundary harmonics through a sphere

The boundary has a constant 1 V term, a 1 V dipole coefficient and an adjustable quadrupole. At half the sphere radius with a 2 V quadrupole, the pole reads 2.00 V and the equator 0.75 V. Compare inside and outside measurements with the same angular resolution.

Open this experiment online

Distinguish angular resolution from total charge

Locate a field null inside a sphere

Take \(b_1=1.2\) V, \(b_2=-1.0\) V, \(a=60\) mm, with all other coefficients zero. Find a point on the positive axis at which the full electric field vanishes.

Work through the solution

On the axis, symmetry sets transverse field to zero. The potential is \(1.2z/a-(z/a)^2\) volts. Its derivative vanishes at \(z/a=0.6\), or 36 mm. The local axial extremum is compatible with Laplace’s equation because transverse curvature has the opposite sign. The point is a saddle of the three-dimensional potential.

Is an interior maximum consistent with the measured boundary?

A code sampling a smooth, charge-free sphere reports 6.0 V at its centre; the largest voltage applied anywhere on the boundary is 4.0 V. Explain the discrepancy using the harmonics.

Work through the solution

At the centre all terms with \(\ell>0\) vanish. The remaining \(b_0\) equals the angular average of the boundary voltage and cannot exceed 4 V. The check isolates a cause to investigate: interior sources, incorrect boundary data or a defective discretisation. It does not require knowing the other coefficients.

Further reading

  • Griffiths, §§3.3.2 and 3.4, spherical separation and multipoles
  • Fließbach, Legendrepolynome, pp. 80–88
  • Fließbach, Kugelfunktionen, pp. 99–107

Normalised spherical harmonics and the field of an arbitrary three-dimensional source · Electrostatic field theory and measurement

An axial voltage scan can determine Legendre coefficients only if the source is rotationally symmetric. A general spherical electrode or molecule needs angular modes with two indices. Their normalisation fixes the conversion from a measured multipole coefficient to a physical voltage.

Chapter 17 · From a measured current to its magnetic field

Construct the magnetic field of a steady source, calculate a coil pair’s uniform region and extract the first magnetic moment that survives at a large distance.

Identify a physically possible source

A wire carries a measured steady current. Its magnetic effect depends on the complete current path, including the return conductor. Charge conservation requires \(\nabla\cdot\mathbf J=0\) for a stationary distribution. A finite wire segment with current suddenly ending at an insulated tip would accumulate charge. The missing return path can be neglected in an approximation only after comparing its distance and field with those of the measured segment.

The magnetostatic field equations in vacuum are

\[\nabla\cdot\mathbf B=0,\]
\[\nabla\times\mathbf B=\mu_0\mathbf J.\]

The first suggests writing \(\mathbf B=\nabla\times\mathbf A\). Adding any gradient to \(\mathbf A\) leaves \(\mathbf B\) unchanged. In unbounded space we may choose \(\nabla\cdot\mathbf A=0\) together with decay for a localised source. Applying curl to the potential gives

\[\nabla\times(\nabla\times\mathbf A)=\nabla(\nabla\cdot\mathbf A)-\nabla^2\mathbf A;\]

the chosen divergence removes the first term.

\[\nabla^2\mathbf A=-\mu_0\mathbf J,\]
\[\mathbf A(\mathbf r)=\frac{\mu_0}{4\pi}\int\frac{\mathbf J(\mathbf r')}{|\mathbf r-\mathbf r'|}\,d^3r'.\]

Each Cartesian component solves a scalar Poisson problem. Taking the observation-coordinate curl under the integral differentiates the distance kernel. Since \(\nabla(1/R)=-\mathbf R/R^3\), exchanging the order of the cross product yields the Biot–Savart integrand \(\mathbf J(\mathbf r')\times\mathbf R/R^3\). Ampère’s circulation law remains true for all steady currents. It gives a field value immediately only when symmetry constrains the field along a chosen path.

Turn the vector integral into an axial measurement

For a thin circular loop of radius \(a\) in the \(xy\)-plane, \(\mathbf J\,d^3r'\) becomes \(I\,d\boldsymbol\ell'\). At a point \(z\) on the axis every element has the same distance \(\sqrt{a^2+z^2}\). Opposite elements produce cancelling transverse fields. The surviving axial numerator integrates to \(2\pi I a^2\) because each tangent crosses the inward radial component of \(\mathbf R\) with the same orientation. Thus

\[B_z(z)=\frac{\mu_0 I a^2}{2(a^2+z^2)^{3/2}} .\]

For a 40 mm loop carrying 0.80 A, the central field is \(12.57\,\mu{\rm T}\). At \(z=a\) it is smaller by \(2^{3/2}\), or \(4.44\,\mu{\rm T}\). Reversing current reverses both readings. No field singularity exists on the axis; evaluating the ideal filament field directly on the wire instead requires a model of its finite cross-section.

Design a locally uniform field by cancelling curvature

Place two identical coaxial loops at \(z=\pm d/2\) carrying the same current. Their combined field is even in \(z\), so its first derivative at the midpoint is automatically zero. The second derivative sets the leading departure from uniformity. For a loop profile \(b(z)=C(a^2+z^2)^{-3/2}\), differentiation gives

\[b''(z)=3C\frac{4z^2-a^2}{(a^2+z^2)^{7/2}},\]
\[B_{\rm pair}''(0)=2b''(d/2).\]

Choosing \(d=a\) cancels the curvature, leaving a fourth-order axial variation near the centre. The midpoint field then equals \(\mu_0 I(4/5)^{3/2}/a\) for one turn on each loop. For \(a=60.0\) mm and \(I=0.50\) A this gives \(7.49\,\mu{\rm T}\). Identical compact \(N\)-turn windings scale that reading by \(N\) while their finite winding dimensions eventually change the profile. A ratio of two nearby field readings is often a better test of spacing than an absolute reading affected by current calibration.

Find which source information a distant detector retains

For \(r\gg a\), the exact axial loop field approaches \(\mu_0 I a^2/(2r^3)\). Define the dipole moment \(\mathbf m=I\pi a^2\hat{\mathbf n}\). The axial far field is then \(\mu_0m/(2\pi r^3)\). Expanding the vector-potential kernel for a general localised steady source explains the same dependence: the term proportional to \(\int\mathbf J\,dV\) vanishes for a closed current. Indeed, applying the divergence theorem to \(x_i\mathbf J\) gives \(\int J_i\,dV=0\) when currents vanish at the outer boundary. The antisymmetric part of the next moment produces

\[\mathbf m=\tfrac12\int\mathbf r'\times\mathbf J\,d^3r',\]
\[\mathbf A_{\rm dip}=\frac{\mu_0}{4\pi}\frac{\mathbf m\times\hat{\mathbf r}}{r^2}.\]

For a planar loop the line-integral moment reduces to current times signed area. A detector far away therefore has difficulty distinguishing small loops with the same moment but different shapes. Closer readings, which retain the higher moments, are needed.

Find a pair of coils with a flat central field

Change the separation of two identical current loops. Each curve is divided by its own central field so that the graph tests uniformity. At Helmholtz spacing, a probe one quarter-radius off centre reads about 0.42% below the centre.

Open this experiment online

Check which coil measurement identifies the source

Test the dipole approximation at a specified distance

At \(z=3a\), how large is the error if the exact loop field is replaced by its axial dipole formula? Express it relative to the exact result.

Work through the solution

The approximation-to-exact ratio is

\[[1+(a/z)^2]^{3/2}=(10/9)^{3/2}=1.171.\]

The distant-source expression overpredicts by about 17.1%. At \(z=10a\) the excess falls to 1.50%. A distance of a few radii may be insufficient for precision work.

Choose a coil polarity for a gradient probe

The second coil of a symmetric pair is reversed. Predict the midpoint field and identify which derivative can now be nonzero there.

Work through the solution

The two equal axial fields cancel at the midpoint. With opposite currents the sum is an odd function, allowing a linear gradient. For a pair \(b(z-d/2)-b(z+d/2)\), its central derivative is \(-2b'(d/2)\). With \(d>0\), \(b'(d/2)<0\), so this wiring gives a positive axial gradient. Checking polarity distinguishes this arrangement from the uniform-field pair.

  • Griffiths, §§5.2–5.4, current sources and vector potential
  • Fließbach, Magnetischer Dipol

An experimenter can measure a flux change with a coil without measuring the magnetic field over every square millimetre of the coil area. The vector potential gives a corresponding computational tool. Its line integral determines flux, while the freedom to choose its gauge can turn a difficult boundary problem into a manageable one.

Chapter 18 · How microscopic dipoles produce macroscopic charge

Derive the volume and surface charges of a polarised body, determine the fields in layers and calculate which electrical work a capacitance measurement includes.

Replace a dense collection of dipoles by a smooth field

A small neutral molecule can have positive and negative charge centres separated by a displacement. Its dipole moment \(\mathbf p\) points from negative to positive. A volume containing many molecules but small compared with the macroscopic variation defines a dipole moment per volume \(\mathbf P\), in C/m². For observation points outside the body the sum of dipole potentials becomes

\[V(\mathbf r)=\frac{1}{4\pi\epsilon_0}\int_\Omega\mathbf P(\mathbf r')\cdot\nabla'\frac1{|\mathbf r-\mathbf r'|}\,d^3r'.\]

The prime matters: differentiation with respect to source position has the opposite sign from differentiation with respect to observation position. Apply the product rule to \(\nabla'\cdot(\mathbf P/R)\) and integrate the divergence over the body. The result has exactly the Coulomb form for a volume distribution \(\rho_b=-\nabla\cdot\mathbf P\) and a surface distribution \(\sigma_b=\mathbf P\cdot\mathbf n\). Together the two carry zero total charge for a bounded polarised neutral object. The volume and surface terms can each be nonzero.

Background · Electric displacement
\[\mathbf D=\epsilon_0\mathbf E+\mathbf P\]

Its flux measures free charge. Polarisation is dipole moment per volume. A discontinuity of normal displacement depends on free surface charge.

Worked slab with a polarisation gradient

In \(0<z<d\), prescribe \(P_z=P_0z/d\) over a broad slab. The bound volume charge is uniform at \(-P_0/d\). The lower face carries zero and the upper face \(+P_0\). Per unit area the negative volume contribution is \(-P_0\), cancelling the positive face. In an isolated large-plane approximation with no applied background, \(D_z=0\) outside and inside. Thus \(E_z=-P_0 z/(\epsilon_0 d)\) in the slab. Voltage rises from bottom to top by \(P_0d/(2\epsilon_0)\). With \(P_0=10\) nC/m² and \(d=2.0\) mm the rise is 1.13 V. Uniformly polarised material is the special case in which only the two faces carry charge.

Separate what an external circuit supplies

Gauss’s law says \(\epsilon_0\nabla\cdot\mathbf E=\rho_{\rm free}+\rho_b\). Substituting the polarisation divergence and collecting terms defines \(\mathbf D=\epsilon_0\mathbf E+\mathbf P\) with \(\nabla\cdot\mathbf D=\rho_{\rm free}\). A small pillbox then gives the jump in the normal component of \(\mathbf D\) as the free surface density. A narrow electrostatic circulation loop gives continuity of tangential \(\mathbf E\). These two statements specify different components. A spatially varying material can make \(\nabla\times\mathbf D\ne0\) even when \(\nabla\times\mathbf E=0\).

For a reversible linear isotropic dielectric, measurements can supply \(\mathbf P=\epsilon_0\chi_e\mathbf E\). Then \(\epsilon=\epsilon_0(1+\chi_e)\) converts between \(\mathbf D\) and \(\mathbf E\). Permanent polarisation and history-dependent dielectrics require additional constitutive information. The prescribed-gradient example deliberately specified \(\mathbf P\) directly.

Turn boundary conditions into a measurable capacitance

Place two clean dielectric layers of thicknesses \(d_1,d_2\) between broad electrodes. There is no free sheet at their interface. Both layers therefore have the same normal \(D=Q/A\) away from edges. Each voltage drop is \(D d_i/\epsilon_i\). Adding the drops gives

\[\frac CA=\frac{1}{d_1/\epsilon_1+d_2/\epsilon_2},\]
\[\frac{V_1}{V_2}=\frac{d_1/\epsilon_1}{d_2/\epsilon_2}.\]

Take one millimetre of relative permittivity 2 and one millimetre of relative permittivity 8. With 10 V applied, the first layer takes 8 V and the second 2 V. Their fields are 8 and 2 kV/m. The free plate density is \(1.42\times10^{-7}\) C/m². A simple arithmetic mean of the permittivities would give a wrong voltage split. The layers share normal displacement in this orientation. For strips lying side by side across the electrode face, the voltage is common and their capacitances add in parallel.

Track the source that holds the voltage

At fixed geometry, adding a small plate charge \(dQ\) requires reversible work \(V\,dQ\). With constant linear capacitance, integrating from zero to \(Q\) gives

\[U=Q^2/(2C).\]

In the layered capacitor this equals \((A/2)\sum_i d_i E_iD_i\). Changing a layer while \(Q\) stays fixed changes the mechanical work by the corresponding change in \(U\). Holding voltage fixed connects a source that supplies or removes charge. If insertion at fixed \(V\) increases capacitance by \(dC\), source work is \(V\,dQ=V^2dC\); the field stores only \(V^2dC/2\). The other half can appear as mechanical work by the electric force. Specifying the electrical control variable resolves an apparent sign ambiguity in capacitor force calculations.

Move a dielectric interface between voltage-controlled plates

The pair has a total thickness of 2 mm and an applied voltage of 10 V. The first dielectric has relative permittivity 2. Equal layer thicknesses and a second permittivity of 8 give slopes of 8 and 2 V/mm. Which physical charge would be missed by forcing those slopes to agree?

Open this experiment online

Infer a hidden material property

Recover a permittivity from a voltage tap

Two layers of thickness 0.80 and 1.20 mm share 9.0 V. A tap shows a 3.0 V drop across the first layer of relative permittivity 4. Find the second relative permittivity.

Work through the solution

Equal normal displacement gives

\[\epsilon_1 V_1/d_1=\epsilon_2 V_2/d_2.\]

The second drop is 6.0 V, hence

\[\epsilon_{r2}=4(3.0/0.80)(1.20/6.0)=3.0.\]

A free interfacial sheet would supply a jump in \(D\) and invalidate this inversion.

Predict which bound charge a probe detects at the internal interface

In the equal-thickness, 10 V example choose the field direction positive from layer 1 to layer 2. Find the combined bound interface density and check against the field jump.

Work through the solution

With \(E_1=8000\), \(E_2=2000\) V/m, \(P_1=\epsilon_0 E_1\) and \(P_2=7\epsilon_0 E_2\). The top face of layer 1 and bottom face of layer 2 together carry \(P_1-P_2=-6000\epsilon_0=-53.1\) nC/m². This agrees with \(\epsilon_0(E_2-E_1)\) from Gauss’s law for total charge.

Practicum · locate free and bound charge from a buried voltage tap

Two broad metal electrodes at \(z=0\) and \(z=d_1+d_2\) are held at 10.0 V and 0 V. Between them lie linear isotropic dielectrics, first \(d_1=1.00\) mm with \(\epsilon_{r1}=2.00\), then \(d_2=2.00\) mm with \(\epsilon_{r2}=6.00\). A very thin immobile sheet of free charge may be trapped at their interface. An ideal nonperturbing probe there reads 4.00 V. Neglect fringing. On paper, sketch a candidate potential and label the electric field, displacement, and source of each surface charge. Can all of your labels fit the three voltage readings simultaneously?

Reconstruct the source from field jumps

Determine both field vectors, both displacement vectors, the free charge sheet and the bound interface charge. State the direction associated with a positive sheet density.

Follow the calculation and check the result

Set the interface normal from layer 1 to layer 2 along \(+\hat{\mathbf z}\). The potentials in the two charge-free interiors must be affine because \(\partial_z(\epsilon\partial_zV)=0\) there. The slopes are \(-6.00\) V/mm and \(-2.00\) V/mm. Therefore \(E_1=6000\) V/m, \(E_2=2000\) V/m and both point along the normal. Their displacements agree: \(D_1=2\epsilon_0(6000)=D_2=6\epsilon_0(2000)=106.25\) nC/m². Gauss's law for free charge gives

\[\sigma_f=D_2-D_1=0.\]

Compute the polarisation separately. \(P_1=\epsilon_0(6000)\) and \(P_2=5\epsilon_0(2000)\). Facing surfaces contribute \(+P_1\) and \(-P_2\), so \(\sigma_b=P_1-P_2=-35.42\) nC/m². A vacuum pillbox that counts all charge gives \(\epsilon_0(E_2-E_1)=-35.42\) nC/m², the same result by a different route. The signed density indicates charge per area, while the oriented normal fixes the sign in each jump equation.

Change one reading without changing either electrode

After a treatment, the tap reads 5.00 V with both plate voltages unchanged. A colleague assumes that equal voltage drops imply equal charge on facing electrodes. Test the inference, find the trapped charge, and close a global charge budget.

Follow the calculation and check the result

Now \(E_1=5000\) V/m and \(E_2=2500\) V/m because the equal voltage drops occur across different thicknesses. So \(D_1=88.54\) nC/m², \(D_2=132.81\) nC/m² and the trapped free sheet is \(+44.27\) nC/m². The conductor face charges are \(+88.54\) nC/m² on the low-\(z\) plate and \(-132.81\) nC/m² on the high-\(z\) plate. Added to the sheet they sum to zero, consistent with zero exterior displacement for the ideal screened setup.

At the internal interface the bound charge is \(P_1-P_2=\epsilon_0(5000-12500)=-66.41\) nC/m². Total charge there is \(-22.14\) nC/m² even though the trapped free sheet is positive. Check it using \(\epsilon_0(E_2-E_1)=-22.14\) nC/m². An instrument sensitive only to the electric-field jump would give the wrong sign if its reading were interpreted as free charge.

Test what the measurements can actually resolve

Suppose the second tap reading has uncertainty ±0.05 V and the other inputs are known exactly. Propagate the uncertainty to the inferred free surface charge, then propose a null experiment.

Follow the calculation and check the result

With \(V_m\) the tap reading,

\[\sigma_f=\epsilon_0[\epsilon_{r2}V_m/d_2-\epsilon_{r1}(10-V_m)/d_1].\]

Its slope is \(\epsilon_0(3000+2000)\) per volt in SI units, namely 44.27 nC/m² per volt. The inferred sheet is \(44.27\pm2.21\) nC/m². The uncertainty in the same tap is correlated between both drops, so treating the two inferred fields as independent would give a different uncertainty.

Remove the trapped charge and repeat with both electrodes at 0 V. The unique solution has zero field, and a residual tap voltage would indicate an offset or a violation of the material assumptions. A stronger differential test keeps the sheet and changes the applied voltage: the inferred jump in displacement should remain fixed while the two plate charges adjust. In a numerical boundary-value calculation, compare the reconstructed fluxes on either side of the interface and the integrated free charge, using the physical face permittivity.

Further reading

  • Griffiths, §§4.2–4.4, bound charge, displacement and energy
  • Tong, Electromagnetism in Matter, polarisation and displacement

Study the full derivation

Anisotropic and nonlinear dielectrics from local measurements to global fields · Electrostatic field theory and measurement

A single dielectric constant cannot describe a crystal whose displacement tilts away from its electric field, or a reversible material whose incremental response changes with bias. Starting with the constitutive measurement clarifies which parts of ordinary electrostatics survive.

Chapter 19 · How a magnet produces an exterior field

Translate microscopic loop moments into volume and surface currents. Derive a shape-dependent internal field and learn which magnetic response a coil measurement can recover.

Add the fields of tiny current loops

A small current loop produces a dipole vector potential \(\mu_0\mathbf m\times\hat{\mathbf R}/(4\pi R^2)\) far from that loop. Coarse-grain a material into a dipole moment per volume \(\mathbf M\), in A/m. With \(\nabla'(1/R)=\hat{\mathbf R}/R^2\), the potential becomes an integral of \(\mathbf M\times\nabla'(1/R)\). Apply the curl product rule to \(\nabla'\times(\mathbf M/R)\), then integrate the curl over the body. For outward normal \(\mathbf n\) this gives

\[\mathbf A(\mathbf r)=\frac{\mu_0}{4\pi}\left[\int_\Omega\frac{\nabla'\times\mathbf M}{R}\,d^3r'+\oint_{\partial\Omega}\frac{\mathbf M\times\mathbf n}{R}\,dS'\right].\]

Comparison with the vector potential of conduction currents identifies \(\mathbf J_b=\nabla\times\mathbf M\) and \(\mathbf K_b=\mathbf M\times\mathbf n\). These currents are a representation of the material dipoles. Neighbouring equal loop currents cancel where they share a boundary. At the outer surface a current remains unpaired. The curl measures how cancellation fails within a nonuniform specimen.

Worked magnetised cylinder

Let a very long cylinder of radius \(a\) have uniform axial \(M_0\hat{\mathbf z}\). Its bound volume current vanishes. Its side carries \(K_\phi=M_0\), and its flat end faces carry none in this model. The remaining current acts like a long solenoid. The internal field far from the ends is \(B_z=\mu_0 M_0\), while the exterior field tends to zero in the infinite-length limit. With \(M_0=4.0\times10^4\) A/m this gives 50.3 mT. A finite specimen has a return field near and beyond its ends; the far field of a finite magnet must eventually be dipolar.

What a loop linking a winding actually counts

Subtracting \(\mathbf J_b\) from magnetostatic Ampère’s law gives \(\nabla\times\mathbf H=\mathbf J_{\rm free}\) with \(\mathbf H=\mathbf B/\mu_0-\mathbf M\). A rectangular loop across an interface yields \(\mathbf n\times(\mathbf H_2-\mathbf H_1)=\mathbf K_{\rm free}\), while \(\nabla\cdot\mathbf B=0\) guarantees continuous normal \(B\). In a region free of conduction currents and with suitable topology one can introduce a magnetic scalar potential \(\mathbf H=-\nabla\phi_m\). Its divergence follows from \(\nabla\cdot\mathbf H=-\nabla\cdot\mathbf M\). This alternative calculation uses the same magnetisation as the current description. Both predict identical \(\mathbf B\).

Derive the demagnetising field of a sphere

Put a sphere of radius \(a\) with fixed uniform \(\mathbf M=M\hat{\mathbf z}\) in vacuum and assume no applied field. Inside and outside, \(\nabla\cdot\mathbf M=0\). The angular structure at the surface is \(M\cos\theta\), so use \(\phi_i=C r\cos\theta\) and \(\phi_o=C a^3\cos\theta/r^2\). They are harmonic, regular at the origin or at infinity, and continuous at \(a\); continuity ensures equal tangential \(H\). At the surface their outward fields are \(H_{i,r}=-C\cos\theta\) and \(H_{o,r}=2C\cos\theta\). With normal \(B\) continuous, \(2C=-C+M\), hence

\[\mathbf H_i=-\tfrac13\mathbf M,\]
\[\mathbf B_i=\tfrac23\mu_0\mathbf M .\]

The factor \(1/3\) encodes specimen shape. A very long axial cylinder with the same magnetisation has almost zero internal \(H\) far from its ends. The sphere’s exterior scalar potential corresponds to a dipole moment equal to magnetisation times volume.

Worked susceptibility seen from outside

For a reversible linear sphere with \(M=\chi H_i\) in a uniform applied field \(H_0\), superposition adds the applied field and the demagnetising contribution: \(H_i=H_0-M/3\). Solving yields

\[M/H_0=\chi/(1+\chi/3).\]

If a moment measurement gives \(M/H_0=1.50\), the intrinsic susceptibility is 3.0. As \(\chi\) grows, \(M/H_0\) approaches 3, and the inversion becomes very sensitive to moment uncertainty. Using \(B=\mu H\) without specifying where the field is measured can conceal this shape dependence.

Separate reversible energy from cycle loss

When ferromagnetic domains rearrange, \(B\) can depend on the prior excursion of \(H\). A single constant susceptibility then cannot describe an entire cycle. In a slow, approximately uniform closed magnetic circuit the source supplies incremental energy density \(H\,dB\). Returning to the initial magnetic state leaves the signed cycle integral \(\oint H\,dB\); its dissipated energy per volume is the positive area for the driven loop orientation. A measured loop area of 180 J/m³ at 50 cycles/s would dissipate 9.0 kW/m³, or 0.090 W in \(10\) cm³. Eddy-current loss can also enlarge a measured dynamic loop, so a rate sweep helps interpret that result.

Infer material response from an external field

The sphere reference curve gives an apparent susceptibility of 2.25 at intrinsic susceptibility 9. The adjustable ellipsoid starts at N = 0.33, giving 2.27. Try smaller demagnetising factors for elongated ellipsoids magnetised along their long axes. Determine when an apparent response would severely underestimate the intrinsic one.

Open this experiment online

Test a surface-current picture

What current remains if magnetisation falls towards the rim?

Take a long cylinder with \(M_z=M_0(1-s^2/a^2)\) inside. Find the azimuthal bound currents and the field on its axis.

Work through the solution

Cylindrical curl gives

\[J_{b,\phi}=-dM_z/ds=2M_0s/a^2.\]

At \(s=a\) the surface current is zero. Regard a shell \(ds\) as a small solenoidal sheet \(K=J_{b,\phi}ds\). At the axis all shells contribute, giving \(B_z(0)=\mu_0\int_0^a J_{b,\phi}\,ds=\mu_0M_0\). Far from the ends the radial profile inside is \(B_z(s)=\mu_0M_z(s)\).

Invert a nearly saturated shape response

If \(M/H_0=2.70\) for a linear sphere, what is \(\chi\)? Estimate how an absolute uncertainty of 0.03 in the measured ratio propagates.

Work through the solution

Writing \(r=M/H_0\), one finds

\[\chi=r/(1-r/3)=27.\]

Its derivative is \((1-r/3)^{-2}=100\), so the local uncertainty is about 3. Distinguishing two high susceptibilities requires precise specimen geometry and much better relative accuracy than the measured moment alone suggests.

Further reading

  • Griffiths, §§6.1–6.4, magnetisation, bound currents and H
  • Tong, Electromagnetism in Matter, magnetic fields in matter

Study the full derivation

From microscopic moments to measured magnetisation · Magnetism, induction and field dynamics

A magnetised sample can make a compass turn without a power supply attached. The macroscopic theory assigns it bound currents in its bulk and on its surface. These are calculated sources for the magnetic field. We will reconstruct them from magnetic moments, predict signals from finite samples, and ask what an exterior field measurement can identify.

Chapter 20 · Where momentum waits between source and receiver

Derive the electromagnetic momentum balance, trace light pressure through a finite pulse, and account for the angular impulse when a magnetic flux decays.

Give a region a mechanical and a field account

Charges respond to Lorentz force density \(\mathbf f=\rho\mathbf E+\mathbf J\times\mathbf B\). To predict the total force on enclosed matter, one can measure the fields on a surrounding vacuum surface. First eliminate the sources. In vacuum Gauss’s law gives \(\rho=\epsilon_0\nabla\cdot\mathbf E\), and the Ampère–Maxwell law gives

\[\mathbf J=(\nabla\times\mathbf B)/\mu_0-\epsilon_0\partial_t\mathbf E.\]

Introduce \(\mathbf g=\epsilon_0\mathbf E\times\mathbf B=\mathbf S/c^2\). Its time derivative supplies both \(\epsilon_0\partial_t\mathbf E\times\mathbf B\) and \(\epsilon_0\mathbf E\times\partial_t\mathbf B\). The first cancels the displacement-current term in the force; Faraday’s law rewrites the second.

For example, the electric terms now read \(\epsilon_0[\mathbf E(\nabla\cdot\mathbf E)-\mathbf E\times(\nabla\times\mathbf E)]\). Component \(i\) is \(\partial_j[\epsilon_0(E_iE_j-\delta_{ij}E^2/2)]\), with repeated Cartesian indices summed. The magnetic terms have the same form because \(\nabla\cdot\mathbf B=0\). Integration gives

\[T_{ij}=\epsilon_0(E_iE_j-\tfrac12 E^2\delta_{ij})+\frac1{\mu_0}(B_iB_j-\tfrac12 B^2\delta_{ij}),\]
\[\mathbf F_{\rm matter}=\oint T\mathbf n\,dA-\frac d{dt}\int\mathbf g\,dV .\]

The normal points out of the chosen volume. Positive \(T_{xx}\) denotes tension along \(x\) in this convention. For a wave travelling in \(+x\) with transverse fields, \(T_{xx}=-u\), where \(u\) is energy density. On an inlet whose outward normal is \(-\hat{\mathbf x}\), the normal traction therefore points in \(+x\).

Measure the time before light reaches a detector

A finite plane pulse in vacuum has \(|\mathbf S|=cu\). Its total momentum is \(U/c\) along the propagation direction. Surround a freely absorbing target and a length of initially empty space upstream with a vacuum control surface. While a pulse enters but has yet to reach the target, the inlet stress integral is nonzero. The electromagnetic momentum inside grows at exactly the same rate. The minus time derivative in the total force cancels the inlet contribution and the target has zero force during this interval.

Worked optical impulse

A 0.60 mJ pulse is fully absorbed after crossing the inlet. Initially and finally the region contains no pulse. Integrating the balance over that full time removes the stored-field term. The target gains \(0.60\times10^{-3}/c=2.00\times10^{-12}\) N s. For ideal normal reflection the exiting pulse carries the opposite momentum, giving twice that impulse. For a transparent window with parallel faces at normal incidence the outgoing pulse may eventually have the same vacuum momentum as the incoming pulse, while the two faces still experience transient forces.

Convert distributed field momentum into a turning impulse

Now take a long coaxial arrangement: an inner narrow cylindrical shell of radius \(a\) carries free charge \(+\lambda\) per length; an outer shell of radius \(b\) carries \(-\lambda\). There is a uniform axial magnetic field \(B_0\) over the annular gap, with end effects negligible. For a definite preparation take an ideal long solenoid producing uniform field throughout \(r<b\), and confine the initial electric field to the gap. Between shells \(E_r=\lambda/(2\pi\epsilon_0 r)\). The field momentum density points towards negative azimuth because \(\hat{\mathbf r}\times\hat{\mathbf z}=-\hat{\boldsymbol\phi}\).

\[g_\phi=-\lambda B_0/(2\pi r),\]
\[L_{{\rm field},z}'=\int_a^b r g_\phi\,2\pi r\,dr=-\tfrac12\lambda B_0(b^2-a^2).\]

The prime denotes angular momentum per length. While the coil current decays slowly, Faraday’s law gives \(2\pi r E_\phi=-\pi r^2\dot B\) for radii up to \(b\). The torque on each shell per length is \(r\lambda_{\rm shell}E_\phi(r)\). Integrating from \(B_0\) to zero yields \(+\lambda B_0a^2/2\) on the inner shell and \(-\lambda B_0b^2/2\) on the outer. Their sum reproduces the initial field angular momentum. Clamps would receive those impulses if the shells were held fixed.

Worked sign and magnitude

With \(\lambda=20\) nC/m, \(B_0=0.25\) T, \(a=10\) mm and \(b=30\) mm, the initial \(L'_z=-2.0\times10^{-12}\) kg m/s. That is angular momentum per metre of apparatus. The outer shell receives nine times the inner impulse magnitude and rotates in the opposite sense. Torque from the induced azimuthal electric field supplies this transfer even though both shells started at rest.

Transfer angular momentum from a field into two shells

The inner radius is 10 mm and its line charge is +20 nC/m. For a 30 mm outer radius and an initial field of 0.25 T, the final shell impulses are +0.25 and −2.25 in units of 10⁻¹² kg m/s. Trace the four accounts during switch-off.

Open this experiment online

Choose a control surface for momentum

Find a pressure when transmission and reflection coexist

A normal beam of intensity 300 W/m² reaches a free-standing film in vacuum. Reflected power fraction is 0.20 and transmitted fraction is 0.50. Find the time-averaged pressure and identify the momentum carried away.

Work through the solution

With incident direction positive, outgoing momentum per area and time is \((T-R)I/c\). The deposited amount is

\[(1-T+R)I/c=0.70(300)/c=0.700\,\mu{\rm Pa}.\]

The absorbed part contributes \(0.30I/c\) and reflection adds \(0.40I/c\). The result assumes forward and backward beams remain normal to the film.

Reverse just the charges

In the coaxial example reverse both shell charges while keeping the axial field and current decay unchanged. Which quantities reverse?

Work through the solution

The radial field, stored azimuthal momentum and angular momentum reverse. Faraday’s induced \(E_\phi\) follows the same history because the flux decay is unchanged. Each electric force and angular impulse reverses since the charge signs reverse. This independent sign argument checks the cross product in the original momentum density.

Practicum · audit a pulse bouncing inside a partly absorbing cavity

A shutter has just prepared a short \(U_0=1.20\) mJ pulse travelling to the right in an otherwise empty one-dimensional cavity. Start the accounting after preparation. The left mirror reflects perfectly. At every encounter with the right mirror 60% of incident pulse energy is reflected, 30% passes into vacuum on the right, and 10% is absorbed. Pulse duration is short compared with the flight time across the cavity. Mirrors are mounted on massive force probes; neglect their displacement and delay any re-emission of heat. The challenge is to reconcile two large, oppositely signed readings with a small net impulse.

Audit one encounter and decide which surface terms matter

For energy \(U\) just before an encounter with the right mirror, calculate its mechanical impulse. Then find the impulse when the reflected packet hits the left mirror. Which momentum is still present between those events?

Follow the calculation and check the result

The incoming momentum is \(+U/c\). The two outgoing packets carry \(+0.30U/c\) and \(-0.60U/c\). Momentum balance therefore assigns the right mirror \(+(1-0.30+0.60)U/c=+1.30U/c\). This includes reversing the reflected packet and stopping the absorbed packet. The left mirror receives \(-2(0.60U)/c=-1.20U/c\) at the next collision. Between those events the cavity still contains \(-0.60U/c\) of field momentum. The complete system also contains the \(+0.30U/c\) transmitted packet outside the cavity.

Stop the movie at a specified time

Freeze the experiment just after the third right-mirror encounter and before the next left-mirror encounter. Find the remaining energy, radiated output, deposited heat, both probe impulses, and total field momentum.

Follow the calculation and check the result

Three incident energies in units of \(U_0\) form the sequence \(1,0.6,0.36\). Their sum is 1.96. The output energy is \(0.30(1.96)U_0=0.588U_0\), heat is \(0.196U_0\), and \(0.216U_0\) remains. The three fractions sum to unity. Right-probe impulse is

\[+1.30(1.96)U_0/c=+2.548U_0/c.\]

Only two left reflections have occurred, so the left probe reads \(-2(0.60+0.36)U_0/c=-1.920U_0/c\). Their sum is \(+0.628U_0/c\).

The escaped packets carry \(+0.588U_0/c\), but the packet still inside carries \(-0.216U_0/c\). Including these two contributions gives measured plus field momentum \((0.628+0.588-0.216)U_0/c=U_0/c\), the initial value. Counting a third left-hand reflection at this time would violate the preselected event boundary. Since \(U_0/c=4.00\times10^{-12}\) N s, the probe readings are approximately \(+10.2\) and \(-7.68\) pN s.

Sum the full history in two independent ways

Continue until no macroscopic pulse remains. Find the impulse on each mirror, then derive their combined reading directly from exterior measurements without examining any reflection.

Follow the calculation and check the result

The geometric series of right hits sums to \(U_0/(1-0.6)=2.5U_0\). The right impulse is \(3.25U_0/c\). Summing every left hit gives

\[-2(0.60)U_0/[(1-0.60)c]=-3.00U_0/c.\]

Thus the pair receives \(+0.25U_0/c\). All transmitted packets travel right and together carry \(0.30U_0/(1-0.60)=0.75U_0\). An external vacuum control surface therefore gives \((1-0.75)U_0/c\) immediately. The absorbed \(0.25U_0\) accounts for the energy stored as heat.

A detector without enough time resolution can recover the integrated exterior momentum even though it cannot resolve the alternating internal forces. Conversely, two large internal probe signals can coexist with a modest net exterior impulse. In a numerical time march record separate signed transfers and the energy still in flight after each boundary update, then vary the stopping time. A budget that closes only after the very last encounter cannot diagnose an intermediate sign mistake.

  • Tong, Electromagnetism and Relativity, energy-momentum and angular momentum

Energy flow and mechanical force from vacuum fields · Magnetism, induction and field dynamics

An external support holds a charged capacitor plate or a current-carrying coil in place. One can infer the support force from fields just outside the body, without summing forces on every microscopic charge. A second surface integral tracks the energy feeding the same apparatus. Both methods start with Maxwell's equations, but they transport different conserved quantities.

Chapter 21 · What an interface does to phase, field and power

Match fields at an optical surface, derive reflection for each polarisation and follow energy when the refracted wave becomes evanescent.

Read refraction from the clock shared by two media

A plane wave strikes a flat interface \(z=0\) between transparent isotropic dielectrics. Their permeabilities are \(\mu_0\); the refractive indices \(n_1,n_2\) are real at the chosen frequency. Write every field as the real part of a complex amplitude times \(e^{i(\mathbf k\cdot\mathbf r-\omega t)}\). Tangential electric and magnetic fields must match at every point \(x\) and every time \(t\) on the surface. This is impossible for independent exponential factors except where their temporal frequencies and tangential wave numbers agree. Therefore \(\omega_i=\omega_r=\omega_t\), \(\theta_r=\theta_i\), and

\[k_{\parallel}=\frac{\omega}{c}n_1\sin\theta_i=\frac{\omega}{c}n_2\sin\theta_t .\]

The interface fixes phase matching before it fixes amplitudes. Which amplitudes match depends on polarisation. Choose the \(xz\)-plane of incidence so that s polarisation has electric field along \(y\) and p polarisation has magnetic field along \(y\).

Use one amplitude convention that works for both polarisations

Use the tangential electric component for all amplitudes. Let \(Y\) be the ratio of the tangential magnetic magnitude to that electric component for a forward wave, with the corresponding sign reversing for a backward wave. From \(\mathbf H=(n/Z_0)\hat{\mathbf k}\times\mathbf E\), \(Z_0=\sqrt{\mu_0/\epsilon_0}\), the forward admittances are \(Y_s=n\cos\theta/Z_0\) and \(Y_p=n/(Z_0\cos\theta)\). The factors differ because an oblique p field has only a fraction \(\cos\theta\) of its magnitude tangential to the surface.

\[E_i+E_r=E_t,\]
\[Y_1(E_i-E_r)=Y_2E_t,\]
\[r=\frac{Y_1-Y_2}{Y_1+Y_2},\]
\[t=\frac{2Y_1}{Y_1+Y_2}.\]

For propagating waves the normal component of mean energy flux is \(Y|E_\parallel|^2/2\). Hence \(R=|r|^2\) and \(T=(Y_2/Y_1)|t|^2\). In a lossless interface \(R+T=1\). Some conventions reverse the reflected p-polarisation unit vector and therefore reverse the sign called \(r_p\). Comparing tangential components explicitly removes that ambiguity.

Worked oblique reading

For air to glass with \(n_1=1.0\), \(n_2=1.5\) at \(45^\circ\), Snell’s law gives

\[\theta_t=28.13^\circ.\]

Dropping the common factor \(1/Z_0\), the s admittances are 0.707 and 1.323. Their reflection amplitude is \(-0.303\), giving 9.20% reflected power. The p admittances are 1.414 and 1.701. Their tangential reflection amplitude is \(-0.0920\), giving 0.847%. Giving only one reflectance for an unpolarised beam would hide this nearly elevenfold difference. At normal incidence the two admittances coincide for each medium, providing a sign and magnitude check.

Find the angle that cancels one reflected component

An interface is reflection-free for p polarisation when \(n_1/\cos\theta_i=n_2/\cos\theta_t\). Combine this condition with Snell’s law for distinct indices to get

\[\theta_i+\theta_t=\pi/2,\]
\[\tan\theta_B=n_2/n_1.\]

At the air–glass interface this angle is \(56.31^\circ\). A small index change shifts that angular minimum, making a polarised measurement a way to infer index. Absorption introduces a complex admittance and generally turns the exact zero into a finite minimum.

Keep phase matching beyond the critical angle

For incidence from large to small index, \(k_\parallel\) can exceed the magnitude \(n_2\omega/c\) allowed for medium 2. Solve the dispersion relation there for the normal wave number:

\[k_{z,2}^2=(n_2\omega/c)^2-k_\parallel^2,\]
\[k_{z,2}=i\kappa,\]
\[\kappa=\frac{2\pi}{\lambda_0}\sqrt{n_1^2\sin^2\theta_i-n_2^2}.\]

The positive imaginary branch gives decay into \(z>0\). For a single such interface \(Y_2\) is imaginary, so \(|r|=1\); a reactive magnetic-to-electric ratio means zero average normal flux there. A field still extends into the second medium and can carry energy parallel to the surface. Another material brought within a decay length changes the boundary problem and can enable transmission.

Worked length-scale distinction

For \(n_1=1.5,n_2=1.0,\theta_i=50^\circ,\lambda_0=600\) nm, the critical angle is \(41.81^\circ\). The amplitude length \(1/\kappa\) is 169 nm. Intensity follows squared field and therefore falls by \(e\) over 84.3 nm. A detector using intensity must state which length it reports. Close to the critical angle the penetration length becomes large; finite beams then sample a range of angles around the ideal plane-wave value.

Find a polarisation zero and the onset of total reflection

Air into glass of index 1.5 gives a p-polarised reflection zero at 56.3°. Reverse the indices, predict the critical angle, then inspect what happens to each reflected power fraction as incidence becomes more oblique.

Open this experiment online

Read an amplitude measurement correctly

How can a transmitted field exceed the incident amplitude?

At normal incidence from index 1.8 to 1.2, calculate the reflected and transmitted tangential electric amplitudes and powers.

Work through the solution

Here \(r=(1.8-1.2)/(1.8+1.2)=0.20\), \(t=1.20\). Reflected power fraction is 0.04. The transmitted power fraction is

\[(1.2/1.8)(1.20)^2=0.96.\]

The reduced wave admittance converts the larger electric amplitude to a smaller power than the incident beam.

Find the angular acceptance of a total-reflection measurement

A liquid has unknown index \(n\). Light is incident from known glass of index 1.60, and total internal reflection first appears at \(57.0^\circ\pm0.2^\circ\). Infer \(n\) and a first-order uncertainty.

Work through the solution

The grazing transmitted wave obeys \(n=1.60\sin57.0^\circ=1.342\). Differentiation gives

\[dn=1.60\cos57.0^\circ d\theta,\]

with \(d\theta\) in radians. The quoted angular interval corresponds to about 0.0030 in index. Index uncertainty of the glass would add another contribution.

Oblique interfaces and films whose reflections cancel · Waves, radiation and relativity

A film only one quarter of a wavelength thick can suppress reflection from a transparent surface. Follow the boundary conditions all the way from an oblique incident wave to the input admittance of a stack, then calculate how much reflection returns when the wavelength, angle or layer order changes.

Chapter 22 · Why dispersion and absorption belong together

Obtain complex permittivity from a damped charge, relate its imaginary part to heating and distinguish wave crests, envelopes and a causal change in a signal.

Replace an instantaneous spring constant by a delayed response

A static dielectric constant is measured after the material has relaxed. At optical frequencies the bound charges have inertia and damping. Model a density \(N\) of independent bound charges of mass \(m\), charge \(q\), natural angular frequency \(\omega_0\) and damping rate \(\gamma>0\). A weak field gives a displacement satisfying \(m\ddot x+m\gamma\dot x+m\omega_0^2x=qE(t)\). The resulting polarisation is \(P=Nqx\). This model assumes small displacements and an isotropic response. A crystal with several resonances needs additional modes and oscillator strengths.

For a sinusoidal field with the convention \(e^{-i\omega t}\), differentiation multiplies a phasor by \(-i\omega\). Dividing the equation by its dynamic stiffness gives

\[\chi(\omega)=\frac{P}{\epsilon_0E}=\frac{\omega_p^2}{\omega_0^2-\omega^2-i\gamma\omega},\]
\[\omega_p^2=\frac{Nq^2}{m\epsilon_0}.\]

Rationalise the denominator using \(A=\omega_0^2-\omega^2,\ B=\gamma\omega\). Then \(\chi'=\omega_p^2A/(A^2+B^2)\) and \(\chi''=\omega_p^2B/(A^2+B^2)\). The real part changes sign across the resonance. The imaginary part stays positive at positive frequencies with our convention. In the low-frequency limit the static spring law reappears,

\[\chi(0)=\omega_p^2/\omega_0^2.\]

Decide which part of the response dissipates work

The field delivers power density \(E\dot P\) to the bound charges. The polarisation current phasor is \(-i\omega\epsilon_0\chi E\). For peak-amplitude phasors the cycle average of two real oscillating quantities is half the real part of one phasor times the complex conjugate of the other. Thus

\[\langle E\dot P\rangle=\tfrac12\omega\epsilon_0\chi''|E|^2 .\]

This result also follows by multiplying the oscillator equation by \(N\dot x\). The kinetic and spring energy changes integrate to zero over one steady period, leaving \(Nm\gamma\langle\dot x^2\rangle\) as heat. Positive loss therefore has a mechanical interpretation independent of any phasor notation. Changing to an \(e^{+i\omega t}\) convention reverses the sign attached to the imaginary part, while the heat remains positive.

Worked response at resonance

Take \(\omega_p^2=0.20\,\omega_0^2\) and \(\gamma=0.10\,\omega_0\). At \(\omega=\omega_0\), \(A=0\) and \(\chi=2i\). If \(\omega_0=2.0\times10^{12}\) rad/s and \(E=100\) V/m peak, the absorbed power density is \(1.77\times10^5\) W/m³. This is local power where the field has that amplitude. Applying it throughout a thick absorbing slab would neglect attenuation of the field with depth.

Recover the actual lengths and speeds in a material

For relative permeability one and a plane wave \(e^{ikz-i\omega t}\),

\[k=(\omega/c)\sqrt{1+\chi}.\]

Choose \(n=n'+i\kappa\) with \(\kappa\ge0\) for a passive medium. The field amplitude decays as \(e^{-\omega\kappa z/c}\) and intensity as \(e^{-2\omega\kappa z/c}\). At the resonance of the previous example, \(1+\chi=1+2i\). Equating real and imaginary parts of the squared index gives

\[n'^2-\kappa^2=1,\]
\[2n'\kappa=2,\]
\[n'=\sqrt{\tfrac12(\sqrt5+1)},\]
\[\kappa=\sqrt{\tfrac12(\sqrt5-1)} .\]

Here \(n'=1.272,\ \kappa=0.786\). At the stated angular frequency the intensity attenuation length \(c/(2\omega\kappa)=95.3\,\mu{\rm m}\). A finite slab also reflects at its surfaces. Inferring bulk loss from transmitted power alone requires accounting for those reflections.

For a narrow packet, expand the real propagation constant around its carrier:

\[k'(\omega)\simeq k'_c+(\omega-\omega_c)\,dk'/d\omega,\]

where \(k'\) here denotes the real part of \(k\). The carrier phase moves at \(\omega_c/k'_c\). If attenuation and curvature vary little across the packet bandwidth, the envelope delay over length \(L\) is \(L\,dk'/d\omega\). Strong frequency-selective loss can reshape the peak so much that tracking it no longer measures the arrival of new information.

Link the two parts of susceptibility through causality

A causal linear material obeys \(P(t)=\epsilon_0\int_0^\infty h(\tau)E(t-\tau)\,d\tau\). Its susceptibility for our convention is \(\int_0^\infty h(\tau)e^{i\omega\tau}d\tau\). For a decaying response this expression is analytic when \({\rm Im}\,\omega>0\). Closing a contour in that half plane relates real and imaginary components by principal-value integrals. For a response decaying at large frequency one useful form is

\[\chi'(\omega)=\frac2\pi\,{\cal P}\int_0^\infty\frac{\omega'\chi''(\omega')}{\omega'^2-\omega^2}\,d\omega'.\]

Thus a narrow absorption band contributes to index variation at frequencies where the local absorption is small. A measurement over a short spectral window cannot uniquely evaluate the integral without information about loss outside it. The damped-oscillator poles lie below the real axis, as the causal convention requires.

Change the damping of a bound charge

Track the in-phase and out-of-phase parts of one oscillator response. With strength 0.50 and damping 0.20 in the plotted units, the absorptive part at resonance is 2.50. Compare that point with the frequency of maximum absorption as damping increases.

Open this experiment online

Use attenuation and loss as independent checks

Infer an extinction coefficient

After correcting for both surfaces, a liquid transmits 25% of its incident intensity in 0.50 mm at vacuum wavelength 1.00 µm. Find \(\kappa\) and the field-amplitude ratio.

Work through the solution

With \(T=\exp(-4\pi\kappa L/\lambda_0)\),

\[\kappa=-\lambda_0\ln(0.25)/(4\pi L)=2.21\times10^{-4}.\]

The amplitude ratio is

\[\sqrt T=0.50.\]

Using the amplitude decay law on intensity would overestimate \(\kappa\) by a factor of two.

Recover the conductivity limit

Set \(\omega_0=0\) in the charge model and express the response as \(J=\sigma E\). Find the low-frequency real conductivity.

Work through the solution

Using \(J=-i\omega P\) yields

\[\sigma(\omega)=\epsilon_0\omega_p^2/(\gamma-i\omega).\]

At \(\omega\ll\gamma\),

\[\sigma\simeq\epsilon_0\omega_p^2/\gamma=Nq^2/(m\gamma).\]

The absence of a restoring force lets charges drift steadily instead of settling to a finite static polarisation.

An optical pulse entering a transparent slab is delayed, broadened and sometimes reshaped. Derive these effects from the motion of bound charge, and learn what a measured group delay actually says about a pulse carrying information.

Chapter 23 · Potentials, gauge freedom and the arrival of a signal

When a source changes at noon, which part of its history can affect a detector at twelve o’clock and one nanosecond? The answer emerges from Maxwell’s equations once we specify both the source and the boundary condition in time.

Why introduce two potentials?

A magnetic field with zero divergence can, on a contractible region, be written as \(\mathbf B=\nabla\times\mathbf A\). Faraday's law then says that \(\mathbf E+\partial_t\mathbf A\) has zero curl. Define its scalar potential as \(-\nabla\phi\). These two definitions solve the homogeneous Maxwell equations identically. Two inhomogeneous equations still determine how charge and current generate the fields. The potentials contain more components than necessary. For any smooth function \(\chi\), put

\[\mathbf A'=\mathbf A+\nabla\chi,\]
\[\phi'=\phi-\partial_t\chi.\]

The curl of a gradient vanishes. The two extra terms in the electric field cancel because mixed derivatives commute. This freedom lets us choose which equations to solve while keeping every force measurement identical.

Background · Retarded time
\[t-t_r=|\mathbf r-\mathbf r_s(t_r)|/c\]

The source is evaluated at emission. For a moving source its location on the right also depends on the unknown emission time.

Uncoupling the field equations

Insert the potentials into Gauss's law. This gives

\[\nabla^2\phi+\partial_t\nabla\cdot\mathbf A=-\rho/\epsilon_0.\]

Now substitute them in Ampère–Maxwell and use the curl-of-curl identity. Keeping the gradient terms together gives

\[(\nabla^2-c^{-2}\partial_t^2)\mathbf A=-\mu_0\mathbf J+\nabla(\nabla\cdot\mathbf A+c^{-2}\partial_t\phi).\]

Choose the Lorenz condition \(\nabla\cdot\mathbf A+c^{-2}\partial_t\phi=0\). A gauge transformation can achieve it by solving the scalar wave equation for \(\chi\) with the negative of the original condition as source. Both potentials then obey wave equations with the same propagation speed. Under this choice, charge continuity is essential. Applying the wave operator to the Lorenz condition returns \(-\mu_0(\nabla\cdot\mathbf J+\partial_t\rho)\), which vanishes for a conserved source. Residual gauge functions obey the homogeneous wave equation.

Constructing the retarded kernel

In a source-free spherical shell a radial scalar field \(\psi\) obeys \(\partial_r^2(r\psi)=c^{-2}\partial_t^2(r\psi)\). The one-dimensional equation has an outgoing branch \(r\psi=f(t-r/c)\) and an incoming branch \(g(t+r/c)\). An isolated source with no incident wave selects the outgoing branch. The response to an instantaneous impulse is supported at \(t=r/c\). Its spatial normalisation follows by integrating the static kernel over a tiny sphere, where \(-\nabla^2(1/4\pi r)=\delta^3(\mathbf r)\). The causal kernel is therefore \(\delta(t-r/c)/(4\pi r)\). Integrating the source over time removes the delta function:

\[\phi(\mathbf x,t)=\frac{1}{4\pi\epsilon_0}\int \frac{\rho(\mathbf x',t-R/c)}{R}\,d^3x',\]
\[\mathbf A(\mathbf x,t)=\frac{\mu_0}{4\pi}\int \frac{\mathbf J(\mathbf x',t-R/c)}{R}\,d^3x',\]
\[R=|\mathbf x-\mathbf x'|.\]

Every volume element contributes at its own source time. If an incident wave is already present, add its homogeneous solution. In Coulomb gauge the scalar potential instead satisfies an instantaneous Poisson equation. Its instantaneous contribution to \(-\nabla\phi\) combines with \(-\partial_t\mathbf A\) to give the same causal electric field.

Two calculations with potentials

A pulse recorded at two distances

Measure an isolated outgoing spherical wave component in a source-free exterior. At radius \(0.30\) m its field trace peaks at \(10.0\) ns. At \(1.80\) m its peak arrives \(1.50/c=5.00\) ns later. The peak amplitude is \(0.30/1.80=1/6\) of the first. Multiplying each trace by its radius removes spreading. Shifting the second trace back by \(5.00\) ns then superposes them. For an electromagnetic dipole these statements describe its outgoing transverse radiation term along the same ray. Reactive near-field terms have different radial dependences.

Two vector potentials for a uniform field

For a constant magnetic field \(B\hat{\mathbf z}\) one choice is \(\mathbf A=Bx\hat{\mathbf y}\), \(\phi=0\). Choose \(\chi=-Bxy/2\). Its gradient adds \(-By\hat{\mathbf x}/2-Bx\hat{\mathbf y}/2\), giving \(\mathbf A'=(-By\hat{\mathbf x}+Bx\hat{\mathbf y})/2\). Its curl has \(z\) component \(B/2-(-B/2)=B\). The line integrals around any closed loop match because the integral of the added gradient is zero.

Compare the arrival of a compact pulse at two radii

This source-free outgoing component has a finite start and finish. A 1.80 m detector records the front 5.00 ns after a 0.30 m detector and measures one sixth of its amplitude. Can changing the pulse duration change either observation?

Problem sheet · delays and a time-dependent gauge

A finite source

Two ends of a source are 12 cm apart along a detector's line of sight. Bound the difference in retarded source times. At what frequency does the corresponding maximum phase span reach one radian?

Work through the solution

The triangle inequality gives \(|R_1-R_2|\leq0.12\) m. Thus \(\Delta t\leq0.400\) ns. For a harmonic source the maximum phase difference is \(2\pi f\Delta t\). One radian requires \(f=398\) MHz approximately. Well below that frequency one common retarded time can be accurate for this part of the phase. A dipole approximation also requires a source small compared with the observation distance.

A gauge with a time derivative

Start with zero potentials. Set \(\chi=\alpha xt\), where \(\alpha\) is constant. Determine both transformed potentials and check the fields.

Work through the solution

The new potentials are \(\mathbf A'=\alpha t\hat{\mathbf x}\) and \(\phi'=-\alpha x\). Hence \(-\nabla\phi'=+\alpha\hat{\mathbf x}\) and \(-\partial_t\mathbf A'=-\alpha\hat{\mathbf x}\). Their sum and the curl of the spatially uniform vector potential are both zero. The example also satisfies the Lorenz condition, consistent with \(\chi\) solving the homogeneous wave equation.

Chapter 24 · A moving charge, its retarded position and its radiation

A moving source moves while its field travels. Finding its position on the past light cone supplies an extra factor in its potential and explains why an accelerated charge can carry energy to arbitrarily large distances.

Liénard–Wiechert potentials from the emission event

Let the charge follow the prescribed path \(\mathbf z(s)\). At time \(t\) and detector position \(\mathbf x\), define \(R(s)=|\mathbf x-\mathbf z(s)|\) and \(\mathbf n=(\mathbf x-\mathbf z)/R\). The emission time \(s\) solves \(h(s)=s+R(s)/c-t=0\). Differentiate to obtain

\[h'=1-\mathbf n\cdot\boldsymbol\beta=\kappa,\]

with \(\boldsymbol\beta=\dot{\mathbf z}/c\). For a subluminal charge \(\kappa>0\), so the root is unique when it exists. Two emissions a time \(ds\) apart arrive only \(\kappa ds\) apart. Looking forwards along a fast charge's path shortens this interval.

Insert \(\rho=q\delta^3(\mathbf x'-\mathbf z(s))\) into the spacetime integral for the retarded potential. Integrate over \(\mathbf x'\) first. The remaining integral is proportional to \(\int ds\,\delta(h(s))/R(s)\). Changing variable from \(s\) to \(h\) introduces \(1/\kappa\). With the current density \(q\dot{\mathbf z}\delta^3(\mathbf x'-\mathbf z)\), the same argument yields the vector potential:

\[\phi=\frac{q}{4\pi\epsilon_0}\left[\frac{1}{\kappa R}\right]_{\rm ret},\]
\[\mathbf A=\left[\frac{\mathbf v}{c^2}\right]_{\rm ret}\phi .\]

Simply replacing the position of a static charge with its retarded position misses the Jacobian. Both the geometry and the current vary when taking derivatives of these potentials.

Distinguish persistent and radiative parts

Implicit differentiation of \(h=0\) gives

\[\partial_t s=1/\kappa,\]
\[\nabla s=-\mathbf n/(c\kappa).\]

Apply these identities in \(-\nabla\phi-\partial_t\mathbf A\). Derivatives of the velocity supply an acceleration term, while the remainder can be expressed using the retarded velocity and geometry:

\[\mathbf E=\frac{q}{4\pi\epsilon_0}\left[\frac{(1-\beta^2)(\mathbf n-\boldsymbol\beta)}{\kappa^3R^2}+\frac{\mathbf n\times[(\mathbf n-\boldsymbol\beta)\times\dot{\boldsymbol\beta}]}{c\kappa^3R}\right]_{\rm ret},\]
\[\mathbf B=\frac{\mathbf n\times\mathbf E}{c}.\]

A detector subtends a fixed solid angle with area proportional to \(R^2\). The square of the first field falls as \(R^{-4}\) and its flux through the detector vanishes at large radius. The second field is transverse and its square falls as \(R^{-2}\), so finite power travels to infinity. Uniform motion leaves only the first term.

Recover the nonrelativistic radiation law

For \(\beta\ll1\), \(\kappa\simeq1\). If \(\theta\) is measured from the acceleration, the radiative electric-field magnitude is \(q a\sin\theta/(4\pi\epsilon_0c^2R)\) in absolute value. Its magnetic partner has magnitude \(E/c\). Therefore the outward Poynting flux is \(\epsilon_0cE^2\), and integration over a distant sphere gives

\[\frac{dP}{d\Omega}=\frac{q^2a^2}{16\pi^2\epsilon_0c^3}\sin^2\theta,\]
\[P=\frac{q^2a^2}{6\pi\epsilon_0c^3}.\]

The angular factor integrates to \(2\pi\int_0^\pi\sin^3\theta\,d\theta=8\pi/3\). At finite speed with acceleration parallel to velocity, the vector triple product in the numerator has magnitude \((a/c)\sin\theta\). The flux per unit arrival time contains \(\kappa^{-6}\). Converting to power per unit emission time multiplies by \(dt/ds=\kappa\), leaving the angular dependence \(\sin^2\theta/(1-\beta\cos\theta)^5\). The distinction matters whenever emissions bunch up at the detector.

Reading charge motion from a signal

A moving source changes its pulse spacing

A charge moving at \(0.60c\) directly toward a distant observer emits two brief disturbances \(2.0\) ns apart in the lab frame. It travels \(0.36\) m between emissions. The second propagation time is shorter by \(1.2\) ns, leaving an arrival interval of \(0.80\) ns. Viewed from behind, the interval is \(3.2\) ns. This calculation concerns arrival times. An observer exactly along a parallel acceleration sees zero radiation in that direction.

How much power misses the polar caps?

For a slow charge, collect radiation at angles \(60^\circ\leq\theta\leq120^\circ\). Put \(u=\cos\theta\). The collected fraction is

\[\int_{-1/2}^{1/2}(1-u^2)\,du/(4/3)=11/16.\]

This equatorial belt spans half the solid angle but receives 68.75% of the power. Integrating with respect to \(\theta\) alone would overcount the polar regions.

Track the brightest direction of an accelerating charge

The two angular curves are each normalised to their own maximum. For parallel acceleration and β = 0.60, the maximum moves from 90° to about 31.8°. Compare peak location and the separately reported unnormalised peak height.
