Problem sheet · inversion and beaming

Solve a retarded time

A charge moves along \(z=0.4cs\). At \(t=0\) a detector at \(z=3.0\) m receives its field. Find the emission time and the distance travelled by the signal.

Work through the solution

Before arrival the charge is behind the origin. Here \(R=3.0-0.4cs\) in metres, so \(0=0.6s+3.0/c\). The emission time is \(-16.7\) ns, at \(z=-2.0\) m. The propagation distance is 5.0 m. Using the current separation would predict only \(10.0\) ns of travel.

Locate the angular maximum

For parallel acceleration differentiate \(F(u)=(1-u^2)/(1-\beta u)^5\), \(u=\cos\theta\), and predict the maximum for \(\beta=0.6\).

Work through the solution

The numerator of \(F'\), after dropping positive factors, is \(5\beta-2u-3\beta u^2\). The physical root is \(u=5\beta/(1+\sqrt{1+15\beta^2})\). At 0.6 it equals 0.850, giving \(\theta\simeq31.8^\circ\). The other root lies outside the physical interval. At zero speed the limiting angle is \(90^\circ\), matching the dipole pattern.

Practicum · distinguish a large near field from outgoing power

A neutral dipole of size much less than the wavelength oscillates with complex moment \(p\,\hat{\mathbf z}\) at angular frequency \(\omega\). Two probes lie in its equatorial plane. An experimentalist proposes to estimate outgoing power as \(\epsilon_0c|E_\theta|^2/2\) times detector area at each radius. Is this plane-wave calibration valid close to the source? Compare field amplitudes, phases and a conserved flux before forming an opinion.

Recover the two equatorial fields from potentials

Use \(e^{-i\omega t}\), \(k=\omega/c\), \(x=kr\), and the Lorenz-gauge dipole potentials \(\phi=p\cos\theta\,(1-ikr)e^{ikr}/(4\pi\epsilon_0r^2)\),

\[\mathbf A=-i\mu_0\omega p\,e^{ikr}\hat{\mathbf z}/(4\pi r).\]

Recover \(E_\theta\) and \(B_\phi\) at \(\theta=\pi/2\).

Follow the calculation and check the result

At the equator \(\hat{\mathbf z}=-\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}\). Applying \(-r^{-1}\partial_\theta\) to the scalar potential gives \(p(1-ix)e^{ix}/(4\pi\epsilon_0r^3)\). The vector part \(i\omega A_\theta\) adds \(-p x^2 e^{ix}/(4\pi\epsilon_0r^3)\). Define the common complex scale \(K=p e^{ix}/(4\pi\epsilon_0r^3)\). Then

\[E_\theta=K(1-ix-x^2),\]
\[c B_\phi=K(-ix-x^2).\]

For the magnetic field use \(\nabla\times[f(r)\hat{\mathbf z}]=f'(r)\hat{\mathbf r}\times\hat{\mathbf z}\) with \(f=-i\mu_0\omega p\,e^{ikr}/(4\pi r)\). Both fields contain induction and radiation terms. The extra electrostatic term appears only in \(E_\theta\). It prevents the local field impedance from equalling the plane-wave value.

Find what two phase-sensitive probes would report

Multiply \(E_\theta(cB_\phi)^*\), retaining both quadratures. Determine the mean outward energy flux. How quickly does the out-of-phase component disappear relative to it?

Follow the calculation and check the result

The complex product is \(|K|^2(1-ix-x^2)(ix-x^2)=|K|^2(x^4+ix)\). Radiation measurements average real instantaneous products, so the mean radial flux is \(\epsilon_0c|K|^2x^4/2\), proportional to \(r^{-2}\) at every radius outside the ideal source. The imaginary component of the complex Poynting vector measures quadrature exchange; its ratio to the real part is \(x^{-3}\) in this convention. It does not add a second time-averaged outward power.

At \(kr=0.50\) the quadrature component is eight times the real part. At \(kr=2.00\) it is one eighth. A spherical integral restores the angular factor \(\sin^2\theta\) and area \(r^2\), yielding \(\omega^4|p|^2/(12\pi\epsilon_0c^3)\), independent of radius. This checks the result against the dipole radiation formula while retaining the full near-zone amplitudes.

Quantify the bias of an electric-only reading

Compute the ratio of the proposed plane-wave estimate to the true mean radial flux for the two probes. Design a measurement that can separate reactive and radiative fields.

Follow the calculation and check the result

The ratio is

\[|1-ix-x^2|^2/x^4=1-x^{-2}+x^{-4}.\]

It is 13 at \(x=0.5\): a large electric field can coexist with comparatively little outward energy transport. At \(x=2\) the ratio is 0.8125; the same calibration now underestimates the flux by 18.75%. A monotonic intuition based on discarding all inverse powers except \(1/r\) can even miss the sign of the error.

For a phase-sensitive measurement, record \(E_\theta\) and \(B_\phi\) against the same clock, form the real part of their cross-product and compare \(r^2\langle S_r\rangle\) at several radii. Simultaneously examine the imaginary-to-real ratio and check its \(r^{-3}\) trend. For a finite-sized source keep the closest probe outside the source and test the dipole approximation by changing the observation angle. Other multipoles or a reflected wave break the simple three-term model.

Chapter 25 · Changing observers and classifying electromagnetic fields

Can an observer move so that a measured electric field disappears? Two numbers constructed from the fields settle the question before a velocity is chosen. The moving observer's force measurements explain why the classification works.

Measure fields at the same event

Take two inertial laboratories with parallel axes. The primed laboratory moves with constant velocity \(v\hat{\mathbf x}\) relative to the unprimed one. Compare fields at one spacetime event. The position labels and times assigned to that event differ by \(x'=\gamma(x-vt)\) and \(t'=\gamma(t-vx/c^2)\), where \(\gamma=(1-v^2/c^2)^{-1/2}\). Comparing both experiments at identical numerical position and time labels would usually compare different events.

How can a primed observer measure \(E'_y\)? Release a probe initially at rest in the primed frame. In the unprimed frame the probe has velocity \(v\hat{\mathbf x}\), so its transverse force is \(q(E_y-vB_z)\). The transverse momentum \(p_y\) is invariant under this boost, but along the probe's instantaneous trajectory \(dt'=dt/\gamma\). Thus \(dp'_y/dt'=\gamma dp_y/dt\), and \(E'_y=\gamma(E_y-vB_z)\). The other transverse component is \(E'_z=\gamma(E_z+vB_y)\). Longitudinal electric field is unchanged. A probe with adjustable primed velocity can also distinguish the magnetic force. The complete pair of rules is

\[\mathbf E'_\parallel=\mathbf E_\parallel,\]
\[\mathbf B'_\parallel=\mathbf B_\parallel,\]
\[\mathbf E'_\perp=\gamma(\mathbf E_\perp+\mathbf v\times\mathbf B),\]
\[\mathbf B'_\perp=\gamma(\mathbf B_\perp-\mathbf v\times\mathbf E/c^2).\]

Which differences survive a boost?

Examine perpendicular laboratory fields \(E_y=E\), \(cB_z=b\). In their common units the transformed pair is \(e'=\gamma(E-\beta b)\),

\[b'=\gamma(b-\beta E).\]

Squaring and subtracting cancels the cross terms. The factor \(\gamma^2(1-\beta^2)\) is unity. In a general orientation the parallel parts remain unchanged and the other pair of transverse components cancels in the same manner. The scalar product also remains unchanged. The two invariants are

\[I_1=|\mathbf E|^2-c^2|\mathbf B|^2,\]
\[I_2=\mathbf E\cdot\mathbf B .\]

If \(I_2\neq0\), neither field can be transformed away. For nonzero orthogonal fields with \(I_1<0\), choose \(\mathbf v=\mathbf E\times\mathbf B/B^2\). Its speed is \(E/B<c\), and it cancels \(\mathbf E'\). If \(I_1>0\) choose \(\mathbf v=c^2\mathbf E\times\mathbf B/E^2\) to cancel \(\mathbf B'\). For nonzero orthogonal fields of equal strength in common units the required speed would be \(c\). A plane wave illustrates this null case. A zero field also has both invariants zero, so both vanishing invariants alone do not prove that a wave is present.

Two changes of observer

An observer travelling with drifting charges

Let \(E_y=1.80\times10^5\) V/m and \(B_z=1.00\) mT. The cancelling velocity is \(+1.80\times10^8\) m/s along \(x\), approximately \(0.600c\). Then \(B'_z=B_z\sqrt{1-E^2/(cB_z)^2}\simeq0.800\) mT. A charge moving with that primed laboratory feels zero force at the chosen event. In the laboratory, the electric and magnetic terms cancel directly. The statements concern one probe velocity; charges moving differently in the primed frame can experience magnetic force.

Devices following a light pulse

A plane pulse travelling in \(+x\) has \(E_y=cB_z\). A detector moving along \(+x\) measures

\[E'_y/E_y=\gamma(1-\beta)=\sqrt{(1-\beta)/(1+\beta)}.\]

At \(\beta=0.60\) this is \(1/2\), and the intensity ratio is \(1/4\). Transform a phase \(kx-\omega t\) using \(k=\omega/c\). Its frequency receives the same factor \(1/2\). Both detectors obtain \(E'/B'=c\).

Why a neutral wire can have a charge density

For enclosed charge to agree between inertial descriptions, the charge and current densities must form the four-current \(J^\mu=(c\rho,\mathbf J)\). A boost gives

\[\rho'=\gamma(\rho-vJ_x/c^2),\]
\[J'_x=\gamma(J_x-v\rho).\]

For equal positive and negative charge densities producing a laboratory current, \(\rho=0\) but \(J_x\neq0\). In the moving laboratory the densities do not cancel. The change comes from how a simultaneous spatial slice intersects the worldlines of moving charge. Dividing a fixed list of particles by a contracted segment while keeping its endpoint events fixed would miscount particles crossing either endpoint.

Find a frame that cancels a field by varying its velocity

The axes are oriented as in the crossed-field derivation. For perpendicular fields E = 90 and cB = 150 kV/m, a boost at 0.60c cancels E and leaves cB′ = 120 kV/m. Exchange the two inputs and predict which field can now vanish.

Open this experiment online

Problem sheet · classification and measurements

Classify before calculating

Take a field with \(\mathbf E=E_0\hat{\mathbf y}\) and \(c\mathbf B=2E_0\hat{\mathbf y}+E_0\hat{\mathbf z}\). Could either field disappear? Explain why consulting the difference of squares alone gives incomplete information.

Work through the solution

The magnetic magnitude is \(\sqrt{5}E_0/c\), making \(I_1=-4E_0^2\). However \(I_2=2E_0^2/c\neq0\). A frame with either field zero would have \(I_2=0\), contradicting its observed invariant value.

A density reconstructed from a current

A laboratory measures \(\rho=0\) and \(J_x=9.0\) A/m². A second lab moves at \(0.60c\). Determine its current density and charge density, including signs.

Work through the solution

Here \(\gamma=1.25\). The transformed current is \(+11.25\) A/m². The transformed density is \(-1.25(0.60)(9.0)/c=-2.25\times10^{-8}\) C/m³. Inserting these into \(c^2\rho'^2-J_x'^2\) returns \(-81\) in squared current-density units, a check independent of sign conventions in the voltage probes.

Practicum · reconstruct a crossed-field trajectory from two clocks

A positron initially rests in a laboratory with uniform crossed fields \(\mathbf B=B\hat{\mathbf z}\),

\[\mathbf E=E\hat{\mathbf y},\]

with \(B=10.0\) mT and \(E/(cB)=0.600\). Ignore radiation losses and edge effects. Predict its maximum speed, arrival point after one cycle, and energy gain halfway through the cycle. Work by transforming whole events between observers. A velocity transformation alone cannot predict the travel time.

Choose the frame in which the trajectory is simplest

Find a frame with zero electric field, transform the initial particle velocity, and derive the orbit radius and frequency in that frame. Define what a “cycle” means for this measurement.

Follow the calculation and check the result

Boost along \(+x\) at \(v_d=E/B=0.600c\) with \(\gamma_d=1.25\). Then \(E'_y=0\) and \(B'_z=B/\gamma_d=8.00\) mT. Initially the particle has \(v'_x=-v_d\), so its primed energy is constant at \(\gamma_dmc^2\). With positive charge \(e\), its initial magnetic force points towards \(+y\). Defining \(\Omega'=eB'/(\gamma_dm)\) and \(R'=\gamma_dm v_d/(eB')\), one obtains

\[x'=-R'\sin(\Omega't'),\]
\[y'=R'[1-\cos(\Omega't')].\]

Differentiating verifies the initial velocity and yields the rotating transverse acceleration. The primed radius is approximately 0.160 m and the primed period \(T'=2\pi/\Omega'\) is 5.58 ns. One cycle means two successive events at which the primed particle returns to its initial location and velocity. In the laboratory these events occur at different positions.

Measure time and the maximum lab speed

Transform the coordinates of the first return event to the laboratory. At what part of its orbit does the particle reach its maximum lab speed? Why is it incorrect to use a single constant \(\gamma_d\) to convert every subinterval along the curved path?

Follow the calculation and check the result

For a full primed period \(\Delta x'=0\). The inverse Lorentz transformation gives

\[\Delta t=\gamma_dT'=6.98\,\mathrm{ns},\]
\[\Delta x=\gamma_dv_dT'=1.26\,\mathrm{m}.\]

Hence the average lab drift is \(0.600c\) along \(+x\). For an arbitrary subinterval the formula is instead \(\Delta t=\gamma_d(\Delta t'+v_d\Delta x'/c^2)\). Away from rest or half-period endpoints its second term generally contributes.

The primed momentum has largest positive \(x'\) component at half a period, when \(v'_x=v_d\). Then \(v_x=2v_d/(1+v_d^2/c^2)=0.88235c\), \(v_y=0\). The lab energy transformation \(\mathcal E=\gamma_d(\mathcal E'+v_dp'_x)\) confirms that this is the energy maximum and hence the speed maximum. At the end of a period the particle returns to laboratory rest even though the apparatus has seen a net displacement.

Check the energy with an independent voltage measurement

At half a cycle compute the work performed by the actual laboratory electric field from the displacement alone. Compare with the relativistic kinetic energy and explain how it can be zero over a whole cycle.

Follow the calculation and check the result

At the top of the primed orbit \(y'=2R'\). A boost along \(x\) leaves \(y=2R'\) unchanged. The electric work is \(eE(2R')=2\gamma_d^2\beta_d^2mc^2=1.125mc^2\), or about 575 keV. The lab maximum speed gives \(\gamma_{\max}=(1+\beta_d^2)/(1-\beta_d^2)=2.125\), so its kinetic energy is the same \(1.125mc^2\). The magnetic force performs zero work throughout. During the second half the particle moves back down in \(y\), and the electric field removes exactly this kinetic energy.

At a fixed laboratory event a numerical trajectory can be checked against both \(\mathcal E-mc^2=eEy\) and the parametric orbit. Comparing the two paths at equal numerical values of \(t\) and \(t'\) would compare different events and could create apparent errors in both period and speed. At each successive cusp the lab velocity momentarily vanishes; the motion on either side reverses its transverse component. The cusp spacing supplies an additional check on the drift distance.

Study the full derivation

What different observers measure · Waves, radiation and relativity

A moving observer carries clocks, rulers and a calibrated test charge. A statement about the electric field must specify which observer held that test charge at rest. In this chapter we derive how different measurements can agree on the force law and yet assign different electric fields, magnetic fields and charge densities to the same physical apparatus. A current-carrying wire and a light pulse will provide independent checks.

Chapter 26 · From local symmetry to Maxwell’s equations

Some electromagnetic equations describe the geometry of a potential. Others describe its response to charge. Tensor notation identifies the distinction precisely, and a variational argument shows why the source must obey a local conservation law.

Build an antisymmetric tensor from four potentials

Write \(x^\mu=(ct,x,y,z)\), \(\eta_{\mu\nu}=\operatorname{diag}(1,-1,-1,-1)\),

\[A^\mu=(\phi/c,\mathbf A),\]
\[J^\mu=(c\rho,\mathbf J).\]

Greek indices run from 0 to 3 and repeated upper and lower indices are summed. Lowering a spatial index changes its sign. Thus

\[\partial^\mu=(c^{-1}\partial_t,-\nabla).\]

This convention fixes every sign below.

Form \(F^{\mu\nu}=\partial^\mu A^\nu-\partial^\nu A^\mu\). Then

\[F^{0i}=\partial_t A_i^{\rm cart}/c+\partial_i\phi/c=-E_i^{\rm cart}/c.\]

For spatial components \(F^{12}=-\partial_x A_y+\partial_y A_x=-B_z\) with Cartesian subscripts on the right. Antisymmetry leaves six independent quantities. These are the three electric and three magnetic components. Adding a four-gradient to the potential leaves \(F\) unchanged because its mixed derivatives commute.

Unpack the two tensor equations

Consider \(\partial_\mu F^{\mu\nu}=\mu_0J^\nu\). For \(\nu=0\) the only terms are spatial:

\[\partial_iF^{i0}=\nabla\cdot\mathbf E/c=\mu_0c\rho,\]

which is Gauss's law. For \(\nu=1\), \(F^{01}=-E_x/c\), \(F^{21}=B_z\), \(F^{31}=-B_y\). The equation gives

\[(\nabla\times\mathbf B)_x-c^{-2}\partial_tE_x=\mu_0J_x.\]

Cyclic permutations give the remaining components. The other half of Maxwell's equations is an identity:

\[\partial_\lambda F_{\mu\nu}+\partial_\mu F_{\nu\lambda}+\partial_\nu F_{\lambda\mu}=0 .\]

Insert the definition of \(F\). Each second derivative cancels a partner of opposite sign. With three spatial indices the identity says \(\nabla\cdot\mathbf B=0\); with a time index it gives Faraday's law. Applying \(\partial_\nu\) to the sourced equation also gives zero on the left by antisymmetry, enforcing \(\partial_\nu J^\nu=0\).

Vary the potential at fixed external current

We seek a Lorentz scalar built quadratically from the fields, linearly from the source and potential, and locally from their values at a spacetime event. In SI units choose

\[S=\frac1c\int d^4x\left[-\frac{1}{4\mu_0}F_{\mu\nu}F^{\mu\nu}-J^\mu A_\mu\right].\]

The factor \(1/c\) converts \(dx^0\) to seconds. The two antisymmetric terms in \(\delta F_{\mu\nu}\) contribute equally. Thus the field part varies as \(-F^{\mu\nu}\partial_\mu\delta A_\nu/\mu_0\). Integrate by parts, fixing \(\delta A_\nu=0\) on the boundary. The remaining arbitrary variation multiplies

\[\frac1{\mu_0}\partial_\mu F^{\mu\nu}-J^\nu=0 .\]

Under \(A_\mu\mapsto A_\mu+\partial_\mu\chi\) the source term changes by \(-J^\mu\partial_\mu\chi\). Integration by parts leaves a boundary term and \(+\chi\partial_\mu J^\mu\). Gauge independence of the action for arbitrary interior \(\chi\) therefore requires charge continuity. The same conservation law has appeared by a second route.

Read the action in familiar variables

Why a plane wave has zero field Lagrangian density

A direct contraction gives

\[F_{\mu\nu}F^{\mu\nu}=2(B^2-E^2/c^2).\]

The vacuum field Lagrangian density is \(\epsilon_0E^2/2-B^2/(2\mu_0)\), whereas the physical energy density is the sum of those two positive terms. For a plane wave \(E=cB\), the Lagrangian density vanishes; the energy density equals \(\epsilon_0E^2\). At \(E=100\) V/m instantaneous energy density is \(8.85\times10^{-8}\) J/m³. The cancellation in the action carries a distinct physical meaning from an empty field.

Test the stationary potential inside a capacitor

Between plane electrodes at \(0,V_0\), take \(\phi=V_0[x/L+\eta\sin(\pi x/L)]\). Each trial curve has the correct endpoints. For no space charge the static functional per area is \(U=\epsilon_0\int_0^L(\partial_x\phi)^2dx/2\). Its cross term integrates to zero because the sine perturbation vanishes on the boundaries, and the squared cosine averages to \(1/2\). Consequently

\[U/U_{\rm exact}=1+\pi^2\eta^2/2.\]

A perturbation with \(\eta=0.10\) raises the functional by 4.93%. The flattening of the energy near \(\eta=0\) tests stationarity directly.

Perturb the potential while keeping both electrodes fixed

Every trial curve has the prescribed endpoints. At amplitude 0.10 the trial energy is 4.93% above the exact value. Compare positive and negative perturbations, then double the amplitude and predict how the energy penalty changes.

Problem sheet · gauge and variational checks

Introduce a known static charge

For fixed boundary potentials, vary \(I[\phi]=\int (\epsilon_0|\nabla\phi|^2/2-\rho\phi)\,dV\). Which PDE follows? Why is it necessary to specify the sign of the linear term?

Work through the solution

Integrating the gradient term by parts produces \(\delta I=\int(-\epsilon_0\nabla^2\phi-\rho)\delta\phi\,dV\), because \(\delta\phi\) vanishes on the electrodes. Stationarity gives

\[-\epsilon_0\nabla^2\phi=\rho.\]

Reversing the source sign would reverse the curvature induced by positive charge. This functional includes a source coupling and generally differs from just the stored field energy.

Contract with a particle velocity

At an instant a particle is at rest. Insert \(u^\mu=(c,0,0,0)\) in \(f^\mu=qF^{\mu\nu}u_\nu\) to recover its spatial force. Why is the time component zero?

Work through the solution

Here \(F^{i0}=E_i/c\) and \(u_0=c\), so \(f^i=qE_i\). Antisymmetry gives \(F^{00}=0\). At that instant the velocity vanishes and hence so does the rate of work. More generally \(u_\mu f^\mu=q u_\mu F^{\mu\nu}u_\nu=0\), since the velocity product is symmetric. This preserves the particle's invariant rest mass.

Relativistic particle dynamics and the field tensor · Waves, radiation and relativity

A circular track measures momentum per charge. A clock following the particle registers proper time, and a detector records how much kinetic energy it has gained. We will put these observations in one dynamical equation, solve that equation in uniform fields and exhibit a numerical pusher that can get the energy right while its orbit phase slowly slips.

Chapter 27 · Cavity eigenmodes, measured linewidth and ring-down

A cavity has both a pitch and a decay time. One is set predominantly by the field pattern and the boundaries. The other measures how much stored energy escapes per cycle. A spatial perturbation can reveal where a particular mode stores its electric energy.

Make a conducting box satisfy every boundary condition

Let the empty cavity occupy \(0<x<a,\ 0<y<b,\ 0<z<d\). Its ideal conducting walls require zero tangential electric field. Choose an electric field in the \(y\) direction independent of \(y\). This automatically gives

\[\nabla\cdot\mathbf E=0.\]

The field is normal to the two \(y\)-walls and must vanish at the four \(x,z\)-walls. Write \(E_y=X(x)Z(z)e^{-i\omega t}\). The wave equation reduces to

\[X''/X+Z''/Z=-\omega^2/c^2.\]

Sines separately satisfy the vanishing boundary values. Thus a family of normal modes is

\[E_y=E_0\sin(m\pi x/a)\sin(p\pi z/d)e^{-i\omega t},\]
\[f_{m0p}=\frac c2\sqrt{(m/a)^2+(p/d)^2},\]
\[m,p=1,2,\ldots .\]

Faraday's law then gives

\[\mathbf B=(\nabla\times\mathbf E)/(i\omega).\]

Its components are proportional to \(-\partial_zE_y\) and \(+\partial_xE_y\); its normal component vanishes at the appropriate walls. This family is transverse electric relative to the \(z\) axis. It does not exhaust the transverse magnetic modes or the modes with \(y\)-dependence. Whether a particular solution is excited depends on the overlap of the source with its field pattern.

Track energy between electric and magnetic form

Choose a real mode proportional to \(\cos\omega t\). The associated magnetic field is proportional to \(\sin\omega t\). At an electric maximum the stored energy is

\[U=\epsilon_0\int E_{\rm peak}^2dV/2.\]

Both squared sines average to \(1/2\), giving \(U=\epsilon_0 E_0^2 abd/8\). A quarter-cycle later the magnetic field stores the same energy. For a weakly leaking resonator, define \(Q=\omega U/P_{\rm lost}\) using cycle-averaged lost power and slowly varying total energy. At fixed \(Q\),

\[\frac{dU}{dt}=-\frac{\omega}{Q}U,\]
\[U(t)=U_0e^{-\omega t/Q},\]
\[E_{\rm env}(t)=E_{\rm env}(0)e^{-\omega t/(2Q)} .\]

A field probe measuring voltage follows the amplitude envelope. A square-law power detector follows the energy envelope. A ring-down fit delivers \(Q=\omega\tau_U=\omega\tau_E/2\), depending on which time constant is reported. Independent weak loss channels have additive powers and therefore additive inverse quality factors.

Connect a time trace to a frequency scan

The Fourier amplitude of a decaying positive-frequency signal is proportional to \(\int_0^\infty e^{-\omega_0t/(2Q)}e^{i(\omega-\omega_0)t}dt=[\omega_0/(2Q)-i(\omega-\omega_0)]^{-1}\). Its squared modulus is a Lorentzian with full width at half power \(\Delta\omega=\omega_0/Q\). This derivation resolves a common experimental ambiguity: the two half-power points have opposite detunings, and the width spans both. The approximation assumes a single mode and damping small on the scale of the carrier frequency.

Measuring geometry and locating an antinode

A rectangular resonator

Set \(a=60.0\) mm, \(d=80.0\) mm, \(b=25.0\) mm. The \(101\) mode gives \(f=3.123\) GHz. At \(Q=6000\) the energy decay time is \(306\) ns and the field decay time is \(612\) ns. The full power linewidth is \(520\) kHz. Increasing \(b\) changes the stored energy at fixed peak field but leaves this ideal mode frequency unchanged. Other mode families can move as \(b\) changes.

A small dielectric probe

Write the electric eigenproblem as \(\nabla\times\mu_0^{-1}\nabla\times\mathbf E=\omega^2\epsilon\mathbf E\). Multiply by the complex conjugate field and integrate. The wall term vanishes and the numerator becomes \(\int |\nabla\times\mathbf E|^2/\mu_0\,dV\). First-order perturbation of the stationary quotient gives

\[\delta f/f=-\int\delta\epsilon|\mathbf E|^2dV/(2\int\epsilon|\mathbf E|^2dV).\]

A weak permittivity increase of 2% in a region containing 3% of the original electric-field integral shifts the mode down by \(3\times10^{-4}\), approximately \(0.94\) MHz here. At an electric node the first-order shift vanishes. Large beads distort the field and require a new eigenproblem.

Read a cavity decay with an amplitude or power detector

The cavity width is fixed at 60 mm. With 80 mm length and Q = 6000, the energy falls to 1/e in 0.306 µs. Read the field amplitude there and decide which trace a square-law detector would follow.

Problem sheet · two ways to measure loss

Extract internal loss

A port-coupled resonator has measured \(Q_L=3000\). An independent calibration gives external \(Q_e=12000\). Find internal \(Q_i\) and the fraction of power leaving through the port.

Work through the solution

Since \(1/Q_L=1/Q_i+1/Q_e\), the internal quality factor is 4000. The port power fraction is

\[(1/Q_e)/(1/Q_L)=1/4.\]

Closing the port in the idealised model leaves \(Q=4000\).

Compare scans and ring-downs

A single mode near 500 MHz has a half-power width of 100 kHz. After drive removal how long until the field amplitude halves?

Work through the solution

The linewidth gives \(Q=5000\), so \(\tau_E=Q/(\pi f)=3.18\) μs. The field halves after \(\tau_E\ln2=2.21\) μs. At the same instant the energy has fallen to one quarter. This inference requires that frequency jitter has not broadened the measured line.

Chapter 28 · Why a small transparent sphere scatters light

A particle can redistribute light without consuming it. The calculation starts with an electrostatic boundary-value problem and ends with power crossing a faraway sphere. Connecting the two limits predicts a wavelength dependence that can be tested with colour.

Find the induced dipole by matching two potentials

Take a sphere of radius \(a\) and relative permittivity \(\epsilon_r\) in vacuum. Its size must be small compared with the wavelength everywhere, including inside the particle. Across its diameter, the incident wave then looks almost like a uniform electric field \(E_0\hat{\mathbf z}\). Spherical symmetry and the applied field single out the angular factor \(\cos\theta\). Choose \(\phi_{\rm in}=-Cr\cos\theta\) and \(\phi_{\rm out}=-E_0r\cos\theta+D\cos\theta/r^2\). Continuity of tangential electric field is equivalent here to continuity of potential. With zero free surface charge, the normal displacement is also continuous. At \(r=a\),

\[C=E_0-D/a^3,\]
\[\epsilon_r C=E_0+2D/a^3.\]

Eliminate \(C\) to obtain

\[D=a^3E_0(\epsilon_r-1)/(\epsilon_r+2).\]

The coefficient of the dipole potential is \(p/(4\pi\epsilon_0)\). Hence \(p=\alpha_0 E_0\) with \(\alpha_0=4\pi\epsilon_0a^3(\epsilon_r-1)/(\epsilon_r+2)\). The internal field \(3E_0/(\epsilon_r+2)\) explains the denominator. For \(\epsilon_r=1\) the disturbance vanishes. In the perfectly polarizable limit the internal field tends to zero.

Match a small dipole to an outgoing wave

Use complex amplitudes with time dependence \(e^{-i\omega t}\). The far electric field is \((k^2/4\pi\epsilon_0 r)[(\hat{\mathbf n}\times\mathbf p)\times\hat{\mathbf n}]e^{ikr}\), \(k=\omega/c\). Squaring its amplitude and multiplying by \(\epsilon_0 c/2\) gives the mean intensity. Divide by the incident intensity \(\epsilon_0c|E_0|^2/2\). The differential scattering cross section is then \(k^4|\alpha|^2\sin^2\theta/(16\pi^2\epsilon_0^2)\), with \(\theta\) measured from the dipole axis. Integrating the angular factor gives \(8\pi/3\):

\[\sigma_{\rm sca}=\frac{k^4|\alpha|^2}{6\pi\epsilon_0^2}\simeq\frac{8\pi}3 k^4a^6\left|\frac{\epsilon_r-1}{\epsilon_r+2}\right|^2 .\]

The sixth power originates in the coherent addition of dipoles throughout a volume proportional to \(a^3\). The fourth power in frequency comes from the second time derivative of the dipole in the radiative electric field. A cross section has units of area and measures removed power divided by incident intensity.

Where the scattered energy comes from

The incident field does work at mean rate \(\langle\mathbf E\cdot\dot{\mathbf p}\rangle=(\omega/2)\operatorname{Im}(\alpha)|E_0|^2\). Dividing by incident intensity yields

\[\sigma_{\rm ext}=k\operatorname{Im}(\alpha)/\epsilon_0.\]

A strictly real electrostatic \(\alpha_0\) would predict no extracted power while predicting positive scattered power. The static calculation captured the leading dipole amplitude but omitted its small radiation-induced phase delay. For a lossless electric dipole its leading radiative correction satisfies

\[\frac1\alpha=\frac1{\alpha_0}-i\frac{k^3}{6\pi\epsilon_0}.\]

Indeed \(\operatorname{Im}\alpha=k^3|\alpha|^2/(6\pi\epsilon_0)\), making extinction equal to scattering. In an absorbing particle their difference is absorbed power per incident intensity. Finite-size dispersion and higher multipoles require additional terms once \(ka\) grows.

Size, colour and the limits of inference

A particle doubles in radius

For dilute spheres of the same weakly dispersive material, doubling \(a\) gives \(2^6=64\) times the scattered power per particle at fixed incident intensity. If the total volume of dielectric is held fixed, the number of spheres falls by eight. The whole sample then scatters eight times the power, provided phases between different particles are effectively uncorrelated and multiple scattering is negligible. The two questions describe different samples.

A frequency-independent contrast

For \(a=20\) nm, \(\epsilon_r=2.25\) and vacuum wavelength \(600\) nm, \(ka=0.209\) and \((\epsilon_r-1)/(\epsilon_r+2)=0.2941\). The leading cross section is \(5.58\times10^{-19}\) m², around \(4.4\times10^{-4}\) of the geometric area. At \(450\) nm the model predicts 3.16 times that cross section. A large discrepancy can indicate dispersion, additional multipoles, or a distribution of particle sizes.

Compare the scattering of several particle sizes

For radius 20 nm, relative permittivity 2.25 and wavelength 600 nm, the predicted cross section is about 0.56 nm². Halve the radius and estimate the drop before reading the plot. The curve uses a frequency-independent dielectric contrast.

Problem sheet · inverse measurements

Estimate a radius ratio

Two dilute suspensions have the same number density, composition and optical path length. In the single-scattering regime one produces twice the scattered intensity at the same angle. Infer the ratio of particle radii.

Work through the solution

The proportionality to \(a^6\) gives

\[a_2/a_1=2^{1/6}=1.122.\]

A 12.2% change in radius doubles the signal. If counts or material contrasts are unknown, the same intensity change has multiple explanations.

Recover Thomson scattering

A free electron is driven by a weak field. Use \(m\ddot x=-eE_0e^{-i\omega t}\) to find its dipole and cross section. Why does the wavelength law change?

Work through the solution

The displacement amplitude is \(eE_0/(m\omega^2)\). Multiplying by electronic charge gives

\[\alpha=-e^2/(m\omega^2).\]

The \(\omega^{-4}\) in \(|\alpha|^2\) cancels \(k^4\). The cross section becomes \((8\pi/3)[e^2/(4\pi\epsilon_0mc^2)]^2\). This classical approximation assumes nonrelativistic electron motion and negligible recoil.

Chapter 29 · When a circuit element must be treated as a field

Can a short pair of conductors be called a capacitor? At low frequencies it stores energy almost electrostatically. As propagation time becomes important, the same open conductors support standing waves and their input current no longer grows proportionally to frequency.

Build a transmission line from small field volumes

Consider a uniform two-conductor line supporting a transverse electromagnetic wave. Let \(V(z,t)\) measure the transverse potential difference and \(I(z,t)\) the current toward \(+z\). Denote its inductance and capacitance per unit length by \(L'\) and \(C'\). For the moment assume ideal conductors, a linear lossless dielectric and negligible radiation. A segment \(dz\) stores charge \(C'V\,dz\). Charge balance gives

\[I(z)-I(z+dz)=C' dz\,\partial_t V.\]

Its linked magnetic flux is \(L'I\,dz\); Faraday's law gives the voltage drop \(V(z)-V(z+dz)=L' dz\,\partial_t I\). Division by \(dz\) yields

\[\partial_z I=-C'\partial_t V,\]
\[\partial_z V=-L'\partial_t I .\]

Differentiate the second relation with respect to \(z\) and substitute the first. The result is

\[\partial_z^2 V=L'C'\partial_t^2V,\]

with speed \(u=1/\sqrt{L'C'}\). An outgoing wave \(F(t-z/u)\) satisfies

\[V/I=Z_0=\sqrt{L'/C'}.\]

The electric and magnetic field energies per length are \(C'V^2/2\) and \(L'I^2/2\), and they are equal for this travelling wave. Multiplying the two equations by \(V\) and \(I\) also gives a one-dimensional conservation law:

\[\partial_z(VI)=-\partial_t(C'V^2/2+L'I^2/2).\]

Derive the input admittance of an open end

Use \(e^{-i\omega t}\) time dependence, and let the far end \(z=\ell\) be open so \(I(\ell)=0\). Then \(\partial_zV(\ell)=0\). The solution is

\[V(z)=V_L\cos k(\ell-z),\]

where \(k=\omega/u\). Since \(\partial_zV=i\omega L'I\), the current is \(-i V_L\sin k(\ell-z)/Z_0\). At the input,

\[Y_{\rm in}=-\frac{i}{Z_0}\tan(k\ell),\]
\[Y_{\rm lumped}=-i\omega C'\ell,\]
\[\frac{Y_{\rm in}}{Y_{\rm lumped}}=\frac{\tan x}{x},\]
\[x=\frac{\omega\ell}{u} .\]

At small \(x\),

\[\tan x/x=1+x^2/3+O(x^4).\]

Thus a circuit approximation can be assigned an error estimate. Near \(x=\pi/2\) the input voltage approaches a node and the ideal input admittance diverges. Losses round the pole in a real line. Beyond this frequency even the sign can change, although the far end remains open.

Two decisions about model size

A 15 cm open lead

Take \(u=2.00\times10^8\) m/s and \(Z_0=50.0\,\Omega\). Then \(C'=1/(Z_0u)=100\) pF/m and the lumped capacitance is 15.0 pF. At 20.0 MHz, \(x=0.09425\); the exact admittance exceeds the capacitive prediction by 0.297%. At 200 MHz, \(x=0.9425\), and the excess is about 46.0%. A component measured on an open fixture can therefore appear to acquire substantial extra capacitance at high frequency.

A time trace on the same lead

The one-way flight time is \(0.75\) ns. A step launched down the line first sees the characteristic impedance. Information about the open end returns only after \(1.50\) ns. At an open end an incident positive voltage wave is reflected with the same sign. The current waves cancel there, enforcing zero terminal current, while the terminal voltage doubles at their first overlap. For a source matched to \(Z_0\), the returning wave is absorbed at the source. This time-domain argument provides a check on the origin of the standing-wave solution.

A second circuit limit from magnetic energy

In the slow-variation limit, linked flux in two fixed coils is linear in both currents. For a reciprocal medium,

\[\lambda_1=L_1I_1+MI_2,\]
\[\lambda_2=MI_1+L_2I_2.\]

Integrate the supplied power \(I_1\dot\lambda_1+I_2\dot\lambda_2\) to obtain

\[U=(L_1I_1^2+2MI_1I_2+L_2I_2^2)/2.\]

Completing the square gives

\[2U=L_1(I_1+MI_2/L_1)^2+(L_2-M^2/L_1)I_2^2.\]

A passive magnetic energy requires

\[|M|\leq\sqrt{L_1L_2}.\]

The sign of \(M\) depends on terminal orientations. This bound is an independent way to check a measured or numerically inferred circuit model.

Measure the range of a lumped capacitor model

The line has speed 2.00 × 10⁸ m/s and impedance 50 Ω. For a 15 cm open section its first quarter-wave pole is 333 MHz. At 60% of that frequency the distributed admittance exceeds the lumped value by 46%. Move the open end and compare the two curves.

Problem sheet · estimating the cost of a circuit approximation

Set a one-percent frequency limit

For a 0.30 m open line with speed \(1.8\times10^8\) m/s, estimate the highest frequency for a 1% correction in input admittance. State the approximation used.

Work through the solution

Set \(x^2/3=0.01\), giving \(x\simeq0.173\) and \(f=xu/(2\pi\ell)=16.5\) MHz. The next term is \(2x^4/15\simeq0.00012\), so the estimate slightly overstates the allowable frequency. Bisection on \(\tan x/x=1.01\) gives \(x\simeq0.1722\).

Check a claimed mutual inductance

A two-coil model has \(L_1=4\) mH, \(L_2=9\) mH and \(M=7\) mH. Find the current combination that reveals a problem.

Work through the solution

Choose \(I_1=-MI_2/L_1=-1.75I_2\). The surviving coefficient is \(9-49/4=-3.25\) mH, giving a negative stored energy for every nonzero \(I_2\). A passive reciprocal model with these self-inductances can support at most 6 mH of mutual inductance in magnitude.

  • Fließbach, chapter 26 · oscillating circuits
  • Griffiths, 5th ed., §§7.2, 9.5 · inductance and guided waves

Study the full derivation

Field momentum, momentum exchange and the quasistatic limits · Magnetism, induction and field dynamics

A system can have static electric and magnetic fields with nonzero local electromagnetic momentum density. A circuit can also be electrically small while either induction or displacement current remains indispensable. Both puzzles become clearer when one follows the relevant conservation law and compares the scales of the discarded terms.

Chapter 30 · From wavefronts to rays, focusing and caustics

A ray is a prediction extracted from the phase of a wave. Following its amplitude at the same time reveals the point at which a ray calculation loses its validity. A gently graded transparent material gives a solvable example of both effects.

Derive the phase and transport equations together

In a lossless isotropic dielectric with a slowly varying refractive index \(n(\mathbf r)\), consider one scalar polarisation component satisfying \(\nabla^2\psi+k_0^2 n^2\psi=0\), where \(k_0=\omega/c\). This scalar description works when vector-polarisation coupling is negligible over the scales of interest. Set \(\psi=A(\mathbf r)e^{ik_0S(\mathbf r)}\) with a slowly varying real amplitude. Differentiation twice gives

\[0=\nabla^2 A+i k_0[2\nabla A\cdot\nabla S+A\nabla^2S]+k_0^2 A(n^2-|\nabla S|^2).\]

If the material and amplitude vary little over a wavelength, first equate the leading \(k_0^2\) term to zero. At the next order the \(k_0\) term vanishes. The two results are the eikonal equation and transport equation:

\[|\nabla S|^2=n^2,\]
\[\nabla\cdot(A^2\nabla S)=0 .\]

The first fixes the optical length accumulated between neighbouring wavefronts. The second transports energy down a thin ray tube. Across a tube of area \(\mathcal A\) perpendicular to the phase gradient, \(A^2 n\mathcal A\) is constant to this order. In a uniform medium a spherical tube grows as \(r^2\), giving \(A\propto1/r\), consistent with the outgoing wave.

Follow the normal to a wavefront

Choose arclength \(s\) along the ray and \(\hat{\mathbf t}=\nabla S/n\). In the eikonal equation take a spatial derivative. Since \(\nabla S\) is a gradient,

\[(\nabla S\cdot\nabla)\nabla S=\nabla(|\nabla S|^2)/2=n\nabla n.\]

Divide by \(n\). The ray equation is

\[\frac{d}{ds}(n\hat{\mathbf t})=\nabla n .\]

A transverse increase of index bends the ray toward larger optical index. If \(n\) depends only on the coordinate normal to layers, the component of \(n\hat{\mathbf t}\) parallel to them stays constant. Thus \(n\sin\theta\) is conserved for an angle measured from the normal, recovering Snell's law. The same equation follows by requiring stationary optical length \(\int n\,ds\) when varying the path with fixed endpoints.

Solve a graded-index profile

For paraxial rays travelling close to \(+z\), take \(n(y)\simeq n_0(1-g^2y^2/2)\). Assume \(|gy|\ll1\) and \(|dy/dz|\ll1\). Then \(ds\simeq dz\), \(\hat t_y\simeq y'\), and \(d(ny')/dz\simeq n_0y''\) to leading order. Since \(\partial_y n=-n_0g^2y\), the trajectory solves \(y''+g^2y=0\). Initial height \(y_0\) and slope \(s_0\) give

\[y(z)=y_0\cos(gz)+\frac{s_0}{g}\sin(gz),\]
\[y'(z)=-g y_0\sin(gz)+s_0\cos(gz).\]

For a collimated bundle, all \(s_0=0\). The transverse magnification \(\partial y/\partial y_0=\cos(gz)\) vanishes simultaneously for all rays at \(z_f=\pi/(2g)\). This is a caustic of the ray description. In this planar example the ray density grows as \(1/|\cos(gz)|\). Its divergence signals that the neglected \(\nabla^2 A\) becomes important. The underlying wave stays finite and develops diffraction near the focus.

A focus and a reconstructed gradient

Refocus an off-axis bundle

Take \(g=20\ {\rm m^{-1}}\), initial heights between \(-1\) and \(+1\) mm and zero slopes. The predicted first focus is \(78.5\) mm downstream. The extreme rays acquire slopes of magnitude \(0.020\) at the focus, well within the paraxial regime. Tilt every initial ray by 0.010 rad. At \(z_f\) the common height shifts to \(s_0/g=0.50\) mm. The focal length is insensitive to this common tilt in the parabolic approximation.

Estimate the index from a photograph

Two successive crossings of initially parallel symmetric rays are 120 mm apart. Crossings occur at \(gz=\pi/2+m\pi\), so

\[g=\pi/0.120=26.2\ {\rm m^{-1}}.\]

At a height of 2 mm, the predicted fractional index decrease from the central index is

\[g^2y^2/2=1.37\times10^{-3}.\]

Resolving this small contrast through repeated bending can be easier than resolving it through a single refraction measurement.

Focus and tilt a bundle of paraxial rays

At gradient 20 m⁻¹, five parallel rays meet after 78.5 mm. A common tilt of 10 mrad displaces their meeting point by 0.50 mm. Follow the bundle through a crossing and decide why the geometric density ceases to predict a finite intensity there.

Open this experiment online

Problem sheet · optical path and diffraction

A travel-time check

A ray passes through two homogeneous layers of thicknesses \(a,b\), indices \(n_1,n_2\), with lateral endpoint separation \(D\). Write travel time as a function of crossing coordinate \(x\). Recover the interface condition.

Work through the solution

The time is

\[T(x)=[n_1\sqrt{a^2+x^2}+n_2\sqrt{b^2+(D-x)^2}]/c.\]

The derivative vanishes when \(n_1 x/\sqrt{a^2+x^2}=n_2(D-x)/\sqrt{b^2+(D-x)^2}\). The two fractions are the sines of the angles to the interface normal. Each segment's length has positive second derivative, making this stationary path a local minimum in this geometry.

Estimate the diffraction scale

A circular pupil of numerical aperture 0.030 focuses vacuum light of wavelength 600 nm. Estimate the first dark-ring radius and compare it with a ray focus.

Work through the solution

For a uniformly illuminated circular aperture in the paraxial limit the first Airy minimum is \(0.61\lambda_0/\mathrm{NA}\), giving \(12.2\) μm. Different pupil shapes change the numerical factor. The wavelength dependence is absent from the ray crossing, so a ray trace alone cannot distinguish two experiments with identical geometry but different wavelengths.

  • Fließbach, chapter 36 · interference and diffraction

An illuminated aperture is a boundary condition for a wave. A screen a millimetre away, an intensity camera at a lens focus and a microscope measuring an evanescent field sample different consequences of the same condition. We will derive operators for propagating the field, estimate the approximations each instrument makes and use energy and sampling checks to tell numerical structure from a measurable fringe.

Chapter 31 · Radiation reaction and the energy stored near a charge

A charge can radiate at an instant when a proposed frictional force would do no work. To account for the energy one needs three measurements: mechanical work on the charge, power leaving in radiation and a reversible change in its nearby field.

A moving oscillator tests a friction hypothesis

For a point charge moving nonrelativistically in SI units define \(\tau=q^2/(6\pi\epsilon_0mc^3)\). The Larmor formula gives

\[P_{\rm rad}=m\tau a^2.\]

Suppose a charge reaches a turning point of a slow sinusoidal oscillation. Its velocity there is zero and its acceleration is maximal. Radiation carries positive power away, yet any finite force on the particle does zero mechanical work at that instant. Equating instantaneous mechanical loss to instantaneous radiated power cannot account for the turning point.

Integrate over a smooth acceleration history. The product rule gives

\[d(\mathbf a\cdot\mathbf v)/dt=\dot{\mathbf a}\cdot\mathbf v+a^2.\]

Rearranging shows that a local force \(\mathbf F_{\rm self}=m\tau\dot{\mathbf a}\) can recover the Larmor loss between endpoints where \(\mathbf a\cdot\mathbf v\) agrees:

\[\int_{t_1}^{t_2}\mathbf F_{\rm self}\cdot\mathbf v\,dt=m\tau[\mathbf a\cdot\mathbf v]_{t_1}^{t_2}-\int_{t_1}^{t_2}P_{\rm rad}\,dt .\]

This identity motivates the nonrelativistic Abraham–Lorentz term. An integrated energy argument only fixes its work under the chosen endpoint conditions. Deriving the full local self-force requires analysing the near field, regularising the point-source singularity and identifying the measured particle mass. These assumptions delimit the classical effective equation.

Follow the energy that can return to the particle

Let \(K=mv^2/2\), \(E_S=-m\tau\,\mathbf a\cdot\mathbf v\). Write \(m\mathbf a=\mathbf F_{\rm ext}+\mathbf F_{\rm self}\), dot with \(\mathbf v\), and use the product rule once more. The result is

\[\mathbf F_{\rm ext}\cdot\mathbf v=\frac{d}{dt}(K+E_S)+P_{\rm rad}.\]

The acceleration-dependent quantity \(E_S\), called the Schott energy, represents a reversible bound-field term after regularisation. Its sign depends on motion; it is a changeable contribution relative to an energy reference. For constant acceleration over a short nonrelativistic interval, the self-force vanishes, but \(dE_S/dt=-m\tau a^2\). The decrease supplies the radiated energy. Switching the acceleration on and off modifies the budget near the endpoints. Extending a constant-acceleration segment to infinite time would break the assumed slow-speed model.

Why taking the third-order equation literally fails

Take a constant mass and one Cartesian direction. With no external force the equation becomes \(a-\tau\dot a=0\), whose general solution includes \(a=Ae^{t/\tau}\). Standard position and velocity data leave \(A\) undetermined. This runaway is incompatible with a passive free particle. The prescription \(a(t)\to0\) after an applied force has ended removes that branch, but integrating backward gives

\[a(t)=\frac1{m\tau}\int_t^\infty e^{-(s-t)/\tau}F_{\rm ext}(s)\,ds .\]

The integral samples future forces. A discontinuous idealised force can give apparent preacceleration over order \(\tau\). For an electron \(\tau\simeq6.27\times10^{-24}\) s. On such scales an elementary classical point-charge description is inadequate. For smooth forcing varying over \(T\gg\tau\), instead use the leading equation \(a=F_{\rm ext}/m+O(\tau/T)\) on the right. To first order in \(\tau/T\),

\[m a=F_{\rm ext}+\tau\,\frac{dF_{\rm ext}}{dt}.\]

For a force depending on position and velocity, evaluate its total derivative along the leading-order motion. This reduced-order equation selects the smooth, perturbative dynamics without adding independent initial acceleration data.

A spectral width and a phase-resolved budget

Radiative damping of a weakly bound oscillator

Let \(F_{\rm ext}=-m\omega_0^2x\). Then \(\ddot x+\tau\omega_0^2\dot x+\omega_0^2x=0\) to first order. The amplitude falls with e-folding time \(2/(\tau\omega_0^2)\). At \(\omega_0=3.0\times10^{15}\) s⁻¹ the formal electron model gives \(35.4\) ns, with \(\tau\omega_0=1.88\times10^{-8}\). The weak-damping approximation is internally consistent. Actual atomic linewidths additionally depend on quantum matrix elements and other decay channels. The calculation describes a classical bound oscillator with a chosen restoring force.

The same energy viewed at two phases

Impose \(v=v_a\sin\omega t\), so \(a=\omega v_a\cos\omega t\) and \(\dot a=-\omega^2v_a\sin\omega t\). In units \(P_0=m\tau\omega^2v_a^2\), radiation power is \(\cos^2\omega t\) while mechanical self-force power is \(-\sin^2\omega t\). At phase zero all the instantaneous radiation is supplied by decreasing bound-field energy. A quarter period later the radiation vanishes at the corresponding retarded emission phase, but the self-force still removes mechanical energy. Over one period the integrated bound-field term vanishes, so the mean mechanical loss is \(P_0/2\).

Close the energy accounts at a chosen emission phase

The radiated power, the self-force work on the particle and the rate of change of bound-field energy sum to zero at every emission phase. With zero mean speed and phase zero, their dimensionless values are +1, 0 and −1. Shift the mean speed and decide which of the three readings must stay the same.

Open this experiment online

Problem sheet · how local is radiative friction?

Calculate a complete pulse budget

Take \(a(t)=a_0\sin(\pi t/T)\) for \(0<t<T\), zero elsewhere, with initial velocity zero. Calculate final speed, total radiated energy and the ratio of radiation to final kinetic energy.

Work through the solution

The velocity gain is \(2a_0T/\pi\). Integrating \(a^2\) yields

\[E_{\rm rad}=m\tau a_0^2T/2.\]

The final kinetic energy is \(2ma_0^2T^2/\pi^2\), so the ratio is \(\pi^2\tau/(4T)\). Both endpoints have zero acceleration. The time-integrated external work must therefore equal the sum of the final kinetic energy and radiated energy. Choose \(a_0T\ll c\) and \(T\gg\tau\) for this calculation.

Diagnose a spurious trajectory

A computation with no force doubles its acceleration every few multiples of the electron radiation-reaction time. Would closer timesteps necessarily remove the instability?

Work through the solution

The exact homogeneous third-order equation already has \(a=Ae^{t/\tau}\). A smaller step can track that unphysical branch more accurately. A model restricted to smooth weak radiation reaction instead evolves the reduced second-order equation. In free motion this gives \(a=0\) identically. Compare physical timescales and equations before interpreting a converged numerical trajectory as an observable.

Radiated power, mechanical work and energy limits · Waves, radiation and relativity

A charge can radiate while its speed is constant. A source can exchange energy with its nearby field before a pulse reaches a receiver. We will use the flux through a distant sphere, the work at the charge and the energy stored in a local field as three operationally distinct measurements. Agreement requires the relevant integration times and the range of validity of the particle model.

Chapter 32 · Diffraction from an aperture of finite width

Geometrical optics predicts a sharp edge and an infinitely narrow ideal focus. A scalar diffraction integral describes how contributions with different phase interfere. A slit gives an exact far-field reference against which to test an oscillatory numerical integral.

Accumulate phase across an aperture

Let coherent monochromatic light pass through a slit of full width \(a\) in the plane \(z=0\). The slit is long in its other direction and illuminated by a normally incident uniform plane wave. Work with a scalar component in free space. Suppose observation distance \(z\) is large compared with \(a,|x|\) and the wavelength \(\lambda\). Contributions from aperture point \(\xi\) to detector position \(x\) carry a phase \(kR\), \(k=2\pi/\lambda\). The path expansion is

\[R=\sqrt{z^2+(x-\xi)^2}=z+\frac{(x-\xi)^2}{2z}-\frac{(x-\xi)^4}{8z^3}+\cdots .\]

Approximating slow amplitude and obliquity factors by their axial values while retaining the quadratic phase gives the Fresnel integral. Check the dropped phase \(k|x-\xi|^4/(8z^3)\ll1\) over both the aperture and detector range. Its smallness is more restrictive than simply calling the angle small in a high-frequency problem. The scalar aperture model also assumes that edge polarisation and finite screen thickness are negligible.

Reduce the integral to two dimensionless variables

Set \(s=\xi/a\), \(u=ax/(\lambda z)\) and \(N=a^2/(\lambda z)\). Expanding the square splits off a common phase depending only on \(x,z\). Normalise away that phase and the common geometrical amplitude, leaving the shape integral

\[F(u,N)=\int_{-1/2}^{1/2}\exp[i\pi N s^2-2\pi ius]\,ds,\]
\[I_{\rm rel}=|F|^2 .\]

Here \(a\) denotes the full slit width. Definitions using the half-width produce Fresnel numbers four times smaller. The maximum phase of the \(s^2\) term is \(\pi N/4\). This sets a quantitative criterion for dropping it. In the far-field limit \(N\to0\), direct integration of the remaining exponential gives \(F(u,0)=\sin(\pi u)/(\pi u)\) and \(F(0,0)=1\) by continuity. The first zeros occur at \(u=\pm1\). Each slit half has an opposite-phase partner at this observation angle.

Discretise complex amplitude before forming intensity

Divide the slit into \(M\) equal cells. For their midpoint coordinates \(s_j=(j+1/2)/M-1/2\), evaluate \(\phi_j=\pi N s_j^2-2\pi us_j\) and accumulate the real and imaginary parts:

\[F_M=\frac1M\sum_{j=0}^{M-1}(\cos\phi_j+i\sin\phi_j),\]
\[I_M=(\operatorname{Re}F_M)^2+(\operatorname{Im}F_M)^2 .\]

Summing \(|e^{i\phi_j}|^2\) first gives a flat result and loses all interference. An estimate for the largest phase step is \(\pi(N+2|u|)/M\). Reduce it while checking convergence at specified points. For a smooth integrand, composite midpoint quadrature has error of order \(M^{-2}\) in complex amplitude at fixed \(u,N\). Relative error in intensity near a zero can be arbitrarily large. There compare absolute intensities or complex amplitudes. Agreement between a coarse grid and the far-field formula at large \(N\) is not a valid convergence test.

Design a detector scan and identify a false minimum

Choose a distance that resolves the first minimum

A slit has full width \(a=100\) μm in light of \(\lambda=500\) nm. At \(z=1.0\) m the Fresnel number is 0.020 and the dropped aperture phase is at most 0.0157 rad. The first far-field minimum lies at \(x=\lambda z/a=5.0\) mm. At \(z=20\) mm the same slit gives \(N=1\). Dropping 0.785 rad at the aperture edge can materially change the measured distribution. Moving the detector closer also changes the physical width associated with one unit of \(u\).

How much light fills the nominal dark point?

At \(u=1\) the Fraunhofer amplitude vanishes. For small \(N\), expand the chirp to first order. The remaining integral is \(i\pi N\int_{-1/2}^{1/2}s^2e^{-2\pi is}ds\). The imaginary odd integrand vanishes; two integrations by parts give the real integral \(-1/(2\pi^2)\). Hence \(F(1,N)\simeq-iN/(2\pi)\) and \(I_{\rm rel}(1,N)\simeq N^2/(4\pi^2)\). At \(N=0.10\) the predicted residual intensity is \(2.53\times10^{-4}\). A correctly converged computation can have a nonzero value at a nominal far-field dark point.

Integrate the slit and refine the aperture mesh

Here the slit width is the entire opening. At Fresnel number 0.10 the first far-field dark point has residual intensity about 0.000253 on the converged scale. Change the mesh and the Fresnel number independently to distinguish numerical error from a physical filling of the minimum.

Problem sheet · reconstruction and convergence

Use two measured minima

For wavelength 630 nm and distance 1.20 m, the separation of the first minima is 9.0 mm. Recover the slit width and check the implied far-field assumption.

Work through the solution

The distance from the centre to either first zero is 4.5 mm. Thus \(a=\lambda z/x=168\) μm. Then \(N=a^2/(\lambda z)=0.0373\), and the maximum neglected quadratic phase is 0.0293 rad. With the stated precision the use of the far-field formula is plausible. The relevant length in the inverse calculation was half the measured separation.

Choose and validate a quadrature

For \(|u|\leq3\) and \(N=4\), require the estimated phase change between adjacent source nodes to remain below 0.25 rad. What grid size is suggested? How would you estimate the remaining error?

Work through the solution

The bound gives \(M>\pi(4+6)/0.25\simeq126\), so 128 cells meet the criterion. Compare 128 and 256 cells at the centre and near the first fringes. In the second-order convergence regime the fine-grid amplitude error is approximately one third of the coarse-to-fine difference. Verify the trend with 512 cells if high accuracy is needed. Refining the detector sampling alone cannot fix inadequate sampling of the slit.

A screen a millimetre away, an intensity camera at a lens focus and a microscope measuring an evanescent field sample different consequences of the same condition. We will derive operators for propagating the field, estimate the approximations each instrument makes and use energy and sampling checks to tell numerical structure from a measurable fringe.

Chapter 33 · Energy, momentum and a charged particle’s worldline

A field may turn the momentum, change its magnitude, or do both. Beginning with a measurable clock carried by the particle gives a force law that remains well behaved even when increasing momentum produces little visible change in speed.

Use ticks of a comoving clock

A massive particle has a timelike worldline. In a laboratory with spacetime coordinates \(x^\mu=(ct,\mathbf x)\), the invariant interval along its path gives \(c^2d\tau^2=c^2dt^2-d\mathbf x^2\), so \(d\tau=dt/\gamma\),

\[\gamma=(1-v^2/c^2)^{-1/2}.\]

Its four-velocity \(u^\mu=dx^\mu/d\tau=\gamma(c,\mathbf v)\) has fixed squared norm \(c^2\). Multiplication by the measured rest mass gives four-momentum \(p^\mu=(\mathcal E/c,\mathbf p)\), with \(\mathcal E=\gamma mc^2\),

\[\mathbf p=\gamma m\mathbf v.\]

Squaring and differentiating at fixed rest mass gives

\[\mathcal E^2=m^2c^4+p^2c^2,\]
\[d\mathcal E=\frac{c^2\mathbf p}{\mathcal E}\cdot d\mathbf p=\mathbf v\cdot d\mathbf p .\]

Use \(\dot{\mathbf p}=q(\mathbf E+\mathbf v\times\mathbf B)\). Taking its scalar product with \(\mathbf v\) shows \(d\mathcal E/dt=q\mathbf E\cdot\mathbf v\). A uniform magnetic field changes momentum direction while conserving its magnitude and energy. Resolving a general force along and across the velocity gives

\[F_\parallel=\gamma^3 m a_\parallel,\]
\[F_\perp=\gamma m a_\perp.\]

These factors follow from differentiating \(\gamma\mathbf v\), without assigning the particle a changing rest mass.

Integrate motion in a constant electric field

Choose a positive charge initially at rest with \(E\) along \(+x\), and neglect other forces. A negative charge follows the reflected trajectory. Define \(s=qEt/(mc)\). Lab momentum grows linearly, \(p=qEt\). Substitute it into the energy relation and use \(v=c^2p/\mathcal E\). Integration with \(x(0)=0\) gives

\[\gamma=\sqrt{1+s^2},\]
\[\frac vc=\frac{s}{\sqrt{1+s^2}},\]
\[x=\frac{mc^2}{qE}\left(\sqrt{1+s^2}-1\right).\]

Multiplying the distance by \(qE\) recovers kinetic energy \(\mathcal E-mc^2\). A second check comes from the clock. Integrating \(d\tau=dt/\sqrt{1+s^2}\) gives

\[\tau=(mc/qE)\operatorname{arsinh}s.\]

With rapidity \(\eta=qE\tau/(mc)\),

\[s=\sinh\eta,\ \gamma=\cosh\eta.\]

The comoving proper acceleration is \(qE/m\) even while the laboratory acceleration decreases as \(\gamma^{-3}\). Expanding at early times yields

\[v=qEt/m+O(t^3),\]
\[x=qEt^2/(2m)+O(t^4).\]

Read an energy from the curvature of a track

In a uniform magnetic field along \(z\), longitudinal momentum and energy remain fixed. For transverse motion the change in momentum direction has magnitude \(p_\perp v_\perp/r\). Equating it with \(|q|v_\perp B\) gives

\[r=p_\perp/(|q|B).\]

The angular frequency is \(\omega_c=|q|B/(\gamma m)\), and the longitudinal distance travelled per turn is \(2\pi p_\parallel/(|q|B)\). The sign of the charge determines the sense of rotation for a specified field direction. Radius alone measures transverse momentum. To reconstruct total momentum from a helical path one must also measure the pitch.

Reconstruct two ideal laboratory observations

When does the classical speed fail?

For an electron starting at rest in a uniform field of magnitude 100 kV/m, the momentum magnitude reaches \(mc\) after \(mc/(eE)=17.0\) ns. A Newtonian extrapolation then predicts speed \(c\). The relativistic result is \(c/\sqrt2=0.707c\), kinetic energy \((\sqrt2-1)mc^2=212\) keV and travel distance \(2.12\) m. The potential difference over this distance is 212 kV, giving the same kinetic energy independently. These are ideal constant-field values for a prescribed test particle.

A helical track with a missing component

In \(B=0.20\) T a singly charged particle has circular projection of radius \(5.0\) mm and advances \(20\) mm along the field per revolution. Using elementary charge \(e\), one obtains \(p_\perp=1.60\times10^{-22}\) kg m/s and \(p_\parallel=1.02\times10^{-22}\) kg m/s. For an electron \(p/(mc)=0.696\), \(\gamma\simeq1.22\), and the kinetic energy is \(112\) keV. Assuming the track lay entirely in a transverse plane would underestimate its kinetic energy. A heavier singly charged particle with the same track has the same momentum but a different kinetic energy.

Compare a particle clock with a lab timer

In a 100 kV/m uniform field, an initially stationary electron reaches about 0.706c after 17 ns lab time, while its own clock advances roughly 15 ns. Identify where the Newtonian extrapolation crosses the light-speed line and inspect the kinetic energy at that time.

Open this experiment online

Problem sheet · frame and trajectory checks

Measure the elapsed proper time

For the electric trajectory starting from rest, let the final momentum be \(2mc\). Find the ratio of elapsed proper time to lab time, and compare it with the instantaneous final \(1/\gamma\).

Work through the solution

Since \(s=2\), the elapsed-time ratio is

\[\operatorname{arsinh}(2)/2=0.722.\]

At the endpoint \(1/\gamma=1/\sqrt5=0.447\). The particle was slower earlier. Applying its final clock rate to the entire trajectory would discard its acceleration history.

Predict an orbit in crossed fields

Take perpendicular fields with \(E/(cB)=0.50\) and a particle initially at rest in the laboratory. Describe its motion in the frame moving at \(\mathbf E\times\mathbf B/B^2\), and recover its average transverse drift direction.

Work through the solution

The boost speed is \(0.50c\). The primed electric field vanishes, the magnetic field is \(B/\gamma_d\) and the initial particle velocity is opposite the boost. Its primed motion is circular with constant speed. After every complete primed period its primed position returns to its starting value. Transforming the displacement between successive returns gives \(\Delta x/\Delta t=v_d\) along the drift direction, independently of the sign of charge. Opposite signs reverse the sense of the primed circle.

Chapter 34 · Capacitance as a matrix of electrostatic energies

Three conductors occupy a grounded metal enclosure. Charging one can induce charge on another even when its voltage stays fixed. To predict a measurement we must specify which conductors have fixed voltage, which are isolated and what defines the reference potential.

Construct unit-voltage solutions

Consider a connected dielectric region with stationary geometry, linear reciprocal permittivity tensor \(\boldsymbol\epsilon(\boldsymbol r)\), no free volume charge, and perfectly conducting boundaries. For conductor \(j\), define \(u_j\) as the solution of \(\nabla\cdot(\boldsymbol\epsilon\nabla u_j)=0\) which equals one on conductor \(j\) and zero on all other boundaries. When a grounded enclosing wall is used, each of these basis solutions also vanishes on that wall. Linearity and uniqueness give

\[\phi(\boldsymbol r)=\sum_j V_j u_j(\boldsymbol r).\]

Setting just one conductor to unit voltage determines an entire column of responses, measurable by holding the other potentials fixed.

Take \(\boldsymbol n\) to be the unit normal pointing out of the dielectric, into the conductor. Since \(\boldsymbol D=-\boldsymbol\epsilon\nabla\phi\), the conductor's charge facing the dielectric is \(Q_i=\int_{S_i}\boldsymbol n\cdot\boldsymbol\epsilon\nabla\phi\,dS\). The two sign reversals, one from the electric field and one from the conductor's outward normal, cancel. The coefficients \(C_{ij}=\partial Q_i/\partial V_j\) consequently integrate the flux from each basis solution.

\[Q_i=\sum_jC_{ij}V_j,\]
\[C_{ij}=\int_\Omega \nabla u_i\cdot\boldsymbol\epsilon\nabla u_j\,d^3r .\]

To obtain the volume formula, apply the divergence theorem to \(u_i\boldsymbol\epsilon\nabla u_j\). Only the gradient product survives in the volume. Only boundary \(i\) survives on the surface because it is the sole boundary where \(u_i=1\). Reciprocal permittivity makes the volume formula symmetric under \(i\leftrightarrow j\); capacitance readings must therefore agree when drive and pickup electrodes are exchanged under the same conditions.

Background · Maxwell capacitance coefficient
\[Q_i=\sum_j C_{ij}V_j\]

Potentials are defined relative to a stated reference. A floating electrode has a prescribed total charge and a potential determined by the other electrodes.

Identify the reference and the energy

The electrostatic energy is

\[U=\frac12\int\boldsymbol E\cdot\boldsymbol D\,d^3r=\frac12\boldsymbol V^TC\boldsymbol V.\]

Its derivative with respect to \(V_i\) equals \(Q_i\) at fixed geometry. When the enclosing wall is included as an additional voltage degree of freedom, adding the same constant to all voltages leaves every gradient unchanged. The basis solutions including the wall sum to one. The full matrix then annihilates the vector of ones, its row sums vanish, and energy depends only on potential differences. Fixing the wall voltage removes that null mode. The reduced matrix acting on inner voltages can have nonzero row sums and is positive definite for a connected enclosure with positive permittivity.

For example, two electrodes have pair capacitance \(c=4\) pF, with additional \(g_1=2\) pF and \(g_2=3\) pF from each to the wall. The energy is \([g_1V_1^2+g_2V_2^2+c(V_1-V_2)^2]/2\) in pJ for volt units. Differentiate to obtain reduced \(C_{11}=6,\ C_{22}=7,\ C_{12}=C_{21}=-4\) pF. At \(V_1=2,V_2=-1\) V the charges are \(16,-15\) pC and the energy is 23.5 pJ. Including the wall restores total charge zero for the charges facing the dielectric; the wall carries \(-1\) pC.

Float one terminal and read a different capacitance

Disconnect the second electrode with initial charge zero. Its potential adjusts to satisfy \(0=-cV_1+(g_2+c)V_2\), giving \(V_2=4V_1/7\). Substituting into \(Q_1\) yields

\[C_{\rm in}=g_1+c-c^2/(g_2+c)=26/7\,\mathrm{pF}.\]

With electrode two grounded instead, \(C_{\rm in}=6\) pF. Both results came from the same electrostatic matrix; a voltmeter or guard changes the boundary conditions. The plot compares the charge delivered as the driven voltage changes. Vary the mutual coupling, and check that eliminating an isolated electrode agrees with differentiating the energy after minimising over its voltage for zero charge.

Tutorial on calibrated terminal measurements

A measured reduced matrix has diagonal entries 8 and 9 pF and off-diagonal entries \(-3\) pF. Recover the three pair capacitances to one another and to a reference enclosure. Predict the wall charge at \(V_1=1,V_2=2\) V.

Work through the solution

The mutual pair is 3 pF. Subtracting it from the diagonals gives 5 and 6 pF to the wall. The driven charges are \(8-6=2\) pC and \(-3+18=15\) pC. The enclosure-facing surface supplies the remaining \(-17\) pC.

In the worked example electrode two is isolated with a trapped \(Q_2=7\) pC. Determine the voltage induced when \(V_1=0\), and the small-signal input capacitance measured by varying \(V_1\).

Work through the solution

Solve \(7=-4V_1+7V_2\) to find \(V_2=1+4V_1/7\) V. The input charge is then \(-4+(26/7)V_1\) pC. The trapped charge shifts the intercept while leaving the incremental capacitance \(26/7\) pF in this linear dielectric model.

Why can an inferred matrix with a negative eigenvalue fail even if its two diagonal entries are positive?

Work through the solution

Choosing potentials proportional to that eigenvector would make the quadratic field energy negative. In a passive static dielectric with positive permittivity the field integral is nonnegative for every potential pattern. Positivity constrains the off-diagonal terms as well, for two terminals requiring \(C_{11}C_{22}\ge C_{12}^2\).

Further reading · MIT 8.07, conductors and the capacitance matrix.

A multi-electrode device generally has no single capacitance until the other terminals have been connected or isolated. An energy identity determines the matrix that relates voltages to charges, and a complementary flux identity can certify estimates even when the exact field is unknown.

Chapter 35 · How a conductor admits a field step and a sinusoid

A time-varying magnetic field enters a conducting slab from its surface. A suddenly imposed constant field continues to penetrate with elapsed time. A sinusoid establishes a persistent depth profile. Both behaviours follow from the same initial–boundary value equation.

Reduce Maxwell's equations to a diffusion equation

Use a uniform stationary Ohmic medium with scalar conductivity \(\sigma\) and permeability \(\mu\). Work on length and time scales for which displacement current is small compared with conduction current, \(\omega\epsilon/\sigma\ll1\) for each important Fourier component. Then

\[\nabla\times\boldsymbol B=\mu\sigma\boldsymbol E.\]

Taking a curl and using Faraday's law gives

\[\nabla\times\nabla\times\boldsymbol B=-\mu\sigma\partial_t\boldsymbol B.\]

The identity \(\nabla\times\nabla\times\boldsymbol B=\nabla(\nabla\cdot\boldsymbol B)-\nabla^2\boldsymbol B\), together with absence of magnetic monopoles, leaves

\[\partial_t\boldsymbol B=D_m\nabla^2\boldsymbol B,\]
\[D_m=\frac1{\mu\sigma}.\]

\(D_m\) has units of area per time. Larger conductivity slows penetration: a small electric field can drive larger currents that oppose the changing applied field. An ideal mathematical step contains arbitrarily high frequencies outside this reduction. The result describes observations made after the brief electromagnetic start-up, on distances large enough for a continuum Ohmic description.

Background · Skin depth
\[\delta=\sqrt{2/(\mu\sigma\omega)}\]

In a good homogeneous conductor under sinusoidal excitation this is the amplitude decay length. Intensity decays twice as fast in the exponent.

Solve the initial–boundary value problem for a step

Fill \(x>0\) with conductor and impose a tangential field \(B(0,t)=B_0\) for \(t>0\), with the interior initially field-free. At each finite time require \(B(x,t)\to0\) as \(x\to\infty\). There is no imposed length scale, so try \(B/B_0=F(\eta)\) with \(\eta=x/(2\sqrt{D_mt})\). The time derivative produces \(-\eta F'/(2t)\); the second space derivative times \(D_m\) gives \(F''/(4t)\). Therefore

\[F''+2\eta F'=0.\]

First integrate \(F'=Ae^{-\eta^2}\), then impose \(F(0)=1,F(\infty)=0\). The normalisation \(\int_0^\infty e^{-s^2}ds=\sqrt\pi/2\) gives

\[\frac{B(x,t)}{B_0}=\operatorname{erfc}\!\left(\frac{x}{2\sqrt{D_mt}}\right).\]

Any fixed fractional field level moves with \(\sqrt t\). The depth at half amplitude is

\[x_{1/2}=2\operatorname{erfc}^{-1}(0.5)\sqrt{D_mt}=0.9539\sqrt{D_mt}.\]

For copper represented by \(\sigma=5.8\times10^7\,\mathrm{S/m}\), \(\mu=\mu_0\), \(D_m=0.01372\,\mathrm{m^2/s}\). At \(0.10\,\mathrm{ms}\) the half-depth is \(1.12\,\mathrm{mm}\). Reaching twice that depth requires \(0.40\,\mathrm{ms}\).

Solve for a periodic steady state

At the same surface impose \(B(0,t)=\operatorname{Re}B_0e^{i\omega t}\) for long enough that the transient has passed. Seek \(B=\operatorname{Re}B_0 e^{i\omega t-kx}\). Substitution gives

\[D_m k^2=i\omega.\]

Select the root with positive real part, \(k=(1+i)/\delta\) with \(\delta=\sqrt{2D_m/\omega}\). Thus

\[B(x,t)=B_0e^{-x/\delta}\cos(\omega t-x/\delta).\]

At one skin depth the amplitude is \(e^{-1}\) of the surface amplitude and the oscillation lags by one radian. For the same model copper at 1 kHz, \(\delta=2.09\,\mathrm{mm}\), while the sinusoidal half-amplitude depth is \(\delta\ln2=1.45\,\mathrm{mm}\). A half-step depth and an exponential e-fold depth are different measurement definitions. Frequency and elapsed time are independent controls in the two experiments. In a slab comparable in thickness to either penetration scale the second interface supplies another boundary condition.

Read the two profiles at a shared probe

The graph plots the step response and the sinusoidal envelope against physical depth. Place the probe at 2 mm, vary the step duration and check the square-root law using the half-field depth. Hold that time fixed while quadrupling frequency. Only the periodic envelope shrinks by a factor of two in length. Time-dependent field and envelope both use normalised field-amplitude units.

Open this experiment online

Tutorial on inversion and currents

A step profile has half-field depth \(2.0\,\mathrm{mm}\) after \(0.30\,\mathrm{ms}\). Infer \(D_m\) and \(\sigma\) if \(\mu=\mu_0\).

Work through the solution
\[D_m=(0.002/0.9539)^2/0.00030=0.01465\,\mathrm{m^2/s}.\]

Conductivity is

\[1/(\mu_0D_m)=5.43\times10^7\,\mathrm{S/m}.\]

A single profile measures the product \(\mu\sigma\) unless permeability is independently known.

If \(B=B_z(x,t)\), find the sign and surface magnitude of \(J_y\) for a positive ideal step. Compare the current integrated over depth with the imposed field.

Work through the solution

Ampère gives

\[J_y=-\partial_xB_z/\mu.\]

The surface derivative is \(-B_0/\sqrt{\pi D_mt}\), hence current is positive and its magnitude falls as \(t^{-1/2}\). Its integral over all \(x>0\) is \(B_0/\mu\). The current spreads over a growing region while maintaining the total sheet current dictated by the field difference.

At a probe the AC envelope is 0.10 of the surface amplitude. What is the phase lag, and what is its time-delay equivalent at 1 kHz?

Work through the solution

Solve \(e^{-x/\delta}=0.1\), so

\[x/\delta=\ln10=2.303\,\mathrm{rad}.\]

At 1 kHz this equals

\[2.303/(2\pi\,1000)=0.367\,\mathrm{ms}.\]

This is the phase delay of a single sinusoid. A pulse contains many frequencies with different attenuation and phase shifts.

Further reading · MIT Electromechanical Dynamics, magnetic diffusion and sinusoidal skin effect.
