A conducting sheet initially shields its interior from an applied magnetic step. Given time, a normal resistive metal admits a static tangential magnetic field. The same equations give a finite slab a discrete relaxation spectrum and a periodic drive a complex penetration depth. These are different initial and boundary conditions for one diffusion operator.

Chapter 36 · Static screening and collective charge oscillations

In a neutral ion–electron gas a small positive probe draws an excess of electrons. A displaced electron fluid also experiences a restoring electric field and can oscillate. The equilibrium screening length and the collective frequency involve the same density but describe different experiments.

Count the electrons in a weak electrostatic potential

Assume fixed singly charged positive ions of uniform density \(n_0\), and classical electrons in local thermal equilibrium at temperature \(T_e\). Electron potential energy in an electric potential \(\phi\) is \(-e\phi\), where \(e>0\). The Boltzmann distribution relative to distant neutral plasma is \(n_e=n_0\exp[e\phi/(k_BT_e)]\). The net plasma charge density \(e(n_0-n_e)\) is negative near a small positive potential. Expand the exponential when \(|e\phi|\ll k_BT_e\). Including a prescribed weak external charge density gives

\[(\nabla^2-\lambda_D^{-2})\phi=-\rho_{\rm ext}/\epsilon_0,\]
\[\lambda_D^2=\frac{\epsilon_0 k_BT_e}{n_0e^2}.\]

For a point source in an unbounded uniform plasma the source-free spherical equation at \(r>0\) is \((r\phi)''=(r\phi)/\lambda_D^2\). Discard the growing exponential at infinity. The flux through a sufficiently small sphere fixes the coefficient of the \(1/r\) singularity, yielding \(\phi=Qe^{-r/\lambda_D}/(4\pi\epsilon_0 r)\) as the ideal linear Green function. A literal point charge makes \(\phi\) large arbitrarily close to it. Applying this linear expression as a microscopic prediction there would violate the assumption that produced it.

At \(r=\lambda_D\) the potential is \(e^{-1}\) times the bare Coulomb value at that same radius. The electric field is its derivative, so its ratio to the unscreened field is \((1+r/\lambda_D)e^{-r/\lambda_D}\). At one Debye length this is \(2/e=0.736\). Equating the field ratio to the potential ratio would incorrectly remove a derivative term. If several mobile thermal species can equilibrate, the linear charge responses add, giving inverse squared screening lengths that add.

Displace the electron fluid before the ions move

Now consider a rapid, small longitudinal displacement \(\xi(x,t)\) of a cold electron fluid against the uniform positive background. Particle conservation gives density perturbation \(\delta n=-n_0\partial_x\xi\). The resulting charge perturbation is \(e n_0\partial_x\xi\). For a nonzero spatial Fourier mode Gauss's law gives

\[E=en_0\xi/\epsilon_0,\]

with any uniform externally imposed field excluded. Newton's law \(m_e\ddot\xi=-eE\) then gives

\[\ddot\xi+\omega_p^2\xi=0,\]
\[\omega_p^2=\frac{n_0e^2}{m_e\epsilon_0},\]
\[\omega_p\lambda_D=\sqrt{\frac{k_BT_e}{m_e}}.\]

This frequency is in radians per second. The oscillation cycles at \(f_p=\omega_p/(2\pi)\). The length–frequency product equals a one-dimensional thermal-speed scale. The derivations used different closures: the static density had time to approach thermal equilibrium, while the oscillation neglected pressure gradients, collisions and ion motion. At appreciable \(k\lambda_D\), pressure and kinetic effects change the longitudinal frequency and damping. A fully kinetic model is required to predict Landau damping.

Infer density and temperature from two measurements

At \(n_0=10^{16}\,\mathrm{m^{-3}}\) and \(k_BT_e=2\,\mathrm{eV}\), the expressions give \(\lambda_D=105\,\mu\mathrm m\) and \(f_p=898\,\mathrm{MHz}\). Doubling temperature alone increases screening length by \(\sqrt2\) and leaves this cold oscillation frequency fixed. Quadrupling density at fixed temperature halves the length and doubles the frequency. With a measured frequency \(1.80\,\mathrm{GHz}\), density would be about four times the above value. An independently measured \(\lambda_D\) then determines \(k_BT_e=m_e(2\pi f_p\lambda_D)^2\).

Set density and temperature in the graph and compare screened potential and field ratios at a selected physical distance. Use the readout to turn an oscillation period into a density estimate. Check the continuum hypothesis by estimating \(N_D=4\pi n_0\lambda_D^3/3\), the number of particles in a Debye sphere. It is approximately \(4.9\times10^4\) at the worked point, making a collective description plausible. A small \(N_D\), degeneracy or strong coupling would undermine the thermal mean-field treatment.

Open this experiment online

Tutorial on independent spatial and temporal tests

A probe measures \(f_p=0.90\,\mathrm{GHz}\) and \(\lambda_D=210\,\mu\mathrm m\). Infer approximate density and thermal energy relative to the worked example.

Work through the solution

The frequency is essentially unchanged, so density is approximately \(10^{16}\,\mathrm{m^{-3}}\). The doubled screening length at fixed density requires four times the thermal energy, about 8 eV. The independent product check gives a thermal speed of roughly \(1.19\times10^6\,\mathrm{m/s}\).

How far from a weak source does the screened potential fall to 1 percent of the bare value? Calculate the field ratio at that point.

Work through the solution

The distance is

\[r=\lambda_D\ln100=4.605\lambda_D.\]

The field ratio is

\[(1+4.605)/100=0.0561.\]

These are ratios to the appropriate unscreened quantities at the same physical position.

If both electrons and singly ionised positive ions with equal temperature and density can rearrange in the static experiment, compare the new screening length with the electron-only value. Does this change the electron-frequency formula on a time scale where ions are stationary?

Work through the solution

Both species respond to weak potential with charge-density changes proportional to \(-q_s^2 n_s\phi/(k_BT_s)\). The two identical inverse squared lengths add, yielding \(\lambda_D/\sqrt2\). On the much shorter oscillation time scale the ions remain the fixed background in the cold electron derivation.

Chapter 37 · Reconstructing a partially polarised electromagnetic wave

A detector averages enormous numbers of optical cycles. Its horizontal and vertical readings may be equal for a circularly polarised wave, a diagonal linearly polarised wave, or unpolarised light. Which additional intensities distinguish these preparations?

Start from what a polarising analyser measures

Take a quasi-monochromatic beam propagating in a fixed direction, resolved in transverse axes \(x,y\). Use complex field amplitudes with time factor \(e^{-i\omega t}\). Absorb common power and impedance factors into their units. The time- or ensemble-averaged coherency matrix \(J=\langle\boldsymbol E\boldsymbol E^\dagger\rangle\) has four real degrees of freedom because it is Hermitian. An analyser selecting the normalised complex state \(\boldsymbol a\) passes amplitude \(\boldsymbol a^\dagger\boldsymbol E\) and measures \(I_a=\boldsymbol a^\dagger J\boldsymbol a\). Thus every analyser projects the same matrix onto a distinct polarisation.

Choose \(S_0=J_{xx}+J_{yy}\), \(S_1=J_{xx}-J_{yy}\),

\[S_2=2\operatorname{Re}J_{xy},\]
\[S_3=-2\operatorname{Im}J_{xy}.\]

For this convention the state \((1,i)/\sqrt2\) has positive \(S_3\). Naming it by its explicit Jones vector avoids a handedness ambiguity between observer viewing directions. Inverting those definitions gives

\[J=\frac12\begin{pmatrix}S_0+S_1&S_2-iS_3\\S_2+iS_3&S_0-S_1\end{pmatrix}.\]

Horizontal and vertical linear analysers therefore give \((S_0\pm S_1)/2\). The \(+45^\circ,-45^\circ\) pair gives \((S_0\pm S_2)/2\). The circular pair \((1,\pm i)/\sqrt2\) gives \((S_0\pm S_3)/2\). Every pair sum recovers total intensity, providing an internal calibration check. Subtracting the complementary measurements cancels a common additive detector offset in each Stokes difference, though \(S_0\) still needs a dark correction.

Derive the physically allowed domain

Because \(I_a\ge0\) for every analyser, both eigenvalues of \(J\) are nonnegative. Solve its quadratic characteristic equation using the trace \(S_0\) and determinant \((S_0^2-S_1^2-S_2^2-S_3^2)/4\). The eigenvalues are \((S_0\pm|\boldsymbol S|)/2\), where \(\boldsymbol S=(S_1,S_2,S_3)\). Consequently \(P=|\boldsymbol S|/S_0\) lies between zero and one for a beam with nonzero intensity. A single fully polarised Jones state gives rank one and \(P=1\). An incoherent mixture of two orthogonal states of equal intensity has \(J=(S_0/2)I\) and \(P=0\).

Suppose a corrected data set gives \(I_x,I_y=70,30\); \(I_{+45},I_{-45}=65,35\); \(I_+,I_-=60,40\) in the same units. The pair sums agree at 100. Reconstructed parameters are \((100,40,30,20)\), giving \(P=\sqrt{2900}/100=0.539\). The eigenvalues are 76.93 and 23.07. Subtracting the smaller times the identity leaves a rank-one contribution of intensity 53.85 and an unpolarised remainder of intensity 46.15. This decomposition describes the observed second moments; several microscopic preparations can produce the same \(J\).

Predict a rotating analyser and identify its blind spot

For \(\boldsymbol a=(\cos\alpha,\sin\alpha)\), expanding the projection and using double-angle identities gives

\[I_\alpha=[S_0+S_1\cos2\alpha+S_2\sin2\alpha]/2.\]

A linear analyser alone is blind to \(S_3\), even when sampled at hundreds of angles. In the example the extrema are \(50\pm25\), with the maximum at \(\alpha=\frac12\operatorname{atan2}(30,40)=18.43^\circ\). The linear fringe visibility 0.50 is slightly below the total degree 0.539. Inserting a quarter-wave plate with Jones matrix \(\operatorname{diag}(1,-i)\) before the same analyser transforms \(S_2\) into \(S_3\) in the intensity formula. One can now obtain the previously hidden signed correlation from readings at \(45^\circ\) and \(135^\circ\).

The experiment prepares an adjustable polarised fraction with azimuth \(\psi\) and ellipticity angle \(\chi\), mixed with an unpolarised background. Its normalised Stokes vector is \(P(\cos2\chi\cos2\psi,\cos2\chi\sin2\psi,\sin2\chi)\). Make the unassisted intensity scan flat by choosing circular polarisation, then insert the fixed retarder virtually and predict the recovered difference. Setting \(P=0\) makes both scans flat. This comparison shows which measurement discriminates the two cases.

Open this experiment online

Tutorial on instrument design

A linear scan alone has \(I_{\max}=75,I_{\min}=25\). Give the range of total degrees of polarisation allowed and the maximum possible magnitude of \(S_3\).

Work through the solution

The linear magnitude is 50 and \(S_0=100\). Thus \(0.5\le P\le1\), and the positivity bound gives

\[|S_3|\le\sqrt{100^2-50^2}=86.60.\]

A circular analyser measurement fixes the remaining magnitude and sign.

An ideal beam contains 60 units of pure horizontal light and 40 units of unpolarised light. Compare its Stokes vector with a coherent superposition of horizontal and vertical components with intensities 80 and 20 and zero relative phase.

Work through the solution

The incoherent mixture has \((100,60,0,0)\) and \(P=0.6\). The coherent preparation has \((100,60,80,0)\) since \(2\sqrt{80\times20}=80\), and \(P=1\). Their horizontal and vertical readings coincide. A diagonal analyser gives 50 for the mixture and 90 for the coherent preparation.

All three measured component differences equal 70 at measured total 100. Can a physical beam have these parameters?

Work through the solution

They imply \(|\boldsymbol S|=70\sqrt3=121.2>S_0\) and a negative matrix eigenvalue. Check dark subtraction, gain calibration, alignment and whether the source changed between readings. A physical fit with stated uncertainties is required before interpreting the data as an optical state.

Chapter 38 · Recovering a vector field from divergence, curl and boundary data

A numerical field solver returns three components at every point. Divergence measures sources and curl measures circulation, yet neither measurement detects a spatially uniform offset. Helmholtz decomposition makes precise what can be recovered, how to compute it, and what the boundary must supply.

Invert the vector Laplacian in open space

Let \(\boldsymbol F\) be smooth on all of space and rapidly decreasing, together with its needed derivatives, so integration by parts has no surface term at infinity. The identity \(\nabla^2\boldsymbol F=\nabla(\nabla\cdot\boldsymbol F)-\nabla\times(\nabla\times\boldsymbol F)\) reduces reconstruction to three scalar Poisson inversions. Define \(G(\boldsymbol r)=1/(4\pi|\boldsymbol r|)\); distributionally \(-\nabla^2G=\delta^3\). For \(d=\nabla\cdot\boldsymbol F\) and \(\boldsymbol c=\nabla\times\boldsymbol F\), convolution with \(G\) gives

\[\Phi=G*d,\]
\[\boldsymbol A=G*\boldsymbol c,\]
\[\boldsymbol F=-\nabla\Phi+\nabla\times\boldsymbol A .\]

To verify, first note that \(\nabla\cdot\boldsymbol c=0\); a supplied curl field must satisfy this compatibility condition. Moving the derivative through convolution gives

\[\nabla\cdot\boldsymbol A=G*(\nabla\cdot\boldsymbol c)=0.\]

The divergence of the proposed \(\boldsymbol F\) is \(-\nabla^2\Phi=d\), and its curl is

\[\nabla(\nabla\cdot\boldsymbol A)-\nabla^2\boldsymbol A=\boldsymbol c.\]

Any difference from the original field has zero divergence and curl, hence componentwise zero Laplacian. Smoothness and decay on all space force this harmonic difference to vanish. The reconstructed vector pieces are unique in this setting, while adding a gradient to an unrestricted vector potential still leaves its curl unchanged.

Derive the Fourier projectors

On a periodic grid separate the mean mode first. For a nonzero Fourier wavevector \(\boldsymbol k\) with convention \(e^{i\boldsymbol k\cdot\boldsymbol r}\), differentiation multiplies by \(i\boldsymbol k\). A longitudinal component is parallel to \(\boldsymbol k\), so its amplitude must reproduce the scalar product \(\boldsymbol k\cdot\widehat{\boldsymbol F}\). Subtraction leaves a perpendicular component:

\[\widehat{\boldsymbol F}_L=\frac{\boldsymbol k(\boldsymbol k\cdot\widehat{\boldsymbol F})}{|\boldsymbol k|^2},\]
\[\widehat{\boldsymbol F}_T=\widehat{\boldsymbol F}-\widehat{\boldsymbol F}_L.\]

The first projector squared equals itself, and the two pieces are orthogonal. Thus their squared magnitudes add mode by mode, even for complex amplitudes with the Hermitian inner product. Equivalently the longitudinal piece has zero curl and the transverse piece has zero divergence. At \(\boldsymbol k=0\), the denominator vanishes and both derivative measurements are zero. A known mean, applied uniform field or boundary condition supplies that information. Setting the mean to zero silently would discard an actual applied bias.

Recover a patterned measurement

Take a two-dimensional periodic field \(\boldsymbol F=\boldsymbol b+\boldsymbol a\cos(2x+y)\) in dimensionless periodic coordinates with \(\boldsymbol a=(3,1)\), \(\boldsymbol b=(1,0)\). Its measured divergence is \(-7\sin(2x+y)\). Its out-of-plane curl is \(+\sin(2x+y)\), from \(\partial_xF_y-\partial_yF_x\). Projection with \(\boldsymbol k=(2,1)\) gives \(\boldsymbol a_L=(2.8,1.4)\), \(\boldsymbol a_T=(0.2,-0.4)\). The squared amplitudes are 9.8 and 0.2, summing to the original 10; only 2 percent of the nonconstant modal power is transverse. Neither differentiated pattern contains the bias. At phase zero the observed x-component is four, of which 2.8 is longitudinal, 0.2 transverse and one is uniform.

The graph scans phase, showing the x-component of the measured field, the two recovered varying pieces and the mean. Change the input amplitudes until \(\boldsymbol k\cdot\boldsymbol a=0\), then until \(\boldsymbol k\times\boldsymbol a=0\). Changing the mean should move only the total and constant terms. In a discretised solver the differentiation symbol used in a projection must match the numerical divergence being tested; the exact spectral \(i\boldsymbol k\) and a finite difference need not represent the same grid operator.

Open this experiment online

Specify a boundary on a finite domain

One convenient decomposition writes \(\boldsymbol F=\nabla u+\boldsymbol T\) with \(\nabla\cdot\boldsymbol T=0\) and \(\boldsymbol T\cdot\boldsymbol n=0\) on the boundary. Solve the Neumann problem \(\nabla^2u=\nabla\cdot\boldsymbol F,\ \partial_nu=\boldsymbol F\cdot\boldsymbol n\). The divergence theorem makes these data compatible. The potential is determined up to an additive constant in a connected domain, which does not affect its gradient. Orthogonality follows from integrating \(\nabla u\cdot\boldsymbol T\) by parts: both the volume divergence and boundary normal term vanish. Holes can admit nontrivial fields with zero curl and divergence, so reconstructing a full vector field from its derivatives alone can require additional circulation data.

Tutorial on recovering missing information

With \(\boldsymbol k=(2,1)\), a sensor returns divergence \(-5\sin(2x+y)\) and curl \(-5\sin(2x+y)\). Infer the cosine amplitudes \(a_x,a_y\).

Work through the solution

From the divergence, \(2a_x+a_y=5\). From the curl, \(2a_y-a_x=5\). Solving gives

\[a_x=1,a_y=3.\]

The projected amplitudes are \((2,1)\) and \((-1,2)\), with equal squared magnitude. The mean remains independent of both readings.

On an annulus \(a<r<b\), consider \(\boldsymbol H=\boldsymbol e_\theta/r\). Which derivative and boundary data vanish? Propose one measurement that distinguishes it from zero.

Work through the solution

Its planar divergence vanishes and its out-of-plane curl is \(r^{-1}\partial_r(rH_\theta)=0\) on the annulus. Its normal component vanishes at both circular boundaries. Nevertheless circulation around any circle surrounding the hole is \(2\pi\). The axis where the field is singular is excluded, so the all-space uniqueness argument does not apply.

A computed projection claims longitudinal power 6, transverse power 4, and original power 13 in one nonzero Fourier mode. Is this consistent with exact orthogonal projection in the same norm?

Work through the solution

No. The two projected vectors are perpendicular, so their powers must sum to the original 13. Check whether powers include the same normalisation, whether the mean was included, and whether the solver and diagnostic use the same differentiation symbol and inner product.

Chapter 39 · A ring, a disk and an electric-field maximum in empty space

Gauss’s law gives the flux through a closed surface. For a finite circular source the field varies across that surface. Adding the fields of actual charge elements predicts both the near field and a surprising axial maximum when the centre is removed.

Decide what symmetry eliminates

A uniformly charged ring of radius \(s\) lies in the \(xy\) plane. A detector on the \(z\) axis is a distance \(R=\sqrt{s^2+z^2}\) from every charge element. Contributions transverse to the axis cancel in diametrically opposite pairs. The potential adds as a scalar, giving \(dV=dq/(4\pi\epsilon_0 R)\) for the whole ring charge \(dq\). Choose zero potential at infinity. Differentiating with respect to detector position gives

\[dE_z=z\,dq/(4\pi\epsilon_0R^3).\]

The same factor \(z/R\) appears if each Coulomb force is projected directly onto the axis. At the ring centre the potential is finite and the field is zero.

Construct an annulus with uniform surface density \(\sigma\), inner radius \(a\) and outer radius \(b\). A radial interval \(ds\) contributes \(dq=2\pi\sigma s\,ds\); forgetting \(s\) would assign equal charge to equal widths at the centre and rim. Integrating and differentiating yields

\[V(z)=\frac{\sigma}{2\epsilon_0}\left[\sqrt{z^2+b^2}-\sqrt{z^2+a^2}\right],\]
\[E_z(z)=\frac{\sigma z}{2\epsilon_0}\left[\frac1{\sqrt{z^2+a^2}}-\frac1{\sqrt{z^2+b^2}}\right].\]

The potential is even in \(z\) and the field odd. When \(a>0\) every point on the central axis is in empty space and both functions are smooth there. This smoothness changes in the disk limit.

Investigate two noncommuting limits

Set \(a=0\) before moving the probe to the plane. The potential then contains \(-|z|\) and the field contains \(\operatorname{sgn}(z)\). Thus \(E_z(0^+)-E_z(0^-)=\sigma/\epsilon_0\), just the charge-sheet jump. By contrast, taking \(z\to0\) first at any positive hole radius gives zero field. The order of shrinking the hole and approaching its centre determines whether the probe sits on material. A grid that places its probe exactly at \(z=0\) for both geometries can conceal the difference.

At large positive \(z\), Taylor-expand the two square roots before subtracting. The \(z\) terms cancel. Since \(Q=\pi\sigma(b^2-a^2)\),

\[V(z)=\frac{Q}{4\pi\epsilon_0z}\left[1-\frac{a^2+b^2}{4z^2}+O(b^4/z^4)\right],\]
\[E_z=\frac{Q}{4\pi\epsilon_0z^2}\left[1-\frac{3(a^2+b^2)}{4z^2}+\cdots\right].\]

The axial dipole term is absent by reflection symmetry. For very large \(z\) a numerical difference between almost identical square roots loses precision. Multiply by the conjugate to evaluate \(V=\sigma(b^2-a^2)/[2\epsilon_0(\sqrt{z^2+b^2}+\sqrt{z^2+a^2})]\).

Find an extremum without violating the vacuum field equations

For a nonzero hole the field grows linearly near the origin and decreases as an inverse square in the far field. Differentiate \(z/\sqrt{z^2+s^2}\) to get \(s^2/(z^2+s^2)^{3/2}\). Equating the two edge contributions gives

\[z_{\max}^2=\frac{b^2a^{4/3}-a^2b^{4/3}}{b^{4/3}-a^{4/3}} .\]

This is a maximum of one component along one line. No interior maximum of the electrostatic potential is implied. A lateral displacement would break the ring-pair cancellation and requires integration over the azimuthal coordinate. On axis the field also equals the difference between the fields of two disks of common density.

Plan two field measurements

Locate a peak in a centimetre-scale annulus

Choose \(a=10\) mm, \(b=20\) mm and \(\sigma=1.0\) nC/m². The maximum occurs at \(z=0.4934b=9.87\) mm. At this point \(2\epsilon_0 E_z/\sigma=0.25992\), so \(E_z=14.7\) V/m. A point charge approximation would incorrectly predict that the field increases indefinitely as the detector approaches the hole. The missing charge near the centre matters even though the whole source has nonzero net charge.

Turn a desired error into a measurement distance

For the same radius ratio the leading relative correction to the monopole field is \(0.9375(b/z)^2\). To keep this correction near 1%, choose \(z/b\simeq9.68\), about 0.194 m here. Substituting this distance in the exact expression checks the term neglected in the estimate. For a radial charge distribution with changing sign the monopole could cancel altogether, invalidating the inference.

Integrate an annulus ring by ring

The graph compares midpoint integration over physical ring areas against the analytic axial field. A hole radius of half the outer radius puts the maximum at z/b = 0.4934. Move the inner edge and refine the source cells separately. A changing peak location and a shrinking numerical error have different causes.

Open this experiment online

Problem sheet · what can an axial probe tell you?

Locate the peak of a narrow ring

Shrink the annulus to a narrow ring of fixed total charge and radius \(a\). Find the field maximum directly and compare the answer with the picture above.

Work through the solution

The ring field is proportional to \(z/(z^2+a^2)^{3/2}\). Its derivative is proportional to \((a^2-2z^2)/(z^2+a^2)^{5/2}\). Thus the maximum on the positive axis occurs at \(a/\sqrt2\). Keeping total charge fixed requires the surface density to grow as the width shrinks.

Compute with a nonuniform surface density

Suppose the density increases linearly from zero at the centre of a disk to \(\sigma_0\) at its outer radius \(b\). Describe an integration rule and give two independent checks that do not require an analytic field formula.

Work through the solution

Divide the radius into cells with midpoint \(s_j\). Assign each cell its exact area \(\pi(s_{j,+}^2-s_{j,-}^2)\), multiply by \(\sigma_0s_j/b\), and add the axial ring field. The summed source charge must converge to \(2\pi\sigma_0 b^2/3\). At large \(z\) the computed field times \(4\pi\epsilon_0z^2\) approaches this same charge. At each fixed positive \(z\), double the cell count and check convergence separately from the far-field comparison.

Study the full derivation

From a force reading to Poisson’s equation · Electrostatic field theory and measurement

Imagine trying to infer an invisible charge distribution with a force probe and a voltmeter. Coulomb’s law, Gauss’s law and the electrostatic potential describe the same experiment in three different ways. Deriving the connections also exposes the measurements a single probe cannot make.

Chapter 40 · The same metal sphere connected to ground or electrically isolated

A grounded sphere can draw charge through a wire. An isolated one can only rearrange what is already present. Both are equipotentials, but the second problem needs a different image system and gives a different force at long range.

Find the image by matching distances on a sphere

A positive test charge \(q\) sits at \(z=d>a\) outside a conducting sphere of radius \(a\) centred at the origin. In the exterior vacuum region the potential has the known Coulomb singularity at \(q\) and is otherwise harmonic. Look for an auxiliary point \(s\hat{\mathbf z}\) inside the metal whose distance from each surface point is proportional to the distance from the real charge. The squared distances at polar angle \(\theta\) are \(a^2+s^2-2as\cos\theta\) and \(a^2+d^2-2ad\cos\theta\). Matching their constant and cosine terms yields

\[s=a^2/d,\]
\[R_s=(a/d)R_q.\]

A charge \(q'=-qa/d\) at the auxiliary point then cancels the real potential on the sphere. The superposition vanishes at infinity. Uniqueness for prescribed potentials makes this the actual exterior solution. The mathematical source is outside the physical domain of the solution. A surface enclosing just the conductor can be evaluated using the equivalent exterior field, so the total induced charge is \(q'\). It arrived through the grounding connection.

Change the constraint by adding one image

For an isolated sphere of prescribed total charge \(Q_c\), its surface potential is a constant that must be determined. Add a central charge \(q_0=Q_c-q'\). Its surface contribution \(q_0/(4\pi\epsilon_0 a)\) is uniform, preserving equipotentiality, while the total equivalent enclosed charge becomes \(Q_c\). The resulting sphere potential is \(V_s=Q_c/(4\pi\epsilon_0a)+q/(4\pi\epsilon_0d)\). The grounded and neutral isolated solutions agree only when the geometry or external charge makes their net-charge constraints coincide.

Use Gauss's boundary condition \(\sigma=-\epsilon_0\partial_r V|_{a^+}\). The grounded result and its modification are

\[\sigma_g(\theta)=-\frac{q}{4\pi a}\frac{d^2-a^2}{(d^2+a^2-2ad\cos\theta)^{3/2}},\]
\[\sigma_c(\theta)=\sigma_g(\theta)+\frac{q_0}{4\pi a^2}.\]

For a neutral sphere the charge layer facing the source is negative, while a sufficiently distant part of the surface becomes positive. Integrating over the sphere involves the area element \(2\pi a^2\sin\theta\,d\theta\). A uniform angular average without that weight miscounts the sharply concentrated polar charge.

Take a force at the real charge, then take a large-distance limit

Evaluate the electric field of the image charges only at the real charge. The grounded force \(F_z\) and its neutral-isolated counterpart are

\[F_g=-\frac{q^2}{4\pi\epsilon_0}\frac{ad}{(d^2-a^2)^2},\]
\[F_{\rm neutral}=F_g+\frac{q^2}{4\pi\epsilon_0}\frac{a}{d^3}.\]

At \(d\gg a\), the grounded force begins at order \(d^{-3}\) because the grounded sphere acquires charge proportional to \(1/d\). In the neutral case that leading term cancels, leaving \(-2q^2 a^3/(4\pi\epsilon_0 d^5)\). The conductor responds mainly as an induced dipole. This cancellation offers a demanding numerical check at large separation. For the grounded case the energy relative to infinite separation follows from integrating \(-F_g\) with respect to \(d\), yielding \(U=-q^2a/[8\pi\epsilon_0(d^2-a^2)]\). It also equals \(qV_{\rm image}(d)/2\), with the half arising as the conductor polarises continuously during assembly.

Compare two preparations with identical geometry

Unplug a sphere before approaching it

Set \(a=20\) mm, \(d=40\) mm and \(q=1.0\) nC. The auxiliary image lies at 10 mm and has charge \(-0.50\) nC. Grounding gives \(F_g=-4.99\) μN. For a neutral isolated sphere the added central \(+0.50\) nC exerts \(+2.81\) μN and the total is \(-2.18\) μN. Its surface potential is \(q/(4\pi\epsilon_0d)\simeq225\) V. In both experiments the metal still has no interior electric field in static equilibrium.

Disconnect after the charge is already present

If the wire is removed at \(d=2a\), the sphere keeps its acquired \(-q/2\). With the real charge still at \(2a\) the exterior solution is unchanged. Move it to \(4a\). The new off-centre image is \(-q/4\) and the central image is also \(-q/4\). The net conductor charge remains \(-q/2\), and its potential becomes negative. A calculation that continually sets the sphere voltage to zero after disconnection would model an ongoing exchange of charge with an external reservoir.

Measure the charge density of two spheres with different connections

With the source at two sphere radii, the grounded surface draws a total charge −q/2; the neutral isolated sphere retains zero total charge. Change the distance and the trapped initial conductor charge. Inspect the source-facing pole and the far side before deciding whether a net force can be repulsive.

Problem sheet · charge balance and a near-surface limit

Recover a plane image from a curved surface

Let \(d=a+h\) with \(h\ll a\). Show that the near-surface force on the charge approaches the grounded plane result and determine when the central neutralising image matters.

Work through the solution

Use \(d^2-a^2=2ah+h^2\). The leading grounded force is \(-q^2/(16\pi\epsilon_0h^2)\), identical to attraction to an image \(-q\) a distance \(2h\) away. The central neutralising field is of order \(q/(4\pi\epsilon_0a^2)\), smaller by order \((h/a)^2\) in the force budget.

Where does a neutral sphere change surface charge sign?

For \(d=2a\) and \(Q_c=0\), solve \(\sigma_c=0\) for the polar angle. How can a sphere still attract the external charge with zero net charge?

Work through the solution

In units \(q/(4\pi a^2)\) the equation is

\[-3/(5-4\cos\theta)^{3/2}+1/2=0.\]

Therefore \(\cos\theta=(5-6^{2/3})/4\) and the sign change occurs near \(65^\circ\). Negative surface charge is closer to the positive real charge; the inverse-square field weights its attraction more strongly than repulsion by distant positive charge.

An image source is a construction for a particular physical domain and boundary condition. Three examples show how geometry determines the image position, how material response sets its amplitude, and why an apparent success on part of a boundary is insufficient.

Chapter 41 · How a circular wall selects Bessel modes

A voltage pattern is imposed on the end of a long grounded tube. Its penetration length depends on the tube radius through a number that looks unfamiliar in a Cartesian Fourier series. Deriving that number also explains the proper radial weight for projecting data.

Separate Laplace’s equation without flattening the circular wall

Take an empty cylinder of radius \(a\) extending from \(z=0\) to large positive \(z\). Its side is grounded. A segmented end electrode imposes the continuous axisymmetric potential \(V(r,0)=V_0[1-(r/a)^2]\), matching zero at the rim. In cylindrical coordinates \(\nabla^2V=r^{-1}\partial_r(r\partial_rV)+\partial_z^2V=0\). Set \(V=R(r)Z(z)\). A decaying solution requires \(Z=e^{-kz}\) with \(k>0\). Then

\[(rR')'+k^2rR=0 .\]

Using \(\xi=kr\) gives Bessel's equation of order zero. The regular solution \(J_0(\xi)\) starts at one with zero derivative. Its series follows by substituting \(R=\sum c_m\xi^{2m}\): the recurrence is \(c_{m+1}=-c_m/[4(m+1)^2]\). The independent solution diverges logarithmically at the origin and would introduce an unmodelled line source. The side boundary requires \(J_0(ka)=0\), so \(k_n=j_n/a\) with \(j_n\) the positive zeros of \(J_0\). The first three are approximately \(2.40483,5.52008,8.65373\).

Derive the radial weight and coefficients

Multiply the equation for \(R_m\) by \(R_n\) and subtract the reversed equation. Integration gives \((k_m^2-k_n^2)\int_0^a rR_mR_n\,dr\) equal to a boundary term. At \(a\) both functions vanish; at zero their derivatives are regular and the factor \(r\) vanishes. Hence distinct modes are orthogonal with the radial weight \(r\). That factor represents the area of a circular ring. The squared norm follows from the derivative identities \(J_0'=-J_1\), \((tJ_1)'=tJ_0\), using the known zero at \(a\):

\[\int_0^1 xJ_0(j_nx)^2\,dx=\frac{J_1(j_n)^2}{2},\]
\[b_n=\frac{2\int_0^1 x(1-x^2)J_0(j_nx)\,dx}{J_1(j_n)^2}.\]

Use \((xJ_1(jx))'=jxJ_0(jx)\) to integrate the numerator by parts. The endpoint factor \(1-x^2\) vanishes at \(x=1\); the remaining integral is

\[2j^{-1}\int_0^1 x^2 J_1(jx)\,dx=2J_2(j)/j^2.\]

At a zero of \(J_0\), \(J_2(j)=2J_1(j)/j\). Thus \(b_n=8/[j_n^3J_1(j_n)]\), with alternating signs. The full solution is

\[V(r,z)=V_0\sum_{n=1}^\infty b_n J_0(j_n r/a)e^{-j_n z/a}.\]

Each partial sum exactly grounds the side wall and decays toward infinity. The representation of the end electrode improves as modes are added. For a finite cylinder closed at \(z=L\), replace each exponential by \(\sinh[k_n(L-z)]/\sinh(k_nL)\). This satisfies both end conditions and tends to the long-cylinder result at fixed \(z\) as \(L\) grows.

Estimate a leakage length and a modal error

How far does the slowest mode survive?

For \(a=12\) mm the first modal decay length is

\[a/j_1=4.99\,\mathrm{mm}.\]

Far from the end, two axis probes separated by 5.0 mm should read voltages in ratio about \(e^{-2.40483(5/12)}=0.367\). The first coefficient \(b_1\simeq1.108\) is larger than unity because the higher modes bring the prescribed central boundary value back to exactly \(V_0\). A fit using \(V_0e^{-j_1z/a}\) would get the correct distant slope but the wrong amplitude.

Predict the accuracy of a one-mode model

The second coefficient is about \(-0.140\). On axis the magnitude of its contribution relative to the first is approximately \(0.126\,e^{-(5.520-2.405)z/a}\). At \(z=a\) this is 0.56%. At \(z=0\) higher modes cannot be neglected at the same tolerance. Near a radial node of a chosen reference mode a relative error becomes unstable; use absolute potential error measured in units of \(V_0\) there.

Reconstruct a circular electrode pattern with Bessel modes

Each retained mode exactly satisfies the side-wall condition. At the end, one mode alone overestimates the central voltage by about 10.8%. Move the detector deeper into the tube and compare three and eight modes until their interior traces coincide to the precision you need.

Problem sheet · source weighting and a radial inverse problem

Explain a nonzero axis slope in a file of radial data

Someone fits the central potential by \(V=A+Br\) near the cylinder axis. What does a nonzero \(B\) imply in the continuum problem?

Work through the solution

A smooth axisymmetric Cartesian scalar must have zero radial derivative at the axis. The term \(Br\) would give \(r^{-1}\partial_r(r\partial_rV)=B/r\), incompatible with a smooth source-free interior and finite homogeneous axial curvature. An interpolation can manufacture this feature if it treats the axis as an arbitrary material boundary.

Infer tube radius using only distant measurements

Two distant on-axis probes separated by 3.00 mm have a voltage ratio of 0.500. Infer \(a\) under first-mode dominance, then design a check against residual higher modes.

Work through the solution

From \(e^{-j_1\Delta z/a}=1/2\), \(a=j_1\Delta z/\ln2=10.4\) mm. Move both probes farther from the end by the same amount. A persistent ratio supports the one-mode approximation. If higher modes remain, their changing relative weight changes the ratio. Very small voltages may instead expose the noise floor and lead to an apparently shallower decay.

Chapter 42 · Forces and torques from a matrix of flux linkages

Two measurements made while holding current fixed and flux fixed can produce different torque curves. They agree on the torque of the same physical state. A derivation from electrical work identifies precisely what must be held fixed when differentiating.

Keep track of each electrical and mechanical port

Let \(\theta\) be the mechanical angle of a pair of coils, \(i_j\) the currents entering their positive terminals and \(\lambda_j\) their linked fluxes, including all turns. Use ideal windings, a reversible magnetic medium and negligible radiation. Faraday's terminal relation is

\[v_j=d\lambda_j/dt.\]

With positive torque \(T\) doing work on the moving rotor, energy balance reads

\[dW_m=\sum_j i_j\,d\lambda_j-T\,d\theta .\]

The natural variables of magnetic energy \(W_m\) are fluxes and position. Consequently \(i_j=(\partial W_m/\partial\lambda_j)_\theta\) and \(T=-(\partial W_m/\partial\theta)_\lambda\). A current-controlled experiment supplies or removes electrical work during motion. Define the coenergy \(W'_m=\sum i_j\lambda_j-W_m\). Its differential is \(\sum_j\lambda_j\,di_j+T\,d\theta\), giving \(T=(\partial W'_m/\partial\theta)_i\). Coenergy is a Legendre transform. Its numerical value equals stored energy for linear zero-bias materials but can differ for nonlinear response.

Derive reciprocity, positivity and torque

Take \(\boldsymbol\lambda=L(\theta)\mathbf i\) with a two-port inductance matrix. From the existence of \(W'_m\), mixed derivatives at fixed angle commute, so

\[\partial\lambda_1/\partial i_2=\partial\lambda_2/\partial i_1.\]

This gives \(L_{12}=L_{21}=M\) for the given terminal orientation. With positive self-inductances, positive stored energy requires \(L_1L_2-M^2>0\) for independent currents in a nonsingular model. Integrating coenergy at fixed angle gives

\[W'_m=\mathbf i^T L\mathbf i/2.\]

The energy in its own natural variables is \(W_m=\boldsymbol\lambda^T L^{-1}\boldsymbol\lambda/2\). Differentiate \(L^{-1}L=I\) to obtain

\[(L^{-1})'=-L^{-1}L'L^{-1}.\]

Thus both torque formulas at the same state give

\[T=\tfrac12\mathbf i^T\frac{\partial L}{\partial\theta}\mathbf i .\]

For constant self-inductances and \(M=M_0\cos\theta\),

\[T=-M_0i_1i_2\sin\theta.\]

Reversing one winding reverses the coordinate definitions of its current and mutual inductance together, preserving the physical result. Under prescribed fluxes the same formula holds with currents \(\mathbf i=L(\theta)^{-1}\boldsymbol\lambda\) recalculated at every angle.

Compare a current supply with two flux-conserving loops

Start at the same state, then turn the coils

Use \(L_1=4.0\) mH, \(L_2=9.0\) mH and \(M_0=3.0\) mH. At \(\theta_0=60^\circ\), let currents be \(2.00\) A and \(1.00\) A. The flux linkages are \(9.50\) and \(12.0\) mWb. At this configuration \(T=-5.20\) mN m and the energy is \(15.5\) mJ. The units follow from an inductance times current squared, which is energy, while angle in radians is dimensionless.

Move to \(90^\circ\). Keeping both currents fixed gives \(T=-6.00\) mN m. Keeping both fluxes fixed instead gives \(i_1=9.50/4.0=2.375\) A and \(i_2=12.0/9.0=1.333\) A because the mutual term has vanished. The new torque is \(-9.50\) mN m. The two paths through state space now represent genuinely different experiments. For the fixed-current path the field energy falls by 3.00 mJ. The sources absorb 6.00 mJ and the external mechanical agent supplies 3.00 mJ, consistent with the first law.

A nonlinear constitutive curve

For one winding model a reversible flux linkage \(\lambda=L_\ell i+\Lambda\tanh(i/I_s)\), where positive \(L_\ell,\Lambda,I_s\) may depend on geometry. Integration gives

\[W'_m=L_\ell i^2/2+\Lambda I_s\ln\cosh(i/I_s);\]
\[W_m=i\lambda-W'_m.\]

Only in the linear weak-current limit do they coincide. A measured hysteresis loop would make this single-valued construction invalid without additional state variables describing material history.

Compare turning a rotor at fixed current and at fixed flux

Both protocols start at 60°. With initial currents 2 A and 1 A, the torques there coincide at −5.20 mN m but reach −6.00 and −9.50 mN m at 90°. Reverse one initial current and identify the terms changed by the corresponding constraints.

Problem sheet · independent torque measurements

Test a computed torque numerically

How would a finite-difference experiment recover torque in the preceding fixed-flux state without differentiating any matrix entries symbolically?

Work through the solution

Take the known \(\boldsymbol\lambda\), invert \(L\) at \(\theta\pm h\) separately and compute \(W_\pm=\boldsymbol\lambda^TL_\pm^{-1}\boldsymbol\lambda/2\). Estimate \(T=-(W_+-W_-)/(2h)\) using \(h\) in radians. At \(90^\circ\) the result converges to \(-9.50\) mN m. Reusing the same currents at both perturbations silently changes what the finite difference measures.

Infer the size of the conservative part of coupling

At fixed angle a small current cycle on the \(i_1,i_2\) plane produces \(\oint(\lambda_1di_1+\lambda_2di_2)\neq0\) after correcting lead resistance. What does this say about a proposed coenergy function?

Work through the solution

An exact differential has zero integral around every closed path. A repeatable nonzero result means that a single-valued coenergy of the two currents alone cannot describe these measurements. Check frequency-dependent losses, hysteresis and whether an unmeasured mechanical coordinate moved. Making the inductance matrix symmetric by averaging two readings alone cannot explain the residual work.

A winding links flux through each turn. In two windings the current in either one can change the voltage in the other. A matrix of flux linkages describes this coupling, but predicting power or mechanical force requires specifying the current directions and the control conditions.

Chapter 43 · Where current and energy go in a charging capacitor

A wire carries current to the centre of a plate, yet charge appears across its face and the energy increases in the gap. Following that current over differently chosen surfaces gives a spatial test of charge conservation and an independent power budget.

A circulation must give one answer for every spanning surface

Surround the charging lead by a loop. A flat surface inside the lead intercepts conduction current; a surface stretched into the insulating gap can avoid the lead altogether. Applying the magnetostatic law to both would assign different circulation to the same loop. Charge continuity and Gauss's law instead give

\[\nabla\cdot(\mathbf J+\epsilon_0\partial_t\mathbf E)=-\partial_t\rho+\partial_t\rho=0 .\]

Consequently the flux of this sum through any two surfaces with the same boundary agrees. Ampère–Maxwell equates the circulation of \(\mathbf B/\mu_0\) to that common enclosed current in vacuum. In a material with identified free current the macroscopic balance uses \(\mathbf H,\mathbf J_f,\partial_t\mathbf D\), incorporating polarisation. The divergence identity verifies consistency; the magnetic field generated by the additional term is a physical prediction of Maxwell's equation.

Resolve the charging current across the plate

Take circular metal plates of radius \(a\), separation \(d\ll a\), connected at their centres. Work at times long compared with \(a/c\) and neglect small edge and lead corrections. In the gap \(E_z=V/d\) is approximately uniform with sign chosen from positive to negative plate. \(Q=\epsilon_0\pi a^2 E_z\), so \(\partial_tD_z=I/(\pi a^2)\) where \(I=\dot Q\). A circle of radius \(r<a\) spanning the gap intercepts displacement current \(I r^2/a^2\). Azimuthal symmetry gives

\[B_\phi(r)=\frac{\mu_0 I r}{2\pi a^2}\quad (r<a),\]
\[B_\phi(r)\simeq\frac{\mu_0 I}{2\pi r}\quad (r>a).\]

The exterior expression assumes the return conductor lies farther away and retains the leading large-plate approximation. Magnetic field is continuous at the idealised rim. Now cut a ring of radius \(r\) into the positive plate. The portion of supplied current needed to charge its central disk is \(Ir^2/a^2\); the rest crosses that ring outwards as conduction current. Thus \(2\pi r K_r=I(1-r^2/a^2)\). Its apparent \(1/r\) singularity at the centre is rounded off by the finite contact patch. Distributed charging is compatible with current entering through one point.

Locate the power flow in the gap

The Poynting vector in the gap is

\[\mathbf S=\mathbf E\times\mathbf H=-E_zH_\phi\hat{\mathbf r}.\]

For increasing field it points radially inward. Integrate the inward flux through the cylindrical side of a smaller pillbox of radius \(r<a\) and thickness \(d\):

\[P_{\rm in}(r)=2\pi r d E_z H_\phi(r)=VI\,\frac{r^2}{a^2}\]
\[\frac{d}{dt}\left(\frac{\epsilon_0}{2}E_z^2\pi r^2d\right).\]

Thus energy crosses the side before being stored throughout that subvolume. At \(r=a\) the result equals the terminal power \(VI\). This derivation uses the leading quasistatic fields. A rapidly changing current also produces induction fields and time-varying magnetic energy; in that regime the full Poynting theorem includes them. During discharging, \(\dot Q\) reverses and the direction of radial power flow reverses.

Predict two independent instrument readings

Sample midway to the rim

Let \(a=20\) mm, \(d=0.50\) mm and \(I=4.0\) mA. At \(r=10\) mm a gap circle encloses 1.0 mA displacement current. Its magnetic field is 20.0 nT. The outward conduction current crossing the same radius in the positive metal is 3.0 mA, corresponding to \(K_r=0.0477\) A/m. The gap reading and the plate reading describe different surfaces; their sum recovers the lead current in this construction.

Record a finite charge ramp

The ideal capacitance here is 22.3 pF. A constant \(I=4.0\) mA for 20.0 ns raises the voltage by 3.60 V from zero. The source supplies \(\int VI\,dt=C V_{\rm final}^2/2=144\) pJ. At the half-radius pillbox only one quarter of this energy appears, 36.0 pJ. A real pulse has finite rise and fall times. The simple uniform-field solution is accurate away from abrupt switching transients when the spectral content is well below \(c/a\).

Measure a displaced current and a radial conduction current separately

At 20 mm plate radius, 4 mA lead current and a 10 mm probe radius, 1 mA crosses the gap disk and 3 mA crosses the metal ring. The graph compares both currents over the entire plate. Reverse the current or enlarge the plate and compare the magnetic reading at the selected fractional radius.

Problem sheet · challenge a misleading measurement

Determine the sign during reversal

The capacitor field still points from the positive to the negative plate, but its magnitude is decreasing. Which of \(B_\phi,S_r,E_z\) changes sign relative to an increasing field with the same instantaneous voltage?

Work through the solution

The voltage and \(E_z\) keep their signs. \(I=C\dot V\) reverses, so the azimuthal magnetic field reverses. Hence radial energy flow reverses and leaves the pillbox. A measurement of voltage alone does not determine the direction of energy transport.

What changes if the centre contact is replaced by a rim feed?

Assume a uniform annular feed deposits charge symmetrically at the outer edge. Predict the signed metal current crossing a circle of radius \(r<a\) if positive is radially outward.

Work through the solution

All charge accumulating inside the test circle must now enter from larger radii. The inward flux is \(Ir^2/a^2\), so \(2\pi rK_r=-Ir^2/a^2\). The gap displacement current for the same uniform charging history is unchanged. The external lead and return geometry determines the remainder of the global magnetic field configuration.

Chapter 44 · A lossy half-space seen through its surface impedance

An absorbing medium transmits a complex field and converts electrical work into heat. Matching one complex number at its surface predicts reflection. Integrating the heating through its depth provides an independent check that is especially revealing near the crossover between dielectric and conductor.

Choose a branch that decays into the material

Let a stationary plane wave enter the homogeneous half-space \(z>0\) at normal incidence. Use \(e^{-i\omega t}\) and fields proportional to \(e^{ikz}\), real \(\epsilon,\mu>0\) and Ohmic \(\mathbf J=\sigma\mathbf E\), \(\sigma\geq0\). Ampère's law combines the two currents into \(-i\omega(\epsilon+i\sigma/\omega)\mathbf E\). Faraday's law yields

\[H_y=kE_x/(\omega\mu).\]

Eliminating \(H\) gives

\[k^2=\omega^2\mu\epsilon(1+i t),\]
\[t=\frac{\sigma}{\omega\epsilon},\]
\[k=\beta+i\alpha .\]

Choose \(\beta>0,\alpha\geq0\) so the interior field weakens with depth. Let \(k_d=\omega\sqrt{\mu\epsilon}\). Equating real and imaginary parts gives \(\beta^2-\alpha^2=k_d^2\), \(2\beta\alpha=k_d^2 t\), and hence

\[\frac{\beta}{k_d}=\sqrt{\frac{\sqrt{1+t^2}+1}{2}},\]
\[\frac{\alpha}{k_d}=\frac{t}{2(\beta/k_d)},\]
\[Z=\frac{E_x}{H_y}=\frac{\omega\mu}{k}.\]

The rational expression for \(\alpha\) avoids subtracting nearly equal numbers for small \(t\). As \(t\to0\),

\[\alpha/k_d\simeq t/2.\]

For \(t\gg1\), \(\beta\simeq\alpha\simeq\sqrt{\omega\mu\sigma/2}\): skin depth \(1/\alpha\) measures field-amplitude decay and the power has the shorter e-folding depth \(1/(2\alpha)\).

Read the complex reflection and the power entering the surface

Let the incident medium be lossless with impedance \(Z_1\). Continuity of tangential \(E,H\) gives

\[1+r=h,\ (1-r)/Z_1=h/Z,\]

where \(h=E(0^+)/E_{\rm inc}\). Solving,

\[r=\frac{Z-Z_1}{Z+Z_1},\]
\[h=\frac{2Z}{Z+Z_1},\]
\[1-|r|^2=Z_1\operatorname{Re}(1/Z^*)|h|^2.\]

The flux relation follows by dividing the real part of \(E H^*/2\) by the incident intensity. It includes a real admittance and is generally different from \(|h|^2\). The imaginary part of the complex Poynting vector measures exchange in quadrature with the drive. In the good-conductor limit \(Z\simeq(1-i)\sqrt{\omega\mu/(2\sigma)}\). Its positive real part is essential for passive heating, even where the reflected voltage is almost the negative of the incident one.

Recover the entire inward power from a volume measurement

Ohmic heating per volume is \(\langle p_J\rangle=\sigma|E(0)|^2 e^{-2\alpha z}/2\). Integrating from zero to infinity gives

\[P_J/A=\sigma|E(0)|^2/(4\alpha).\]

Use \(2\beta\alpha=\mu\omega\sigma\) to rewrite it as \(|E(0)|^2\beta/(2\omega\mu)\). This equals the inward mean surface flux from \(E H^*/2\). No separate efficiency factor is needed. The fraction of surface power dissipated before depth \(D\) is \(1-e^{-2\alpha D}\), so 90% of the heat is deposited by \(D=\ln10/(2\alpha)\), about 1.15 field skin depths.

Compare two frequency regimes

A crossover with comparable currents

Consider material whose lossless impedance equals the incident medium’s and whose loss ratio is \(t=2\). Then \(\beta/k_d=1.272\), \(\alpha/k_d=0.786\), and \(Z/Z_1=0.569-0.352i\). Direct complex division gives a reflected power fraction of about 0.120. The balance enters the half-space and ultimately heats it. One lossless phase length \(k_d^{-1}\) into the material, the remaining forward power is \(e^{-1.572}=0.208\) of its surface value. This illustrates substantial heating even though most incident power enters the material.

An amplitude probe and a calorimeter

Suppose a field-amplitude probe reads 1/e of its surface value at depth 0.80 mm. Then \(\alpha=1250\) m⁻¹, the power half-depth is \(\ln2/(2\alpha)=0.277\) mm and 90% of the absorbed energy is deposited by 0.921 mm. These predictions do not require knowing the incident intensity. Disagreement between the two types of measurement can reveal spatially varying \(\sigma\) or a reflected wave from a finite back surface.

Close a reflection and heating budget at every depth

At loss ratio 2 and matched lossless impedances, about 12% of the incident power is reflected. The remaining power gradually becomes heat. Change loss and impedance independently and check that the surface reflection, transmitted flux at depth and integrated heat always add to one.

Problem sheet · determine a material from two probes

Recover material parameters

At frequency \(f\) in a nonmagnetic half-space, phase measurements give \(\beta\) and amplitude measurements give \(\alpha\). Recover \(\sigma,\epsilon\), and specify the consistency condition for the dielectric model used here.

Work through the solution

Solve for \(\sigma=2\beta\alpha/(\mu_0\omega)\) and \(\epsilon=(\beta^2-\alpha^2)/(\mu_0\omega^2)\). A medium with positive real permittivity in this simple Ohmic model requires \(\beta>\alpha\). In the good-conductor limit their difference is small, making the inferred permittivity sensitive to measurement errors.

When does an infinite depth assumption fail?

For a slab of thickness \(D\), the back-face field reflection magnitude is 0.50. Bound the return amplitude at the entrance relative to the forward wave inside, ignoring subsequent round trips. How thick keeps it below 1%?

Work through the solution

The round trip attenuates the field by \(e^{-2\alpha D}\). Require \(0.50e^{-2\alpha D}<0.01\), giving \(D>\ln50/(2\alpha)=1.96/\alpha\). Phase may suppress the measured amplitude at selected frequencies, but the magnitude bound does not depend on that cancellation.

Chapter 45 · Two polarisations moving through a uniaxial crystal

A crystal can send two pulses in different directions even when their wavefronts have the same normal. The distinction emerges by applying the divergence condition to electric displacement and measuring energy flow with the Poynting vector.

A field transverse to the wavevector need not be the electric field

Let a transparent, nonmagnetic uniaxial medium have \(\boldsymbol\epsilon/\epsilon_0=\operatorname{diag}(n_o^2,n_o^2,n_e^2)\). The optic axis is \(z\); dispersion over the bandwidth under study is negligible. For a harmonic plane wave with wavevector in the \(xz\) plane, write \(\mathbf k=(k_x,0,k_z)\). Source-free Maxwell equations require \(\mathbf k\cdot\mathbf D=0\), \(\mathbf k\cdot\mathbf B=0\),

\[\mathbf k\times\mathbf E=\omega\mathbf B,\]
\[\mathbf k\times\mathbf H=-\omega\mathbf D.\]

Eliminating the magnetic field gives

\[\mathbf k\times(\mathbf k\times\mathbf E)+k_0^2(\boldsymbol\epsilon/\epsilon_0)\mathbf E=0,\]
\[k_0=\omega/c.\]

An electric field along \(y\) satisfies this system with \(k^2=k_0^2n_o^2\). This ordinary mode has transverse \(\mathbf E,\mathbf D\) and energy travels parallel to \(\mathbf k\). A second mode has \(\mathbf E\) in the \(xz\) plane; \(\mathbf D\) is transverse but generally not parallel to \(\mathbf E\).

Find the phase index and the direction of energy separately

The remaining two Cartesian equations form a matrix with diagonal \(k_0^2 n_o^2-k_z^2,\ k_0^2 n_e^2-k_x^2\) and off-diagonal elements \(k_xk_z\). Its determinant vanishes for nontrivial fields. Expanding cancels the fourth-order cross term and gives

\[\frac{k_x^2}{n_e^2}+\frac{k_z^2}{n_o^2}=k_0^2,\]
\[\frac1{n_{\rm ph}(\theta)^2}=\frac{\sin^2\theta}{n_e^2}+\frac{\cos^2\theta}{n_o^2},\]

where \(\theta\) is the angle from the optic axis to the wavevector. Along the axis both modes have the same index; perpendicular to it the extraordinary phase index is \(n_e\). For the latter mode choose transverse \(\mathbf D\propto(\cos\theta,0,-\sin\theta)\). Applying the inverse permittivity tensor gives

\[\mathbf E\propto(\cos\theta/n_o^2,0,-\sin\theta/n_e^2).\]

The magnetic field is along \(y\), so the energy flow angle \(\psi\) from \(z\) satisfies

\[\tan\psi=-\frac{E_z}{E_x}=\frac{n_o^2}{n_e^2}\tan\theta.\]

The group velocity obtained by differentiating \(\omega(\mathbf k)=c\sqrt{k_x^2/n_e^2+k_z^2/n_o^2}\) has the same direction in this nondispersive model. This independent construction is normal to the constant-frequency ellipse. At an interface it is the tangential component of \(\mathbf k\), fixed by phase matching, that selects the transmitted wavevector. The energy path can then diverge from the corresponding wave normal.

A crystal plate as a beam displacer and as a retarder

A normally incident beam with an oblique optic axis

Let \(n_o=1.50,\ n_e=1.60\) and let the plate normal make \(45^\circ\) to the optic axis. At normal incidence the phase normal is the plate normal for both modes. For the extraordinary wave \(\psi=\arctan(2.25/2.56)=41.3^\circ\). Relative to its wave normal the energy travels about \(-3.7^\circ\) toward the optic axis. Across a 10.0 mm thick plate the lateral displacement relative to the ordinary beam is approximately 0.65 mm. This describes propagation inside a parallel plate and neglects edge clipping.

A plate that turns linear input into circular output

Propagate perpendicular to the optic axis so both eigenmodes travel in the same direction. Their accumulated phase difference is \(\Delta=k_0(n_e-n_o)d\). Linear incident polarisation at \(45^\circ\) to the eigenaxes has equal amplitudes. When \(|\Delta|=\pi/2\) modulo \(2\pi\), those orthogonal components have a quarter-period phase difference and form circular polarisation, assuming equal transmitted amplitudes. At 600 nm with \(n_e-n_o=0.10\), the smallest such thickness is \(1.50\) μm. A larger multi-order plate can give the same retardance at this wavelength but responds more strongly to bandwidth and thickness errors.

Recover retardance from a pair of polarisers

Place the crystal axes at \(45^\circ\) to the input polariser and use a second polariser crossed with the first. Express the output field in the two crystal axes, then project onto the crossed analyser; its amplitude is proportional to \((e^{i\Delta}-1)/2\). Thus the transmitted fraction is \(\sin^2(\Delta/2)\). An arbitrary phase offset common to both modes disappears. A single intensity reading determines neither the sign of \(\Delta\) nor its full order. Varying thickness or scanning wavelength can resolve the branch; the material dispersion then enters the interpretation.

Predict the transverse displacement of a crystal plate

Choose principal indices 1.50 and 1.60 and a 45° wave normal. The extraordinary beam is displaced by about −0.65 mm through a 10 mm plate; the ordinary beam follows the normal. Swap the principal indices and compare the sign and magnitude of walk-off.

Infer birefringence from a walk-off angle

At \(\theta=45^\circ\), an extraordinary energy ray makes \(\psi=40^\circ\) to the optic axis. Assuming the same model, recover \(n_e/n_o\). Is the medium positive or negative uniaxial?

Work through the solution

The ratio is

\[\sqrt{\tan45^\circ/\tan40^\circ}=1.092.\]

The extraordinary principal index exceeds the ordinary one, a positive uniaxial material. A measurement referenced to the plate normal must first be converted to the angle from the optic axis used in the equation.

Calculate the contrast loss caused by angular misalignment

An ideal half-wave plate has its eigenaxis at angle \(\alpha\) to the input polariser. Keep the analyser crossed and find the intensity transmitted when the angle is \(40^\circ\) instead of \(45^\circ\).

Work through the solution

Projection into the crystal axes and back out gives

\[I/I_0=\sin^2(2\alpha)\sin^2(\Delta/2).\]

At half-wave retardance the factor from phase is unity, and the misaligned transmission is

\[\sin^2 80^\circ=0.970.\]

The reduction alone cannot distinguish angular error from a small error in retardance.

Chapter 46 · Radiation when the electric dipole cancels

Two optical dipoles can cancel in the long-wavelength electric-dipole approximation and still radiate. Expanding their source phase shows which moments survive, where the remaining light goes, and how a small asymmetry restores a different angular pattern.

Keep the source phase inside the radiation integral

For a localised harmonic current \(\mathbf J(\mathbf x')e^{-i\omega t}\), take a detector far compared with source size and wavelength. In the outgoing potential set \(1/R\simeq1/r\), while retaining \(kR\simeq kr-k\mathbf n\cdot\mathbf x'\), where \(\mathbf n=\mathbf r/r\). This approximation requires the quadratic path phase across the source to be negligible. The radiative electric field is proportional to the transverse part of the current integral

\[\mathbf C(\mathbf n)=\int\mathbf J(\mathbf x')e^{-ik\mathbf n\cdot\mathbf x'}\,d^3x',\]
\[\mathbf E_{\rm rad}=\frac{i\mu_0\omega e^{ikr}}{4\pi r}[\mathbf C-\mathbf n(\mathbf n\cdot\mathbf C)] .\]

For small source size \(a\) with \(ka\ll1\), expand the exponential. Continuity and integration by parts give \(\int J_i\,d^3x=\dot p_i\) for electric dipole \(\mathbf p=\int\rho\mathbf x\,d^3x\). The first correction is \(-ik n_j\int J_i x_j\,d^3x\). Split this integral into its symmetric and antisymmetric parts. Define \(Q_{ij}=\int\rho x_i x_j\,d^3x\) and \(\mathbf m=\frac12\int\mathbf x\times\mathbf J\,d^3x\). Differentiating \(Q_{ij}\) and using charge conservation yields

\[\int J_i x_j\,d^3x=\tfrac12\dot Q_{ij}-\epsilon_{ijk}m_k,\]
\[\mathbf C=\dot{\mathbf p}-\frac{ik}2\dot Q\,\mathbf n+ik\,\mathbf n\times\mathbf m+\cdots .\]

The trace of \(Q\) contributes a vector along \(\mathbf n\); the far-field transverse projection removes it. Thus only its traceless electric quadrupole part can radiate. The antisymmetric contribution is the magnetic dipole. Both occur at the next order in this source-phase expansion. Their importance depends on source symmetry and on the actual sizes of their transition moments.

Construct an electric quadrupole with two displaced dipoles

Put narrow identical \(z\)-directed electric dipoles at \(z=\pm d/2\) and drive them with moments \(+p\) and \(-p\), perfectly out of phase. Their total electric dipole is zero. The currents are collinear with their displacement, so this geometry also gives no net magnetic dipole. In direction \(\theta\) to the axis the single-dipole field has factor \(\sin\theta\). The additional two-source factor is \(e^{-ikd\cos\theta/2}-e^{ikd\cos\theta/2}\). In units of the equatorial intensity of one dipole the complete pattern is

\[F(\theta)=4\sin^2\theta\,\sin^2\!\left(\tfrac12kd\cos\theta\right)\simeq(kd)^2\sin^2\theta\cos^2\theta .\]

This has nodes on the axis from transversality and in the equatorial plane from source cancellation. The leading lobes peak at \(45^\circ\) and \(135^\circ\). Integrating over solid angle, \(\int_{-1}^{1}(1-u^2)u^2\,du=4/15\); the single-dipole integral is \(4/3\). The pair-to-single total-power ratio is \((kd)^2/5\) at leading order. A fixed single-dipole amplitude is the reference; normalising each curve to its own maximum would hide this suppression.

Relate the symmetry argument to optical transitions

In the long-wavelength quantum interaction the electric-dipole term contains a matrix element of position, odd under spatial inversion. Between two states of the same definite parity, the integrand for an electric dipole moment changes sign on inversion and integrates to zero. The electric quadrupole contains two position factors and has even parity. The magnetic dipole is an axial vector and also has even parity. Either next-order channel can therefore satisfy parity between such states, subject to angular-momentum and other selection rules. Classical source symmetries illuminate the long-wavelength expansion; actual atomic emission rates require the relevant quantum matrix elements and state populations.

Estimate the strength and detect imperfect cancellation

An optical-scale separation

For \(d=20\) nm and \(\lambda=600\) nm, \(kd=0.2094\). The leading integrated pair-to-single power ratio is \(0.00877\), under 1%. In the \(45^\circ\) direction the dimensionless intensity is \(4(1/2)\sin^2[kd/(2\sqrt2)]\simeq0.01095\). Tripling \(d\) at fixed wavelength should initially give roughly nine times the power; check the exact sine before applying that extrapolation.

An equatorial leak

Reduce the opposing dipole magnitude to \((1-\delta)p\). Expanding the squared two-source factor gives \(\delta^2+4(1-\delta)\sin^2(kd\cos\theta/2)\). At the equator the second term is zero, leaving intensity fraction \(\delta^2\) relative to one dipole. A measured fraction 0.0025 corresponds to a 5% amplitude imbalance if this is the only imperfection. A phase mismatch can also fill the node, so the observation cannot distinguish both mechanisms without additional phase information.

Break the symmetry of an optical dipole pair

Compare a coherent two-source calculation against its first long-wavelength approximation. At d/λ = 0.035, equal and opposite dipoles emit about 1% of the power of a single dipole. Introduce a 5% amplitude mismatch and check the equatorial node. Then increase spacing to test the limit of the expansion.

Separate the amplitude and power scaling

For the symmetric pair suppose the separation is halved with the two moments and frequency unchanged. Predict the leading power change at \(45^\circ\) and at \(90^\circ\). Where is a ratio meaningful?

Work through the solution

At \(45^\circ\) the leading field is proportional to \(kd\), so the intensity drops by a factor of four. At \(90^\circ\) the exact two-source phase difference is zero for every spacing. Both intensities vanish there and their ratio is undefined. A finite measurement at that angle probes symmetry breaking or background light.

Compare with a closed current loop

A small circular loop carries uniform oscillating current \(I\) and has area \(A\). Identify its leading moment and the directions in which its radiation vanishes.

Work through the solution

The net electric dipole of this ideal divergence-free closed current is zero. Its magnetic dipole is \(IA\hat{\mathbf n}_{\rm loop}\). The radiation term contains \(\mathbf n\times\mathbf m\), hence vanishes along the loop axis and peaks transverse to it. At leading order the loop can radiate strongly in its equatorial plane, unlike the collinear electric-quadrupole pair.

Chapter 47 · Four contacts on a conductor of finite thickness

A voltmeter scarcely draws any current, yet its reading depends on how the current from a separate pair of leads spreads inside the specimen. Derive the conversion from a four-terminal reading to resistivity. Decide from the geometry whether the result describes a bulk material or a conducting sheet.

What the two unused current terminals buy us

Place four point contacts on a straight line on the top of a uniform conducting sample. Drive current \(+I\) into the first contact and remove it at the fourth. Attach an ideal high-impedance voltmeter to the second and third contacts. Equal probe spacing is called \(s\); the sample thickness is \(h\). Record \(V=\phi_2-\phi_3\) with the sign convention that positive conventional current flows toward lower electric potential. We seek the resistance of the actual measurement \(V/I\), rather than the terminal resistance between the current contacts.

The voltage lost across a current contact can be large because all the drive current passes through it. That loss does not enter the ideal difference between the inner probe potentials. Likewise a contact resistance in series with an ideal voltmeter has zero \(IR\) drop. The separation does not eliminate all geometric uncertainties. A voltage contact with appreciable area can average the field or perturb it, a voltmeter with finite input impedance draws a small current, and an edge in the conducting specimen redirects current. Derive first what an ideal experiment would do before introducing corrections for a manufactured sample.

In the ohmic, low-frequency limit \(\mathbf J=-\sigma\nabla\phi\) with constant scalar conductivity \(\sigma=1/\rho\). Conservation in the conducting interior means \(\nabla\cdot\mathbf J=0\). A point current lead on an otherwise insulating surface is a boundary flux. Unlike a prescribed voltage, it fixes the strength of a source without fixing its absolute potential. Only currents and differences should survive an arbitrary additive constant. This will be a useful test when we introduce infinitely many reflected current sources.

A spreading experiment in three dimensions

First make the sample so thick that the lower face is inaccessible to the current on the scale of the probes. Around a point input on the surface of a conducting half-space consider a hemisphere of radius \(r\). All its outward current is \(I\); rotational symmetry plus reflection across the ideal upper plane produces a radial field of magnitude \(J=I/(2\pi r^2)\). Integrate \(E_r=\rho J=-d\phi/dr\) inward from infinity. The surface potential relative to infinity is \(\rho I/(2\pi r)\). Subtract a second copy centred on the sink.

At probe 2 the distances from source and sink are \(s\) and \(2s\), respectively. Its potential is \(+\rho I/(4\pi s)\); symmetry gives the opposite sign at probe 3. Therefore

\[R_{\rm bulk}=\frac{V}{I}=\frac{\rho}{2\pi s}.\]

A bulk resistivity in ohm metres can be extracted by multiplying the transfer resistance by \(2\pi s\) in metres. The inverse spacing is not a contact effect. It is the result of spreading current over an area that grows quadratically with radius. In particular, doubling \(s\) halves the measured resistance of a sufficiently thick sample. This scaling is a check independent of the calibration of a fixed current source as long as it remains stable across both measurements.

Confine the same current to a thin sheet

If current rapidly becomes uniform through a thin specimen, the spreading area is instead the circumference of a circle times \(h\). Thus \(J_r=I/(2\pi r h)\). The integral of \(1/r\) is logarithmic and contains an arbitrary reference length. A single source in an infinite sheet cannot be assigned zero potential at infinity by a finite constant. The source–sink pair poses no difficulty because the reference cancels from the potential difference. With \(R_s=\rho/h\) and source and sink distances \(r_+\) and \(r_-\), the sheet potential can be written as

\[\phi=\frac{I R_s}{2\pi}\ln\frac{r_-}{r_+},\]
\[R_{\rm thin}=\frac{R_s\ln 2}{\pi}.\]

At the two inner contacts the ratios are two and one half. The logarithms are equal and opposite, which supplies the extra factor of two. Doubling the probe spacing now leaves the measured transfer resistance unchanged. The name ohms per square refers to \(R_s\), the resistance across opposite complete edges of a square with uniform flow; a four-point probe is a different arrangement and its resistance is smaller by \(\ln 2/\pi\). Attaching the word square to a current probe reading without this conversion would produce a systematic error.

Reflect the current from an insulating lower face

A real film has an upper surface and a back surface. Assume both prevent normal current except at the upper contacts. Reflecting a source with the same sign across an insulating plane cancels the normal derivative there. Continuing the reflection between both parallel faces generates current images displaced vertically by \(2nh\). A grounded conducting backing would impose a different boundary condition and cannot be represented by these signs. On the top surface the half-space spreading result therefore acquires a sequence of image distances. Define \(z=s/h\). After subtracting the source and sink contributions at the inner probes one obtains

\[\frac{h}{\rho}\frac{V}{I}=\frac{1}{\pi}\left[\frac{1}{2z}+2\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\left(\frac{1}{\sqrt{z^2+4n^2}}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{4z^2+4n^2}}\right)\right].\]

Every term in the remaining sum is positive: a nearby reflecting back increases the measured resistance relative to the infinite bulk expression. Individual absolute image potentials have slowly diverging harmonic tails; the paired differences converge. To see why, use \(1/a-1/b=(b^2-a^2)/[ab(a+b)]\). With the two square roots above the numerator is exactly \(3z^2\), independent of \(n\), while the denominator grows as \(n^3\). This form suppresses subtractive cancellation and makes an image-cutoff refinement test meaningful.

The thin-film limit can also be read from the sum without the original sheet argument. For large \(z\) the image spacing is small compared with the distances. Replace the sum over positive and negative images by an integral along the vertical coordinate with density \(1/(2h)\). Integrating the difference of two inverse square roots gives the difference of two inverse hyperbolic sines. At a large upper limit only the ratio of the lateral distances survives. Their ratio is two, returning \(\ln 2\). This second derivation identifies thickness averaging as a long-distance limit of a three-dimensional field, rather than a separate electrical transport law.
